q.q: A student makes a new short video using clips of the 1928 Steamboat Willie and posts it for a school project. Based on the essay, is this acceptable?
opts: No, because Mickey can never be used by anyone
Only if the student also uses the later colour versions
Yes, as long as it doesn't suggest Disney made it
Only if Disney gives written permission for the clips
q.why: 第四、五段：1928 版已屬公共領域，但不能暗示是迪士尼出品。

tz: 1928 年 11 月 18 日，一部七分鐘的卡通在紐約首映，悄悄地重新劃定了大眾娛樂的邊界。嚴格說來，《汽船威利號》並不是米老鼠的第一部影片，但它是第一部上映的；它精準同步的配樂，把一隻愉快吹口哨的老鼠變成了一個現象。
它的天才之處既在技術，也在藝術。親自為角色配音的華特・迪士尼，和他的動畫師烏布・艾沃克斯，讓每一個動作都配合音樂和音效的節奏，讓觀眾相信那些圖畫真的在發出聲音。
從那場不起眼的首映，誕生了史上最有價值的品牌之一，也隨之展開一場漫長的政治角力：創作作品應該維持私有財產多久？美國的著作權期限在二十世紀被延長了不只一次，批評者把這些延長戲稱為「米老鼠保護法」。
然而，時間終究贏了。2024 年 1 月 1 日，原版《汽船威利號》進入美國的公共領域，藝術家和老師都可以自由地重新使用和改編。
限制仍然很重要。後來的版本仍受保護，商標法也仍然禁止任何人暗示某項產品是迪士尼製造的。這件事說明了著作權核心的那份交換：創作者應該得到回報，但文化也需要一個大家都能在上面繼續創作的共同寶庫。

ph.ex: It's not technically a holiday, but many people take the day off.
ph.exzh: 嚴格說來它不是假日，但很多人會請假。

ph.ex: Her success was due to hard work as much as talent.
ph.exzh: 她的成功靠努力，也靠天分。

ph.ex: The company grew from a small shop.
ph.exzh: 這家公司是從一間小店發展起來的。

ph.ex: I have read this book more than once.
ph.exzh: 這本書我讀過不只一次。

ph.ex: Good ideas build upon older ones.
ph.exzh: 好點子是建立在舊點子之上的。

ph.ex: Trust is at the heart of every friendship.
ph.exzh: 信任是每段友誼的核心。

st.m: On November 18, 1928, a seven-minute cartoon premiered in New York and quietly redrew the boundaries of popular entertainment.
st.mz: 《汽船威利》改變了娛樂；它進入公共領域，說明版權要在獎勵創作者與分享文化之間取得平衡。
t: Its genius was technical as much as artistic.
From that modest premiere grew one of the most valuable brands in history, and with it a long political struggle over how long creative works should remain private property.
Yet time eventually won.
st.c: The episode illustrates the bargain at copyright's heart: creators deserve rewards, but culture also needs a common store of works that everyone can build upon.

discuss: Why do you think a whistling mouse became so popular in 1928?
Should famous characters belong to their creators forever, or become free for everyone after some time? Why?
If you could reuse an old story or character for a new project, which one would you choose?

topic: World Toilet Day
zh: 世界廁所日：一間廁所的大學問

a.title: Why Toilets Matter
text: November 19 is World Toilet Day. It sounds funny, but it is a serious day.
Many of us use a clean toilet every day. But billions of people in the world do not have a safe toilet at home.
Without toilets, dirty water can get into rivers and drinking water. This can make people very sick, especially children.
Some girls stay home from school because their school has no clean, private toilet.
A man from Singapore named Jack Sim started this day in 2001. In 2013, it became an official UN day.
Clean toilets protect our health, keep water clean, and help children go to school.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A funny day full of jokes about toilets
How Jack Sim became famous in Singapore
Why toilets are a funny subject for a holiday
Why safe toilets matter for health and school
q.why: 全文說明安全廁所對健康與上學的重要。

q.q: According to the reading, which is TRUE?
opts: World Toilet Day became an official UN day in 2001.
Jack Sim, who started the day, comes from Taiwan.
Some girls miss school because there is no private toilet.
Dirty water from toilets only makes adults sick, not children.
q.why: 第 4 段：Some girls stay home from school because their school has no clean, private toilet。2001 年是開始的年份、2013 年才成為聯合國紀念日；Jack Sim 來自新加坡；第 3 段說孩子特別容易生病。

q.q: In paragraph 3, what does "This" in "This can make people very sick" refer to?
opts: having a clean toilet every day
dirty water in drinking water
a man from Singapore
the river near your school
q.why: This 指的是前一句整件事：髒水流進河川和飲用水。This 常常指「前面一整句話說的事」。

q.q: In the text, “private” means ___.
opts: where other people cannot see you
very large, with lots of room for everyone
very clean and smelling fresh
full of clean, fresh water
q.why: private = 有隱私的。

q.q: Why do some girls stay home from school?
opts: They are tired of doing so much homework
They have to help clean the village river
Their school has no clean, private toilet
The school is too far away to walk to
q.why: 第四段：their school has no clean, private toilet。

q.q: Your school wants to help more girls in a poor village go to school. Based on the text, what is a good plan?
opts: Give each of the girls a new school bag only
Ask the girls to drink more water from the river
Start a fun day of toilet jokes at the school
Build clean, private toilets at the school
q.why: 第四段：沒有乾淨、有隱私的廁所會讓女孩不去上學。

gt.en: It sounds funny, but it is a serious day.
gt.zh: 聽起來很好笑，但這是一個嚴肅的日子。

gt.en: This can make people very sick, especially children.
gt.zh: 這會讓人生重病，特別是兒童。

gt.en: In 2013, it became an official UN day.
gt.zh: 2013 年，它成為聯合國正式的紀念日。

gt.en: Clean toilets protect our health, keep water clean, and help children go to school.
gt.zh: 乾淨的廁所保護我們的健康、維持水源乾淨，也幫助孩子上學。

tz: 11 月 19 日是世界廁所日。聽起來很好笑，但這是一個嚴肅的日子。
我們很多人每天都使用乾淨的廁所。但世界上有好幾十億人，家裡沒有安全的廁所。
沒有廁所，髒水就會流進河川和飲用水裡。這可能讓人病得很重，尤其是孩子。
有些女孩待在家裡不去上學，因為她們的學校沒有乾淨、隱密的廁所。
一位來自新加坡、名叫沈錫賢（Jack Sim）的人在 2001 年發起了這個日子。2013 年，它成為聯合國正式的紀念日。
乾淨的廁所保護我們的健康、讓水保持乾淨，也幫助孩子去上學。

ph.ex: It sounds funny, but it's true!
ph.exzh: 聽起來很好笑，但這是真的！

ph.ex: Don't let water get into your phone.
ph.exzh: 別讓水跑進你的手機。

ph.ex: I stayed home because I had a fever.
ph.exzh: 我發燒所以待在家裡。

ph.ex: Every child should be able to go to school.
ph.exzh: 每個孩子都應該能上學。

st.m: Clean toilets protect our health, keep water clean, and help children go to school.
st.mz: 乾淨的廁所能保護健康、保持水源乾淨，也幫助孩子上學。
t: But billions of people in the world do not have a safe toilet at home.
Without toilets, dirty water can get into rivers and drinking water.
Some girls stay home from school because their school has no clean, private toilet.
A man from Singapore named Jack Sim started this day in 2001.
st.c: Clean toilets protect our health, keep water clean, and help children go to school.

b.title: The Invention That Saves Millions of Lives
text: World Toilet Day, held every November 19, began in 2001 when the Singaporean campaigner Jack Sim founded the World Toilet Organization. In 2013 the United Nations made it an official observance.

The topic makes some people giggle, but the numbers are sobering. According to UN figures, around 3.5 billion people still lack safely managed sanitation, and hundreds of millions have no toilet at all.

When human waste is not safely contained, it contaminates rivers, fields and drinking water. That spreads diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea, which remain major causes of death for young children in poorer countries.
Toilets also affect education and safety. Girls are more likely to miss school if there are no private, hygienic facilities, and women who must go outside at night can face danger.
Experts stress that building toilets is only the first step. Waste must also be collected and treated, or the problem simply moves downstream.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Safe sanitation, still missing for billions, is vital for health and school.
Jack Sim founded the World Toilet Organization in Singapore in 2001.
Toilets are an awkward subject that people would rather not discuss.
Safe sanitation now reaches almost everyone, so the day mainly celebrates success.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：數十億人缺乏安全衛生設施，而它攸關健康、教育與安全。

q.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
opts: About 3.5 billion people have no toilet at all.
The UN started World Toilet Day in 2001.
Cholera mainly affects older people in rich countries.
Building toilets alone does not fully solve the problem.
q.why: 第 5 段：building toilets is only the first step。35 億是缺乏「安全管理的衛生設施」，完全沒有廁所的是數億人；2001 年是沈錫賢發起、聯合國 2013 年才正式認定；霍亂主要奪走貧窮國家幼兒的生命。

q.q: What is the writer's attitude toward the topic of toilets?
opts: Amused, because the topic is mainly a joke
Serious, even though some people find it funny
Uninterested, since toilets are a solved problem
Angry at Jack Sim for starting the day
q.why: 第 2 段：The topic makes some people giggle, but the numbers are sobering——作者認真看待這個話題。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “sobering” means ___.
opts: funny, silly and light
funny, silly and easy to forget
serious and making you think
very small and minor
q.why: sobering = 令人警醒的。

q.q: What does “the problem simply moves downstream” mean?
opts: Toilets should always be built close to rivers
Rivers flow much faster once toilets are built
The problem simply disappears once toilets exist
Untreated waste still pollutes places further along
q.why: 最後一段：廢物沒處理，汙染只是移到下游。

q.q: A charity says: “We built 1,000 toilets, so the village's water is now safe.” Based on the text, what should you ask first?
opts: Is the waste collected and treated?
What colour are all the new toilets?
How many of the girls like the toilets?
When did Jack Sim start his organisation?
q.why: 最後一段：building toilets is only the first step. Waste must also be collected and treated。

tr.en: The topic makes some people giggle, but the numbers are sobering.
tr.zh: 這個主題讓一些人忍不住偷笑，但數字卻令人警醒。

tr.en: Toilets also affect education and safety.
tr.zh: 廁所也影響教育和安全。

tr.en: Experts stress that building toilets is only the first step.
tr.zh: 專家強調，蓋廁所只是第一步。

tz: 每年 11 月 19 日的世界廁所日，始於 2001 年，那一年新加坡的倡議人士沈錫賢創立了世界廁所組織。2013 年，聯合國把它定為正式的紀念日。
這個話題會讓有些人偷笑，但數字卻令人警醒。根據聯合國的資料，大約有 35 億人仍然缺乏安全管理的衛生設施，還有數億人根本沒有廁所。
當人類的排泄物沒有被安全地處理，就會污染河川、田地和飲用水。這會散播霍亂和腹瀉等疾病，而這些疾病仍是貧窮國家幼兒死亡的主要原因。
廁所也影響教育和安全。如果沒有隱密、衛生的設施，女孩比較可能缺課；而晚上必須到戶外上廁所的女性，可能會遇到危險。
專家強調，蓋廁所只是第一步。排泄物還必須被收集和處理，否則問題只是被移到下游而已。

ph.ex: I didn't understand the question at all.
ph.exzh: 我完全看不懂這個題目。

ph.ex: You are more likely to win if you practise.
ph.exzh: 多練習的話，你比較可能會贏。

ph.ex: He missed school for a week because of the flu.
ph.exzh: 他因為流感缺課了一週。

ph.ex: Saying sorry is the first step.
ph.exzh: 說對不起是第一步。

ph.ex: Hurry up, or we'll miss the bus.
ph.exzh: 快一點，否則我們會錯過公車。

st.mz: 世界廁所日提醒我們，數十億人仍缺乏安全的衛生設施，這關係到健康、教育與安全。
t: The topic makes some people giggle, but the numbers are sobering.
When human waste is not safely contained, it contaminates rivers, fields and drinking water.
Toilets also affect education and safety.
st.c: Experts stress that building toilets is only the first step.

c.title: The Unglamorous Revolution
text: Few inventions are less celebrated or more consequential than the humble toilet. World Toilet Day, observed each November 19 and adopted by the United Nations in 2013, exists precisely because the subject is so easy to laugh off.

The scale of the shortfall is striking. Roughly 3.5 billion people lack safely managed sanitation, and hundreds of millions still have no facility at all. Where waste is not contained and treated, it seeps into water supplies and fuels diseases that kill hundreds of thousands of young children every year.

Historians of public health often argue that sanitation saved more lives than almost any medical breakthrough. The sewers built in nineteenth-century cities, prompted by deadly cholera outbreaks, transformed life expectancy long before modern drugs existed.
The consequences extend beyond disease. Without private, safe facilities, girls drop out of school and women face harassment; dignity itself is at stake.

Yet the solution is not merely to install more toilets. Without systems to collect and treat waste, sanitation simply relocates the problem. The real revolution is unglamorous infrastructure, quietly maintained.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Sanitation is an overlooked problem that installing more toilets will completely solve.
Nineteenth-century sewers were the original cause of cholera in cities.
Sanitation is an overlooked foundation that needs whole systems, not just toilets.
Installing more toilets is the complete solution to the sanitation crisis.
q.why: 主旨：衛生設施影響重大卻被忽視，而且需要完整系統。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “consequential” means ___.
opts: very small and minor
having important results
easy to laugh at
very expensive to build
q.why: consequential = 影響重大的。

q.q: Why does the writer mention nineteenth-century sewers?
opts: Old sewers spread cholera, so modern cities should remove them
It explains exactly how cholera first began
It shows that toilets are a modern invention
Sanitation improved health even before modern drugs
q.why: 第三段：下水道在現代藥物出現前就大幅提升平均壽命。

q.q: Why does the writer call the revolution “unglamorous”?
opts: Its success depends on dull, unnoticed systems
Toilets are ugly and largely useless objects
Toilets are always dirty and unpleasant places
The United Nations does not support it at all
q.why: 最後一段：unglamorous infrastructure, quietly maintained。

q.q: How does the essay move from paragraph 2 to paragraph 3?
opts: From present-day numbers to history
From history to predictions about the future
From disease to the world of sport
From examples in Asia to examples in Africa
q.why: 第二段講現況數字，第三段用歷史證據支持。

q.q: A city has money for ONE project. Which choice best matches the essay's view?
opts: A famous new hospital full of the latest machines
Sewage collection and treatment for poor areas
A large statue celebrating the first flush toilet
Free toilet paper for every family for one year
q.why: 第三、五段：衛生系統（收集與處理）比單一醫療突破救更多人。

tz: 很少有發明像不起眼的廁所這樣，既不受讚揚、影響卻又如此深遠。每年 11 月 19 日、並在 2013 年獲聯合國採納的世界廁所日，正是因為這個話題太容易被一笑置之而存在。
缺口的規模令人震驚。大約有 35 億人缺乏安全管理的衛生設施，還有數億人至今完全沒有任何設施。在排泄物沒有被收集和處理的地方，它會滲進水源，助長每年奪走數十萬名幼兒生命的疾病。
公共衛生史學家常說，衛生設施拯救的生命，幾乎比任何醫學突破都多。十九世紀的城市在致命霍亂爆發的推動下興建下水道，早在現代藥物出現之前，就已大幅改變了人們的平均壽命。
影響不只在疾病。沒有隱密、安全的設施，女孩會輟學，女性會遭受騷擾；連人的尊嚴本身都受到威脅。
然而，解決方法並不只是多裝一些廁所。沒有收集和處理排泄物的系統，衛生設施只是把問題搬到別處。真正的革命，是那些不起眼、默默維護著的基礎建設。

ph.ex: She laughed off the mistake and kept going.
ph.exzh: 她把錯誤一笑置之，繼續前進。

ph.ex: Rain seeped into the old house.
ph.exzh: 雨水滲進了這間老房子。

ph.ex: People used boats long before cars were invented.
ph.exzh: 早在汽車發明之前很久，人們就用船了。

ph.ex: He dropped out of the club after a month.
ph.exzh: 他一個月後就退出了社團。

ph.ex: The team's place in the final is at stake.
ph.exzh: 球隊能否進決賽就看這一場了。

ph.ex: Reading is not merely a school subject.
ph.exzh: 閱讀不只是一個學科。

st.m: Few inventions are less celebrated or more consequential than the humble toilet.
st.mz: 廁所是最不受重視、影響卻最大的發明；真正的革命是默默維護的衛生基礎建設。
t: The scale of the shortfall is striking.
Historians of public health often argue that sanitation saved more lives than almost any medical breakthrough.
The consequences extend beyond disease.
st.c: The real revolution is unglamorous infrastructure, quietly maintained.

discuss: Why do you think people find it embarrassing to talk about toilets?
How do clean toilets at school affect students' learning?
What could your school or community do to keep water clean?

topic: World Children's Day: Rights for Every Child
zh: 世界兒童日：每個孩子的權利

a.title: Every Child Has Rights
text: November 20 is World Children's Day. On this day in 1989, the United Nations agreed on a special promise for children.
It is called the Convention on the Rights of the Child. A right is something every person should have.
Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
Children also have the right to give their opinions. Adults should listen when decisions are about them.
Almost every country in the world has signed this promise. Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014.
But many children still cannot go to school or are not safe. World Children's Day reminds us to keep this promise.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How children should play games at school
World Children's Day and every child's rights
World Children's Day and the rights only adults have
How to see a doctor when you are ill
q.why: 全文介紹世界兒童日與兒童權利。

q.q: According to the reading, which is TRUE?
opts: The UN agreed on the promise for children in 2014.
Children have the right to vote in elections.
Today, every child in the world can go to school.
Taiwan made the promise part of its own laws in 2014.
q.why: 第 5 段：Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014。聯合國是 1989 年通過的；文章沒提投票權；第 6 段說很多孩子仍無法上學。

q.q: In paragraph 2, what does "It" in "It is called the Convention on the Rights of the Child" refer to?
opts: the special promise for children
the United Nations in New York
World Children's Day every year
a child's right to play
q.why: It 指第 1 段最後說的 a special promise for children——這份承諾就叫《兒童權利公約》。

q.q: In the text, a “right” is ___.
opts: the opposite of the word left
a kind of game that children play
something every person should have
a rule that every school must follow
q.why: 第二段：A right is something every person should have。

q.q: Why does the day still matter today?
opts: Every child in the world can now go to school and is always safe
Many children still can't go to school or are not safe
The promise made in 1989 has now come to an end
Only adults, and not children, have any rights
q.why: 最後一段：many children still cannot go to school or are not safe。

q.q: Your school is choosing a new lunch menu. Based on the text, what should the school do?
opts: Decide quickly without asking any of the students
Let only the parents choose what children eat
Ask students, because the decision is about them
Choose the cheapest food without asking anyone
q.why: 第四段：Adults should listen when decisions are about them。

gt.en: A right is something every person should have.
gt.zh: 權利是每個人都應該擁有的東西。

gt.en: Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
gt.zh: 兒童有權上學、有權安全、有權看醫生，也有權玩耍。

gt.en: Adults should listen when decisions are about them.
gt.zh: 當決定和兒童有關時，大人應該聆聽。

gt.en: Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014.
gt.zh: 台灣也在 2014 年把它納入自己的法律。

tz: 11 月 20 日是世界兒童日。1989 年的這一天，聯合國通過了一項給孩子的特別承諾。
它叫做《兒童權利公約》。「權利」是每個人都應該擁有的東西。
孩子有權利上學、有權利安全、有權利看醫生，也有權利玩耍。
孩子也有權利表達自己的意見。當決定和孩子有關時，大人應該仔細聽。
世界上幾乎每個國家都簽署了這項承諾。台灣也在 2014 年把它納入自己的法律。
但是仍有許多孩子無法上學，或生活得不安全。世界兒童日提醒我們要遵守這個承諾。

ph.ex: We finally agreed on a name for our team.
ph.exzh: 我們終於決定了隊名。

ph.ex: Everyone can give their opinion in class.
ph.exzh: 每個人在課堂上都可以發表意見。

ph.ex: This book is about friendship.
ph.exzh: 這本書是關於友誼的。

ph.ex: Always keep your promises.
ph.exzh: 一定要遵守你的承諾。

st.m: On this day in 1989, the United Nations agreed on a special promise for children.
st.mz: 世界兒童日紀念《兒童權利公約》，提醒我們要守住保障每個孩子權利的承諾。
t: It is called the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
Children also have the right to give their opinions.
Almost every country in the world has signed this promise.
st.c: World Children's Day reminds us to keep this promise.

b.title: A Promise to the World's Children
text: On November 20, 1989, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, and the date is now celebrated as World Children's Day.

The convention sets out the rights that every person under 18 should enjoy, wherever they live. They include the right to education, to health care, to protection from violence and exploitation, and, in a famous article, the right to rest and play.

One of its most important ideas is that children are not just people to be protected. They have the right to express their views on matters that affect them, and adults must take those views seriously.

It has become the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history: every UN member state except the United States has ratified it. Taiwan, which is not a UN member, passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its own legal system.
Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide. Millions of children are still out of school, working in dangerous jobs, or living through war.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The United States is the only UN member that has not ratified the convention.
The 1989 convention promises every child rights, but many still lack them.
Taiwan passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its legal system.
Children need protection from harm more than they need a voice in decisions.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：公約承諾權利與發聲，但現實仍有落差。

q.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
opts: Taiwan ratified the convention as a full member of the UN in 2014.
The convention covers people under 21 wherever they live.
Every UN member state except the United States has ratified it.
The convention says children only need to be protected by adults.
q.why: 第 4 段：every UN member state except the United States has ratified it。台灣不是聯合國會員，是自己立法；公約適用 18 歲以下；第 3 段說孩子不只是需要被保護。

q.q: What is the purpose of paragraph 5?
opts: To point out that the promises are not yet fully kept
To list all of the rights that the convention includes
To explain why the United States did not sign it
To celebrate that every child is now safe and in school
q.why: 第 5 段：Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide——指出承諾還沒完全實現。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “ratified” means ___.
opts: completely rejected
written by children
translated into English
officially approved
q.why: ratified = 正式批准。

q.q: What does the writer mean by “children are not just people to be protected”?
opts: Children also have the right to be heard
Children do not really need any protection
Children should be the ones protecting adults
Children should be allowed to vote in elections
q.why: 第三段：They have the right to express their views。

q.q: Someone says: “Every country in the world has ratified the convention.” Based on the text, is this accurate?
opts: Yes — every country in the world has ratified it
Yes — and that includes Taiwan at the UN
No — every UN member except the US has ratified it
No — only eighteen countries have ratified it
q.why: 第四段：every UN member state except the United States。

tr.en: One of its most important ideas is that children are not just people to be protected.
tr.zh: 它最重要的觀念之一是：兒童不只是需要被保護的人。

tr.en: Taiwan, which is not a UN member, passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its own legal system.
tr.zh: 台灣雖然不是聯合國會員，仍在 2014 年通過法律，將這項公約納入自己的法律體系。

tr.en: Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide.
tr.zh: 然而，承諾與現實之間的差距仍然很大。

tz: 1989 年 11 月 20 日，聯合國通過了《兒童權利公約》，這一天現在被定為世界兒童日來慶祝。
這項公約列出了每一位 18 歲以下的人，不論住在哪裡都應該享有的權利，包括受教育、獲得醫療照顧、免於暴力和剝削的保護，還有一條很有名的條文：休息和遊戲的權利。
它最重要的觀念之一是：孩子不只是需要被保護的人。他們有權利對影響自己的事情表達看法，而大人必須認真看待這些看法。
它已成為歷史上批准國家最多的人權條約：除了美國以外，每個聯合國會員國都已批准。不是聯合國會員的台灣，則在 2014 年通過一項法律，把這項公約納入自己的法律體系。
然而，承諾和現實之間的落差仍然很大。仍有數百萬名孩子沒有上學、從事危險的工作，或生活在戰爭之中。

ph.ex: The rules are set out on the first page.
ph.exzh: 規則列在第一頁。

ph.ex: Sunscreen gives you protection from the sun.
ph.exzh: 防曬乳能保護你不被曬傷。

ph.ex: Please take your homework seriously.
ph.exzh: 請認真看待你的作業。

ph.ex: She made reading part of her daily life.
ph.exzh: 她讓閱讀成為日常生活的一部分。

ph.ex: Millions of children are still out of school.
ph.exzh: 仍有數百萬名孩子失學。

st.m: On November 20, 1989, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, and the date is now celebrated as World Children's Day.
st.mz: 《兒童權利公約》保障每個孩子的權利，但承諾和現實之間仍有很大的差距。
t: The convention sets out the rights that every person under 18 should enjoy, wherever they live.
One of its most important ideas is that children are not just people to be protected.
It has become the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history: every UN member state except the United States has ratified it.
st.c: Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide.

c.title: Rights Before Adulthood
text: For most of history, children were regarded less as people than as possessions, or as adults in waiting. The Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the UN General Assembly on November 20, 1989, marked a decisive break with that view.

Its premise is that childhood carries rights of its own. Alongside protection from violence, exploitation and neglect, the convention guarantees education, health care and even rest and play, acknowledging that a good childhood is not merely survival.

Its most radical provision concerns participation: children have the right to express their views on matters affecting them, with due weight given according to their age and maturity. This reframes children from passive recipients of care into people whose opinions count.

The treaty has been ratified by every UN member except the United States, making it the most widely accepted human rights agreement ever. Taiwan, excluded from the UN, incorporated it into domestic law in 2014, an example of how norms can spread beyond formal membership.
Ratification, however, is not realisation. Child labour, conflict and unequal schooling persist, a reminder that rights written on paper become real only when adults choose to honour them.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Children are best understood as adults in waiting, not rights-holders.
The United States wrote the convention but chose not to ratify it.
Ratifying the treaty in 1989 largely solved the problem of child labour.
It treats children as rights-holders, but promises need adults to act.
q.why: 主旨：公約視兒童為權利主體並有發聲權，但承諾要靠行動實現。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “provision” means ___.
opts: food packed for a long journey
a part or rule of a legal agreement
a type of school for children
a promise made by children to their parents
q.why: provision = 條款。

q.q: Why does the writer call the participation right “radical”?
opts: It makes children people whose opinions count
It encourages children to use violence
Only adults are allowed to vote on it
It gives children the right to vote in national elections
q.why: 第三段：reframes children from passive recipients … into people whose opinions count。

q.q: What is the writer's attitude in the final paragraph?
opts: Satisfied that all of the work is now done
Angry at children for not using their rights
Realistic: signing is not making rights real
Uninterested in what happens next
q.why: Ratification, however, is not realisation——務實的提醒。

q.q: What does the example of Taiwan in paragraph 4 show?
opts: The UN directly controls Taiwan's laws
A norm can spread without UN membership
Taiwan rejected the treaty in 2014
The United States followed Taiwan's lead
q.why: 第四段：norms can spread beyond formal membership。

q.q: A city council plans to close a children's park without asking anyone. Based on the convention as described, what is the strongest objection?
opts: Parks cost the city a lot of money to keep open every year
Only adults really use the parks in most cities anyway
The council must first ask the United States for permission
Children have rights to play and to be heard on such decisions
q.why: 第二、三段：休息與遊戲的權利，以及對影響自己的事表達意見的權利。

tz: 在歷史上的大部分時間裡，孩子與其說是「人」，不如說被當成財產，或是「還沒長大的大人」。1989 年 11 月 20 日由聯合國大會通過的《兒童權利公約》，標誌著與這種看法的決定性決裂。
它的前提是：童年本身就帶有權利。除了免於暴力、剝削和疏忽的保護之外，公約也保障教育、醫療，甚至休息和遊戲——承認美好的童年不只是活下來而已。
它最具突破性的條款與「參與」有關：孩子有權利對影響他們的事情表達意見，並依照他們的年齡和成熟度給予應有的重視。這把孩子從被動接受照顧的人，重新定位為意見有分量的人。
除了美國以外，每個聯合國會員國都已批准這項條約，使它成為有史以來接受度最高的人權協定。被排除在聯合國之外的台灣，在 2014 年把它納入國內法——這個例子說明了規範可以擴散到正式會員資格之外。
然而，批准並不等於實現。童工、戰爭和不平等的教育依然存在，提醒我們：寫在紙上的權利，只有在大人選擇去尊重它們時，才會成真。

ph.ex: He is less a teacher than a friend to us.
ph.exzh: 對我們來說，他與其說是老師，不如說是朋友。

ph.ex: The new rule marked a break with the past.
ph.exzh: 這條新規定標誌著與過去的決裂。

ph.ex: Seats are given according to age.
ph.exzh: 座位依照年齡安排。

ph.ex: Her kindness makes her the most popular girl in class.
ph.exzh: 她的善良讓她成為班上最受歡迎的女生。
ph.m: making it the most widely accepted

ph.ex: The view was beautiful beyond words.
ph.exzh: 景色美得無法用言語形容。

ph.ex: You can choose to be kind every day.
ph.exzh: 你每天都可以選擇善良。

st.m: The Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the UN General Assembly on November 20, 1989, marked a decisive break with that view.
st.mz: 《兒童權利公約》讓兒童成為擁有權利的人，但權利要靠大人的行動才能真正實現。
t: Its premise is that childhood carries rights of its own.
Its most radical provision concerns participation: children have the right to express their views on matters affecting them, with due weight given according to their age and maturity.
The treaty has been ratified by every UN member except the United States, making it the most widely accepted human rights agreement ever.
st.c: Child labour, conflict and unequal schooling persist, a reminder that rights written on paper become real only when adults choose to honour them.

discuss: Which right in the convention do you think is the most important? Why?
Do adults at your school or home listen to children's opinions? Give an example.
What could students do to help children in other countries who cannot go to school?

topic: Edwin Hubble and the Growing Universe
zh: 哈伯：發現宇宙正在變大的人

a.title: The Man Who Saw Other Galaxies
text: Edwin Hubble was born on November 20, 1889, in the United States. He became a famous astronomer.
An astronomer studies stars and space. Hubble used a very big telescope on a mountain in California.
Long ago, people thought our galaxy, the Milky Way, was the whole universe. Hubble showed that there are many other galaxies far away.
He also found that most galaxies are moving away from us. This means the universe is getting bigger!
Today, a space telescope has his name: the Hubble Space Telescope. It has taken amazing pictures since 1990.
Hubble's work changed how we see our place in space.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The pictures taken by the Hubble Space Telescope
Edwin Hubble and what he found out about space
A tall mountain with a telescope in California
How a young person can become an astronomer
q.why: 全文介紹哈伯和他的發現。

q.q: According to the reading, which is TRUE?
opts: The Hubble Space Telescope has taken pictures since 1889.
Hubble found that most galaxies are moving closer to us.
Hubble used a big telescope on a mountain in California.
Long ago, people thought there were many other galaxies.
q.why: 第 2 段：Hubble used a very big telescope on a mountain in California。太空望遠鏡從 1990 年開始拍照；星系是「遠離」我們；以前的人以為銀河系就是全部。

q.q: In paragraph 4, what does "This" in "This means the universe is getting bigger" refer to?
opts: most galaxies moving away from us
people's old idea about the Milky Way
a big telescope in California
the space telescope's pictures
q.why: This 指前一句的發現：大多數星系正在遠離我們——所以宇宙正在變大。

q.q: In the text, an “astronomer” is a person who ___.
opts: builds tall mountains
takes photos of people
flies a spaceship to the Moon
studies stars and space
q.why: 第二段：An astronomer studies stars and space。

q.q: Why does the text say the universe is getting bigger?
opts: Most galaxies are moving away from us
The telescope on the mountain is very big
There are more new stars every single year
Hubble was born a long time ago, in 1889
q.why: 第四段：most galaxies are moving away from us. This means the universe is getting bigger!

q.q: Your friend says, “The Milky Way is everything in space.” Based on the text, what can you tell your friend?
opts: You are right — Hubble agreed with you
Hubble showed there are many other galaxies
The Milky Way is really a kind of telescope
Only scientists at NASA know the answer
q.why: 第三段：Hubble showed that there are many other galaxies far away。

gt.en: An astronomer studies stars and space.
gt.zh: 天文學家研究星星和太空。

gt.en: Hubble used a very big telescope on a mountain in California.
gt.zh: 哈伯在加州一座山上使用一架非常大的望遠鏡。

gt.en: He also found that most galaxies are moving away from us.
gt.zh: 他也發現大部分星系正在遠離我們。

gt.en: Hubble's work changed how we see our place in space.
gt.zh: 哈伯的研究改變了我們看待自己在宇宙中位置的方式。

tz: 愛德溫・哈伯在 1889 年 11 月 20 日出生於美國。他成為一位有名的天文學家。
天文學家研究星星和太空。哈伯在加州一座山上使用一架非常大的望遠鏡。
很久以前，人們以為我們的銀河系就是整個宇宙。哈伯證明了在很遠的地方還有許多其他的星系。
他也發現大多數星系正在遠離我們。這表示宇宙正在變大！
今天，有一架太空望遠鏡以他的名字命名：哈伯太空望遠鏡。它從 1990 年起就拍下了許多驚人的照片。
哈伯的研究改變了我們看待自己在太空中位置的方式。

ph.ex: I was born on May 5.
ph.exzh: 我在 5 月 5 日出生。

ph.ex: My grandparents live far away.
ph.exzh: 我的爺爺奶奶住得很遠。

ph.ex: The boat slowly moved away from the shore.
ph.exzh: 船慢慢地離開了岸邊。

ph.ex: The puppy gets bigger every week.
ph.exzh: 小狗每週都長大一點。

st.m: Hubble's work changed how we see our place in space.
st.mz: 哈伯發現宇宙中有許多星系，而且宇宙正在膨脹，改變了我們對自己在宇宙中位置的看法。
t: An astronomer studies stars and space.
Hubble showed that there are many other galaxies far away.
He also found that most galaxies are moving away from us.
Today, a space telescope has his name: the Hubble Space Telescope.
st.c: Hubble's work changed how we see our place in space.

b.title: Beyond the Milky Way
text: Edwin Hubble, born in Missouri on November 20, 1889, first studied law at Oxford before returning to his real passion: the stars.

In the early 1920s, astronomers were still arguing about whether fuzzy patches of light called nebulae were inside our galaxy or far beyond it. Using the giant Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson in California, Hubble measured special pulsing stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed that it was far too distant to belong to the Milky Way.
Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.

In 1929 Hubble published another landmark result: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away from us. This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding. The Belgian scientist Georges Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier, which is why the rule is now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law.
In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hubble showed that other galaxies exist and that the universe is expanding.
Hubble studied law at Oxford before he turned to astronomy instead.
Lemaître built the giant Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson in California.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into orbit back in 1929.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：證明其他星系存在、宇宙在膨脹。

q.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
opts: Lemaître proposed his idea two years after Hubble did.
Andromeda turned out to be a cloud inside our own galaxy.
Hubble studied law before he became an astronomer.
NASA launched the space telescope in 1929 to honour him.
q.why: 第 1 段：first studied law at Oxford before returning to … the stars。勒梅特是「早兩年」提出；仙女座是獨立的星系；太空望遠鏡在 1990 年發射。

q.q: In paragraph 2, what does "it" in "showed that it was far too distant to belong to the Milky Way" refer to?
opts: the Hooker telescope
Mount Wilson in California
our own galaxy
the Andromeda nebula
q.why: 哈伯測量的是仙女座星雲裡的星，證明「它」太遠、不屬於銀河系，所以 it = the Andromeda nebula。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “expanding” means ___.
opts: getting colder
getting bigger
staying the same
turning around
q.why: expanding = 擴張、變大。

q.q: Why is the rule now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law?
opts: Lemaître built the telescope Hubble used
The two scientists were brothers
NASA renamed the law in 1990
Lemaître proposed a similar idea earlier
q.why: 第四段：Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier。

q.q: A website says: “Hubble alone came up with the idea that the universe is expanding.” Based on the text, is this fair?
opts: Not fully — Lemaître proposed it two years earlier
Yes — nobody else had ever studied the question
Yes — the space telescope is named after him
No — Hubble studied law, not the stars
q.why: 第四段：勒梅特早兩年提出類似想法。

tr.en: Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.
tr.zh: 仙女座是一個獨立的星系，宇宙一下子變得比任何人想像的都大得多。

tr.en: This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding.
tr.zh: 這是宇宙正在膨脹的有力證據。

tr.en: In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.
tr.zh: 1990 年，NASA 發射了一架以他命名的太空望遠鏡，在地球模糊的大氣層之上延續他的工作。

tz: 愛德溫・哈伯 1889 年 11 月 20 日生於密蘇里州，他先在牛津大學讀法律，後來才回到他真正熱愛的事物：星星。
在 1920 年代初期，天文學家仍在爭論那些叫做「星雲」的模糊光斑，究竟是在我們的銀河系裡面，還是遠在它之外。哈伯使用加州威爾遜山上巨大的胡克望遠鏡，測量仙女座星雲中一種特殊的脈動星，證明它距離太遠，不可能屬於銀河系。
仙女座是一個獨立的星系——宇宙一下子變得比任何人想像的都大得多。
1929 年，哈伯發表了另一項里程碑般的成果：一個星系離我們越遠，它遠離我們的速度看起來就越快。這是宇宙正在膨脹的有力證據。比利時科學家喬治・勒梅特在兩年前就提出過類似的想法，所以這條規律現在常被稱為「哈伯－勒梅特定律」。
1990 年，美國太空總署發射了一架以他命名的太空望遠鏡，在地球模糊的大氣層之上延續他的研究。

ph.ex: The box is far too heavy for me.
ph.exzh: 這個箱子對我來說實在太重了。

ph.ex: Which team do you belong to?
ph.exzh: 你屬於哪一隊？

ph.ex: The more you read, the better you write.
ph.exzh: 讀得越多，寫得越好。
ph.m: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster

ph.ex: A statue was built in her honour.
ph.exzh: 人們為紀念她建了一座雕像。

ph.ex: The plane flew above the clouds.
ph.exzh: 飛機在雲層之上飛行。

st.mz: 哈伯證明仙女座是另一個星系，又發現宇宙正在膨脹。
t: In the early 1920s, astronomers were still arguing about whether fuzzy patches of light called nebulae were inside our galaxy or far beyond it.
Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.
In 1929 Hubble published another landmark result: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away from us.
st.c: In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.

c.title: How Big Is Everything?
text: A century ago, the most basic question in astronomy, how big the universe is, had no agreed answer. Many astronomers believed the Milky Way contained everything; the faint spiral 'nebulae' scattered across the sky were assumed to be clouds within it.

Edwin Hubble, born on November 20, 1889, settled the dispute. In 1923, working with the great Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson, he identified a Cepheid variable, a star whose regular pulsing reveals its true brightness, in the Andromeda nebula. Comparing true and apparent brightness yielded a distance far beyond our galaxy's edge.
The implication was staggering: Andromeda was an 'island universe', and the cosmos contained countless such galaxies.

Six years later he went further, showing that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. The universe was not static but expanding, a conclusion the Belgian priest-physicist Georges Lemaître had already reached theoretically, which is why astronomers now speak of the Hubble–Lemaître law.

Hubble never won a Nobel Prize, which did not then recognise astronomy. Yet his findings demoted humanity twice, from the centre of a single galaxy to one corner of an expanding cosmos, and few scientific discoveries have so thoroughly rescaled our sense of home.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Hubble's main achievement was finally winning the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Hubble proved the Milky Way is the whole universe, which made humans feel more central.
Hubble revealed countless galaxies in an expanding universe, shrinking our place.
The Milky Way, as people once thought, contains everything in the universe.
q.why: 主旨：無數星系＋宇宙膨脹，徹底改變人類的定位。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “recede” means ___.
opts: grow brighter
move away
stop moving
explode
q.why: recede = 後退、遠離。

q.q: Why was the Cepheid variable star so useful?
opts: It was simply the brightest star in the whole night sky
It was located safely inside our own Milky Way galaxy
It proved once and for all that the universe is static
Its regular pulsing shows its true brightness, so distance
q.why: 第二段：its regular pulsing reveals its true brightness——比較真實與視亮度可推算距離。

q.q: How does the writer view Hubble's lack of a Nobel Prize?
opts: A technicality that doesn't reduce his work
Proof that his work was really quite minor
Deeply unfair to the scientist Lemaître
A mistake made by NASA in naming the telescope
q.why: 第五段：諾貝爾獎當時不包含天文學，但他的發現依然極重要（Yet …）。

q.q: What does the phrase “demoted humanity twice” refer to?
opts: Two important prizes that Hubble failed to win
Two different telescopes that Hubble used
Two public arguments he had with Lemaître

tz: 一個世紀以前，天文學最基本的問題——宇宙有多大——還沒有公認的答案。許多天文學家相信銀河系就包含了一切；散布在天空中那些微弱的螺旋狀「星雲」，被認為是銀河系裡的雲氣。
1889 年 11 月 20 日出生的愛德溫・哈伯，解決了這場爭論。1923 年，他使用威爾遜山上偉大的胡克望遠鏡，在仙女座星雲中找到一顆造父變星——一種規律脈動、能透露出自身真實亮度的恆星。比較它的真實亮度和看起來的亮度，就算出一個遠遠超出銀河系邊界的距離。
這個結論驚人至極：仙女座是一個「島宇宙」，而宇宙中有無數個這樣的星系。
六年後他更進一步，證明星系遠離的速度和它們的距離成正比。宇宙不是靜止的，而是在膨脹——比利時的神父兼物理學家喬治・勒梅特早已在理論上得出這個結論，這就是為什麼天文學家現在稱它為「哈伯－勒梅特定律」。
哈伯從未獲得諾貝爾獎，因為當時諾貝爾獎不頒給天文學。然而，他的發現兩度把人類「降級」：從一個星系的中心，降到一個不斷膨脹的宇宙裡的一個角落；很少有科學發現能如此徹底地改變我們對「家」的尺度感。

a.title: Why Does My Horoscope Feel So True?
text: Have you ever read a horoscope or taken a personality quiz online and thought, "Wow, this is exactly me!"? Many people feel this way. Psychologists have a name for it: the Barnum effect.

The Barnum effect happens when we believe that general sentences were written just for us. Look at this one: "You are friendly, but sometimes you like to be alone." It sounds personal, but it is true for almost everyone.

In 1948, a psychologist named Bertram Forer tried a simple test. He gave his students a personality test. A week later, each student got a "personal" result. The students said the results were very good — about 4.3 out of 5.
But there was a secret. Every student got the same result! Forer took most of the sentences from a book about stars and birthdays.
The name comes from P. T. Barnum, a famous American showman. People said his shows had "something for everyone." That is just like these sentences.
Next time a quiz knows you "perfectly," stop and ask: could this be true for my friends, too?
tz: 你有沒有在網路上看過星座運勢或做過性格測驗，然後心想：「哇，這根本就是在說我！」很多人都有這種感覺。心理學家為它取了名字：巴納姆效應。
巴納姆效應是指我們相信一些籠統的句子是專門寫給自己的。看看這一句：「你很友善，但有時候喜歡一個人獨處。」它聽起來很個人，但幾乎對每個人都成立。
1948 年，一位名叫伯特倫・佛瑞的心理學家做了一個簡單的實驗。他讓學生做一份性格測驗。一週後，每個學生都拿到一份「個人」結果。學生們說結果非常準——5 分大約給了 4.3 分。
但這裡面有個祕密：每個學生拿到的結果都一模一樣！佛瑞的句子大多是從一本講星座和生日的書裡抄來的。
這個名字來自美國著名的表演家 P. T. 巴納姆。人們說他的表演「人人都能找到喜歡的東西」，就和這些句子一樣。
下次測驗「完美」說中你的時候，停下來問問自己：這是不是也適用在我的朋友身上？

b.title: The Barnum Effect: Why Vague Words Feel Personal
text: "You have a great need for other people to like and admire you." "At times you are outgoing and sociable, while at other times you are quiet and reserved." If these lines sound like a description of you, you are not alone. Statements like these feel deeply personal, yet they fit almost anyone. Psychologists call our tendency to accept them the Barnum effect.

The effect was famously demonstrated in 1948 by the psychologist Bertram Forer. He gave his students a personality test and, a week later, handed each of them what appeared to be an individual analysis. Asked to rate its accuracy from 0 to 5, the class gave an average score of about 4.3 — a remarkably high result.

Then Forer revealed the trick: every student had received exactly the same text, most of which he had copied from a newsstand astrology book. The students had not been fooled by clever writing so much as by their own minds.

Several factors make such statements convincing. They are vague enough to match many lives, they are mostly flattering, and they often include both sides of a trait — "sometimes shy, sometimes outgoing" — so that nearly every reader can find themselves in them. People also believe a description more when they think it was prepared just for them, or when it comes from an authority.
The name was suggested later by the psychologist Paul Meehl, after the circus owner P. T. Barnum, whose shows were said to offer "something for everyone."

Today the effect helps explain the appeal of horoscopes, fortune tellers and many online personality quizzes, whose results are often shared proudly on social media. Knowing about it does not mean these things can never be fun. It simply reminds us to ask a useful question: would this description fit my classmates just as well?
tz: 「你非常需要別人喜歡、欣賞你。」「有時你外向又合群，有時卻安靜又拘謹。」如果這些句子聽起來像在描述你，你不是唯一一個這麼覺得的人。這類句子讓人感覺非常個人化，卻幾乎適用於任何人。心理學家把我們傾向於相信這類句子的現象稱為巴納姆效應。
1948 年，心理學家伯特倫・佛瑞用一個著名的實驗證明了這個效應。他讓學生做性格測驗，一週後發給每人一份看似專屬的個人分析。請學生用 0 到 5 分評估準確度時，全班平均給了大約 4.3 分——相當高的分數。
接著佛瑞揭開了把戲：每個學生收到的文字一模一樣，其中大部分是他從書報攤買的星座書抄來的。學生們與其說是被巧妙的文字騙了，不如說是被自己的大腦騙了。
有幾個因素讓這類句子特別有說服力。它們夠含糊，能對上很多人的生活；它們大多是好聽話；而且常常同時包含一種特質的兩面——「有時害羞，有時外向」——讓幾乎每個讀者都能在其中看到自己。當人們以為描述是專門為自己準備的，或是出自權威時，也會更相信它。
這個名稱是後來心理學家保羅・米爾提出的，取自馬戲團老闆 P. T. 巴納姆——據說他的表演「人人都能找到喜歡的東西」。
今天，這個效應可以解釋為什麼星座運勢、算命師和許多網路性格測驗那麼吸引人——它們的結果常被人得意地分享到社群媒體上。知道這個效應，並不代表這些東西就不能好玩。它只是提醒我們問一個有用的問題：這段描述是不是也同樣適合我的同學？

c.title: Something for Everyone: The Science of the Barnum Effect
text: Few experiences feel as intimate as being accurately described by a stranger. A horoscope that captures your mood, a quiz that names your hidden fears, a fortune teller who seems to read your past — each can produce a small shock of recognition. Psychologists, however, have long suspected that much of this recognition is manufactured by the reader rather than delivered by the source. They call it the Barnum effect.

The classic demonstration came in 1948. Bertram Forer asked his introductory psychology students to complete a personality questionnaire, then returned a week later with supposedly individual sketches. Students rated how well the sketch described them on a scale from 0 to 5; the average was roughly 4.3. Only then did Forer disclose that all thirty-nine sketches were identical, assembled largely from an astrology book bought at a newsstand.

Later research identified the ingredients that make such descriptions persuasive. Positive statements are accepted more readily than negative ones. Double-headed claims — "you can be talkative, but you also value your quiet time" — cover both ends of a trait and therefore almost never miss. Belief rises further when the description is presented as tailored to the individual, and when it comes from a source that appears scientific or expert.

The term itself was popularised in 1956 by the psychologist Paul Meehl, who borrowed the name of the nineteenth-century showman P. T. Barnum. Meehl was not amused by horoscopes so much as worried about his own profession: he warned that clinical reports full of vague, flattering generalities might impress patients and colleagues while saying almost nothing of substance.

The lesson extends well beyond astrology. Marketing that "understands you", algorithm-generated profiles and even some workplace personality tests can rely on the same mechanism. None of this means that every personality measure is worthless; well-designed tests are checked against real behaviour. But it does suggest a simple discipline: before accepting a description as uniquely yours, ask whether it would be equally convincing if handed to the person sitting next to you.

Being aware of the effect may not be enough to escape it. Because the feeling of recognition arrives instantly, while doubt requires effort, even well-informed readers can be charmed by a description that seems to know them. Recognising a bias, in other words, is only the first step toward resisting it.
tz: 很少有什麼經驗，比被陌生人準確描述更讓人覺得貼心私密。一則抓住你心情的星座運勢、一份說出你隱藏恐懼的測驗、一位彷彿能讀出你過去的算命師——每一種都可能帶來「被看穿」的小小震撼。然而，心理學家很早就懷疑，這種「說中了」的感覺，大多是讀者自己製造出來的，而不是來源真的提供了什麼。他們稱之為巴納姆效應。
經典的實驗出現在 1948 年。伯特倫・佛瑞請修心理學入門課的學生填一份性格問卷，一週後帶回據稱是個人專屬的性格描述。學生用 0 到 5 分評估描述得有多準，平均約 4.3 分。直到那時佛瑞才透露：三十九份描述完全相同，大部分是從書報攤買來的星座書拼湊而成。
後續研究找出了讓這類描述具有說服力的成分。正面的句子比負面的更容易被接受。「兩頭都說」的句子——「你可以很健談，但也重視安靜的時光」——涵蓋了一種特質的兩端，因此幾乎不會失準。當描述被包裝成為個人量身訂做，或來源看起來很科學、很專業時，人們會更加相信。
這個名詞本身是心理學家保羅・米爾在 1956 年推廣開來的，他借用了十九世紀表演家 P. T. 巴納姆的名字。米爾與其說是覺得星座好笑，不如說是擔心自己的專業：他警告，充滿含糊、討好的籠統說法的臨床報告，可能讓病人和同事印象深刻，卻幾乎沒有任何實質內容。
這個教訓遠遠超出星座的範圍。號稱「懂你」的行銷、演算法產生的個人檔案，甚至某些職場性格測驗，都可能依賴同樣的機制。這並不代表所有性格測量都毫無價值；設計良好的測驗會用真實行為來檢驗。但它確實提醒我們一個簡單的習慣：在接受某段描述是「專屬於你」之前，先問問看——如果把它交給坐在你旁邊的人，是否同樣有說服力？
光是知道這個效應，可能還不足以逃離它。因為「被說中」的感覺是瞬間出現的，而懷疑需要花力氣，所以即使是見多識廣的讀者，也可能被一段好像很懂他的描述迷住。換句話說，認出一種偏誤，只是抵抗它的第一步。

topic: The Butterfly Effect: Can Tiny Changes Make a Storm?
zh: 蝴蝶效應：微小的改變能掀起風暴嗎？
discuss: Can you think of a small event that later made a big difference in your life?

a.title: Can a Butterfly Cause a Storm?
text: Can a tiny butterfly in Brazil cause a big storm in Texas? It sounds crazy, but this famous question helps explain an important idea in science: the butterfly effect.

The idea comes from Edward Lorenz, an American scientist who studied the weather. In 1961, he used a computer to predict the weather. One day, he wanted to run the same program again. To save time, he typed a number a little shorter: 0.506 instead of 0.506127.

He went to get a cup of coffee. When he came back, he was very surprised. The new weather was completely different from the first one! A very small change at the start had become a very big change later.

This is the butterfly effect: in some systems, tiny changes can grow into huge results. The weather is one of these systems. That is why weather reports are good for a few days, but no one can say exactly what the weather will be like in a month.
The butterfly effect is also a nice idea for our lives. A small kind word or a few minutes of practice every day can lead to big changes over time.
tz: 巴西一隻小小的蝴蝶，能在美國德州引起一場大風暴嗎？聽起來很瘋狂，但這個有名的問題，幫忙解釋了科學中一個重要的概念：蝴蝶效應。
這個概念來自愛德華・羅倫茲，一位研究天氣的美國科學家。1961 年，他用電腦預測天氣。有一天，他想再跑一次同樣的程式。為了省時間，他輸入了一個短一點的數字：0.506，而不是 0.506127。
他去倒了一杯咖啡。回來時，他非常驚訝：新算出的天氣和第一次完全不一樣！一開始非常小的改變，後來變成了非常大的改變。
這就是蝴蝶效應：在某些系統裡，微小的改變可能變成巨大的結果。天氣就是這樣的系統。這就是為什麼天氣預報準個幾天沒問題，但沒有人能確切說出一個月後的天氣會怎樣。
蝴蝶效應也是一個很適合用在生活中的想法。一句小小的好話，或每天幾分鐘的練習，久而久之都可能帶來很大的改變。

b.title: The Butterfly Effect: How Tiny Changes Shape the Future
text: In 1972, the American meteorologist Edward Lorenz gave a talk with a memorable title: "Does the Flap of a Butterfly's Wings in Brazil Set Off a Tornado in Texas?" The question was not really about insects. It was about a surprising feature of certain natural systems, a feature now known as the butterfly effect.

Lorenz discovered it by accident about a decade earlier. Working at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, he was running a simple computer model of the weather. Wanting to repeat one run, he restarted it from the middle and typed in a value from a printout, 0.506, rather than the full 0.506127 stored in the machine. He then left to get coffee. When he returned about an hour later, the new forecast had drifted so far from the original that the two looked like entirely different weather.

The lesson was startling. In systems like the atmosphere, extremely small differences in starting conditions can grow over time until they completely change the outcome. Scientists call this "sensitive dependence on initial conditions," and it became a founding idea of chaos theory.

The discovery explains why weather forecasts have limits. Even with powerful supercomputers and millions of measurements, tiny errors are unavoidable, and they multiply. Forecasts are generally reliable for a few days, but beyond roughly two weeks, detailed predictions become little better than guesses.

It is important not to misunderstand the idea. The butterfly effect does not mean that every small action causes enormous consequences, or that a real butterfly can create a storm. It means that in certain complex systems, we cannot know which tiny differences will matter.

That humbling idea has spread far beyond meteorology, into ecology, economics and popular culture, reminding us that the future is often less predictable than it seems, and that small causes deserve respect.
tz: 1972 年，美國氣象學家愛德華・羅倫茲發表了一場題目令人難忘的演講：〈巴西一隻蝴蝶拍動翅膀，會在德州引發龍捲風嗎？〉這個問題其實和昆蟲無關，而是關於某些自然系統一個令人意外的特徵——也就是現在所說的蝴蝶效應。
羅倫茲大約在十年前意外發現了它。當時他在麻省理工學院工作，正在執行一個簡單的天氣電腦模型。為了重複其中一次運算，他從中間重新開始，從列印出來的紙上輸入一個數值 0.506，而不是機器裡儲存的完整數值 0.506127。接著他離開去倒咖啡。大約一小時後他回來時，新的預報已經偏離原本的結果太遠，兩者看起來就像完全不同的天氣。
這個教訓令人吃驚。在大氣這樣的系統裡，起始條件極小的差異，可能隨著時間放大，直到完全改變結果。科學家稱之為「對初始條件的敏感依賴」，它也成為混沌理論的奠基概念。
這個發現解釋了為什麼天氣預報有極限。即使有強大的超級電腦和數百萬筆測量資料，微小的誤差仍無法避免，而且會不斷倍增。天氣預報通常在幾天內相當可靠，但超過大約兩週，詳細的預測就跟猜測差不多了。
重要的是不要誤解這個概念。蝴蝶效應並不是說每一個小動作都會造成巨大的後果，也不是說一隻真的蝴蝶能製造風暴。它的意思是：在某些複雜的系統裡，我們無法知道哪些微小的差異會產生影響。
這個讓人謙卑的想法已經遠遠擴散到氣象學之外，進入生態學、經濟學和大眾文化，提醒我們未來往往比看起來更難預測，而微小的原因也值得尊重。

c.title: Chaos, Weather and the Limits of Prediction
text: For much of the twentieth century, many scientists shared an optimistic assumption: with good enough equations and accurate enough measurements, the future behaviour of physical systems — including the weather — could in principle be calculated far in advance. The butterfly effect quietly dismantled that confidence.

Its discovery is one of science's favourite accidents. In 1961, Edward Lorenz, a meteorologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, was running a stripped-down computer model of the atmosphere. To re-examine one sequence, he restarted the simulation midway, entering a value from a printout rounded to three decimal places instead of the six the computer held internally. The difference — about one part in four thousand — seemed negligible. Yet within a couple of months of simulated weather, the new run bore no resemblance to the old one.

Lorenz recognised that this was not a malfunction but a property of the equations themselves. In nonlinear systems, small discrepancies do not stay small; they compound, often exponentially, until the system's path is effectively unpredictable. His 1963 paper on the subject, "Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow", became a cornerstone of what would later be called chaos theory. The vivid butterfly image came later, from the title of a 1972 lecture.

A crucial subtlety is that chaotic systems are deterministic: they obey fixed rules, with no randomness involved. The problem lies in our knowledge rather than in the machinery. Because we can never measure initial conditions with perfect precision, even a flawless model will eventually diverge from reality. Modern forecasters respond by running "ensembles" — dozens of simulations with slightly varied starting points — and reporting probabilities rather than certainties.

The concept has since been borrowed, sometimes loosely, by economists, ecologists and novelists. Popular usage often implies that any trivial act may trigger dramatic consequences, which distorts the original point. Lorenz's insight was not that small causes routinely produce large effects, but that in certain systems we cannot know in advance which small causes will matter.

There is something both humbling and liberating in this. Chaos theory sets hard limits on prediction, yet it also explains why complex systems remain endlessly varied, and why the future, at least in its details, stays genuinely open. For forecasters, that means accepting uncertainty; for everyone else, it may mean a little more humility about predicting anything at all.
tz: 二十世紀的大半時間裡，許多科學家都抱持一個樂觀的假設：只要方程式夠好、測量夠精確，物理系統——包括天氣——未來的行為原則上可以提早很久計算出來。蝴蝶效應悄悄瓦解了這份信心。
它的發現是科學史上最為人津津樂道的意外之一。1961 年，麻省理工學院的氣象學家愛德華・羅倫茲正在執行一個簡化的大氣電腦模型。為了重新檢視其中一段運算，他從中途重新開始模擬，輸入列印紙上四捨五入到小數點後三位的數值，而不是電腦內部保存的六位數。這個差距——大約四千分之一——看起來可以忽略不計。然而，在模擬天氣的短短一兩個月內，新的運算結果就和舊的毫無相似之處。
羅倫茲意識到，這不是機器故障，而是方程式本身的特性。在非線性系統中，小小的差異不會一直很小；它們會累積放大，常常是指數式的，直到系統的走向實際上變得無法預測。他 1963 年關於這個主題的論文〈決定論的非週期流〉，成為後來所稱混沌理論的基石。生動的蝴蝶意象則是後來才出現的，來自 1972 年一場演講的題目。
一個關鍵的細節是：混沌系統是決定論的——它們遵守固定的規則，沒有任何隨機成分。問題出在我們的知識，而不是機制本身。因為我們永遠無法完美精確地測量初始條件，即使是毫無瑕疵的模型，最終也會和現實分道揚鑣。現代預報員的因應方式是執行「系集預報」——用稍微不同的起點跑數十次模擬——並報告機率，而不是確定的結果。
這個概念後來被經濟學家、生態學家和小說家借用，有時用得相當隨意。一般的用法常暗示任何微不足道的舉動都可能引發戲劇性的後果，這扭曲了原本的重點。羅倫茲的洞見並不是「小原因經常造成大結果」，而是：在某些系統中，我們無法事先知道哪些小原因會產生影響。
這件事讓人既謙卑又感到解放。混沌理論為預測設下了嚴格的極限，但它也解釋了為什麼複雜系統永遠變化多端，以及為什麼未來——至少在細節上——始終真正是開放的。對預報員來說，這代表要接受不確定性；對其他人來說，這或許代表在預測任何事情時，都要多一點謙虛。

topic: Confirmation Bias: We See What We Want to See

a.title: We See What We Want to See
text: Do you have a favourite team, singer, or phone brand? If you do, you may notice good news about it more easily than bad news. This is called confirmation bias.
Confirmation bias means we look for information that agrees with what we already believe. At the same time, we often ignore information that does not agree.
Here is an example. Mia thinks her new classmate Leo is rude. When Leo forgets to say hello, Mia thinks, "See? He is rude." But when Leo helps her carry her books, she does not remember it.

In 1960, a British psychologist named Peter Wason studied this. He gave people the numbers 2, 4, 6 and asked them to find the rule. Most people only tested ideas that would prove they were right. Few tried to prove themselves wrong.
The internet can make this bias stronger. Many apps show us more of what we already like, so we see the same opinions again and again.
How can we fight it? Before you decide, ask yourself: "What could show that I am wrong?" Good thinkers look at both sides.
tz: 你有沒有最喜歡的球隊、歌手或手機品牌？如果有，你可能比較容易注意到關於它的好消息，而不是壞消息。這就叫確認偏誤。
確認偏誤是指我們會去找和自己原本想法一致的資訊。同時，我們常常忽略和自己想法不一致的資訊。
舉個例子。米亞覺得新同學里歐很沒禮貌。里歐忘了打招呼時，米亞心想：「看吧？他就是沒禮貌。」但里歐幫她搬書時，她卻不記得這件事。
1960 年，一位名叫彼得・華生的英國心理學家研究了這個現象。他給受試者 2、4、6 三個數字，請他們找出規則。大多數人只測試能證明自己是對的想法，很少人試著證明自己是錯的。
網路會讓這種偏誤更嚴重。很多應用程式會給我們看更多我們本來就喜歡的東西，所以我們一再看到同樣的意見。
要怎麼對抗它？做決定之前，問問自己：「有什麼可以證明我是錯的？」好的思考者會兩面都看。

b.title: Confirmation Bias: Why We Defend What We Already Think
text: Imagine you are convinced that a certain brand of sneakers is the best. You read a glowing review and nod in agreement. Then you see a complaint about the shoes falling apart, and you quickly decide the writer must have been careless. Without realising it, you have just shown confirmation bias: the tendency to search for, interpret and remember information in ways that support what we already believe.

The bias was explored in a famous 1960 experiment by the British psychologist Peter Wason. Participants were told that the numbers 2, 4, 6 followed a hidden rule and were asked to discover it by suggesting other sets of three numbers. Most guessed something like "even numbers going up by two" and then tested only examples that fitted their guess, such as 8, 10, 12. Because every test seemed to succeed, they grew confident — yet the real rule was simply "any three numbers in increasing order."

Wason's participants were not foolish. Testing ideas that might prove us wrong feels uncomfortable, while finding support feels rewarding. The same pattern appears in everyday life: fans remember a referee's mistakes against their team, and people tend to read news from sources that share their views.
Online platforms can deepen the problem. Recommendation systems learn what we click and offer more of it, which may surround us with familiar opinions and make opposing views seem rare or strange.

The good news is that the bias can be reduced. Researchers suggest deliberately asking, "What evidence would change my mind?" and seeking out the strongest version of the opposing argument. Scientists build this habit into their work by designing experiments that could prove their ideas false.
Changing our minds can feel like losing, especially in front of others. In reality, it is often a sign that we are thinking clearly.
tz: 想像你確信某個牌子的球鞋是最好的。你讀到一篇讚不絕口的評論，點頭表示同意。接著你看到有人抱怨那雙鞋很快就壞了，你立刻斷定寫的人一定是自己不小心。不知不覺中，你剛剛就展現了確認偏誤：傾向用支持自己原本信念的方式去搜尋、解讀和記住資訊。
英國心理學家彼得・華生在 1960 年一個著名的實驗中探討了這種偏誤。他告訴受試者，2、4、6 這組數字遵循一個隱藏的規則，請他們提出其他三個數字的組合來找出規則。多數人猜的是「每次加二的偶數」之類，然後只測試符合自己猜測的例子，像是 8、10、12。因為每次測試似乎都成功，他們越來越有信心——但真正的規則只是「任何三個由小到大的數字」。
華生的受試者並不笨。測試可能證明自己錯的想法讓人不舒服，而找到支持的證據則讓人很滿足。同樣的模式也出現在日常生活中：球迷會記得裁判對自己球隊的誤判，人們也傾向從立場相同的來源閱讀新聞。
網路平台可能讓問題更嚴重。推薦系統會學習我們點什麼，然後給我們更多同類內容，這可能讓我們被熟悉的意見包圍，並讓相反的觀點顯得罕見或奇怪。
好消息是，這種偏誤可以減少。研究者建議刻意問自己：「什麼證據會讓我改變想法？」並主動去找反方最有力的論點。科學家把這個習慣融入工作中，設計能證明自己想法錯誤的實驗。
改變想法可能感覺像是輸了，尤其是在別人面前。但實際上，這往往代表我們思考得很清楚。

c.title: The Comfortable Trap of Confirmation Bias
text: Of all the errors that shape human judgement, confirmation bias may be the most pervasive. It describes our habit of gathering, interpreting and recalling evidence in ways that flatter our existing beliefs. The bias rarely feels like a bias from the inside; it feels like being right. Because it operates quietly, we tend to notice it far more easily in others than in ourselves.

Its modern study began with the psychologist Peter Wason. In his 2-4-6 task, first reported in 1960, participants tried to identify a rule by proposing number sequences. Most formed a narrow hypothesis and then proposed only sequences that would confirm it, rarely testing a case that might fail. Their confidence grew even as their understanding stalled. A later Wason puzzle, the selection task, showed that even educated adults struggle to see which evidence could disprove a claim.

Subsequent research revealed how deep the tendency runs. In a well-known 1979 Stanford study, supporters and opponents of the death penalty read the same mixed set of studies. Rather than moving closer together, both groups rated the evidence on their own side as more convincing and left more certain than before — a pattern known as attitude polarisation.

The bias is not simply a failure of intelligence. Several researchers argue that reasoning evolved partly to persuade others and defend our positions, which would explain why we are quick to spot weaknesses in opposing arguments but slow to notice them in our own. In a digital environment that rewards engagement, algorithms that serve us more of what we already click can intensify this tendency, though researchers still debate how strongly.

Remedies exist, but they require effort. One is to "consider the opposite": before reaching a conclusion, list reasons it might be mistaken. Another is to seek out the most persuasive version of an opposing view rather than its weakest caricature. Science itself can be seen as an institutional defence against the bias — a system in which claims must survive serious attempts at disproof.

None of these strategies makes us immune. But they shift the question we ask ourselves from "Can I believe this?" to "Must I believe this?" — a small change that separates thinking from merely agreeing. It is a habit worth practising, especially when the stakes are high.
tz: 在所有影響人類判斷的錯誤中，確認偏誤可能是最普遍的。它描述的是我們用迎合既有信念的方式去蒐集、解讀和回想證據的習慣。從內部看，這種偏誤很少讓人覺得是偏誤；它感覺起來就像「我是對的」。由於它安靜地運作，我們往往在別人身上比在自己身上更容易察覺它。
現代對它的研究始於心理學家彼得・華生。在他 1960 年首次發表的 2-4-6 實驗中，受試者藉由提出數列來找出規則。多數人形成一個狹窄的假設，然後只提出會證實它的數列，很少測試可能失敗的情況。他們的信心越來越高，理解卻停滯不前。華生後來的另一個謎題「選擇作業」顯示，即使受過教育的成年人，也很難看出哪些證據能推翻一個說法。
後續研究揭示了這種傾向有多根深柢固。在 1979 年史丹佛一項知名研究中，支持和反對死刑的人閱讀了同一組正反並陳的研究。兩組人不但沒有更接近，反而都認為支持自己一方的證據更有說服力，離開時比之前更加確信——這種模式被稱為態度兩極化。
這種偏誤不單純是智力不足。有些研究者主張，推理能力的演化有一部分是為了說服他人、捍衛自己的立場，這可以解釋為什麼我們很快就能挑出對立論點的弱點，卻很慢才注意到自己論點的弱點。在一個獎勵互動的數位環境中，給我們更多已點選內容的演算法可能加劇這種傾向，不過研究者對影響有多大仍有爭論。
補救方法是有的，但需要努力。其一是「考慮相反情況」：在下結論前，列出它可能錯誤的理由。其二是主動找出對立觀點最有說服力的版本，而不是它最弱、最扭曲的樣子。科學本身可以被視為一種對抗這種偏誤的制度——在這個系統裡，主張必須經得起認真的反駁嘗試。
這些策略沒有一個能讓我們完全免疫。但它們能把我們問自己的問題，從「我可以相信這個嗎？」轉變成「我非相信這個不可嗎？」——這個小小的改變，正是思考和單純附和的分界。這是一個值得練習的習慣，尤其是在事關重大的時候。

a.title: Fish for Tomorrow
text: November 21 is World Fisheries Day. It reminds us to take care of the fish in our seas, rivers and lakes.
Fish are an important food for billions of people. Millions of people also work as fishers.
But some people catch too many fish. Then there are not enough young fish to grow up and lay eggs. This is called overfishing.
Today, more than one third of the world's fish groups are overfished.
Some fish now come from fish farms. Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too.
If we only catch what the sea can replace, there will be fish for our children in the future.

b.title: Can the Oceans Keep Feeding Us?
text: World Fisheries Day, celebrated on November 21, was started in 1997 by fishing communities who met in New Delhi to call for responsible fishing around the world.
Fish and seafood are a major source of protein for billions of people, and fishing supports the jobs of tens of millions more, from small boats to large factory ships.

However, the oceans are under pressure. According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of the world's fish stocks are now overfished, meaning they are caught faster than they can reproduce.
Illegal fishing, harmful methods that destroy the seabed, and bycatch, the accidental capture of dolphins, turtles and sharks, make the problem worse.
Fish farming, or aquaculture, now produces more than half of the seafood we eat. It can reduce pressure on wild fish, but poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters.
Experts say the solution includes catch limits, protected marine areas and better tracking of where fish come from.

c.title: The Tragedy of the Open Sea
text: The ocean once seemed inexhaustible. Today, World Fisheries Day, marked each November 21 since 1997, serves as an annual reminder that it is not.

According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of assessed fish stocks are overfished, harvested faster than they can replenish themselves. The causes are partly technological: sonar, vast nets and subsidised fleets allow fishers to locate and remove fish with an efficiency earlier generations could not imagine.

Economists describe the dynamic as a 'tragedy of the commons'. Because no single fisher owns the sea, each has an incentive to catch as much as possible before others do, even though restraint would leave everyone better off.

Aquaculture has eased some pressure and now supplies most of the seafood humans eat, but it brings its own costs, including coastal pollution and, for some species, a reliance on wild fish ground into feed.

The most promising answers are institutional rather than technical: enforceable quotas, marine reserves where stocks can recover, and traceability that lets consumers reward responsible fleets. The sea can recover remarkably quickly, but only if people agree to share it.

a.title: Why Do We Forget So Fast?
text: Have you ever studied new words at night and forgotten most of them by the next week? You are not lazy. Your brain is just doing what brains do.

About 140 years ago, a German scientist named Hermann Ebbinghaus wanted to know how fast people forget. He tested himself. He learned long lists of made-up words, like "WID" and "ZOF," and checked how many he still remembered later.

His results surprised many people. He forgot a lot in the first hour, and even more in the first day. After that, he forgot more slowly. If you draw this on paper, it looks like a slide going down. We call it the forgetting curve.
But Ebbinghaus found good news, too. When he reviewed a list again, he learned it faster than the first time. Each review made the memory stronger and the curve flatter.
So, how can you remember new words? Don't study everything in one night. Review them after one day, then after a few days, and then after a week. This is called spaced review.
A little review, again and again, works better than a lot of study at one time.
tz: 你有沒有在晚上背了新單字，結果到了下週大部分都忘光了？你不是懶惰，你的大腦只是在做大腦會做的事。
大約 140 年前，一位名叫赫爾曼・艾賓浩斯的德國科學家想知道人忘記得有多快。他拿自己做實驗。他背了一長串編造出來的字，像是 "WID" 和 "ZOF"，然後檢查之後還記得多少。
他的結果讓很多人驚訝。他在第一個小時忘了很多，第一天又忘了更多。之後，他忘記的速度就變慢了。如果把這畫在紙上，看起來就像一座往下的溜滑梯。我們稱它為遺忘曲線。
不過艾賓浩斯也發現了好消息。當他再次複習一份清單時，他學得比第一次更快。每一次複習都讓記憶更牢固，曲線也更平緩。
那麼，要怎麼記住新單字呢？不要在一個晚上讀完所有東西。一天後複習一次，幾天後再複習，然後一週後再複習。這叫做間隔複習。
一點一點地反覆複習，比一次讀很多更有效。

b.title: The Forgetting Curve: How Memory Fades — and How to Stop It
text: Every student knows the frustration: you study a list of vocabulary carefully, feel confident, and then discover a week later that most of it has vanished. Almost everyone has felt it. This experience is not a personal failing. It follows a pattern first measured more than a century ago.

In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus set out to study memory scientifically. To avoid the influence of meaning, he invented thousands of nonsense syllables such as "DAX" and "BOK", memorised lists of them, and tested how much effort it took to relearn each list after different periods of time. He published his findings in 1885 in a short but influential book.

The results produced what is now called the forgetting curve. Memory dropped sharply within the first hour and continued to fall during the first day, after which the decline slowed. Ebbinghaus measured this through "savings" — how much less time relearning took — and found that the savings shrank quickly at first and then levelled off. In 2015, Dutch researchers repeated his experiment and obtained a very similar curve.

Crucially, Ebbinghaus also discovered how to fight forgetting. Each time he reviewed a list, it took less effort to relearn, and the memory lasted longer. Spreading reviews out over time worked better than cramming them into a single session — a finding now known as the spacing effect.

Modern research supports him. Studies show that students who space their practice, and who test themselves instead of simply rereading, remember far more weeks or even months later. Many flashcard apps now schedule reviews automatically, just before a word is likely to be forgotten.
The lesson is encouraging. Forgetting is natural, but it is not final. With short, well-timed reviews, information can move from fragile short-term memory into knowledge that lasts for years.
tz: 每個學生都懂那種挫折感：你仔細背了一張單字表、覺得很有把握，結果一週後發現大部分都不見了。幾乎每個人都有過這種感覺。這種經驗不是你個人的缺點，它遵循一個在一百多年前就首次被測量出來的模式。
1880 年代，德國心理學家赫爾曼・艾賓浩斯著手用科學方法研究記憶。為了避免字義的影響，他發明了數千個像 "DAX"、"BOK" 這樣沒有意義的音節，把它們背成清單，再測試經過不同時間後，重新記住每份清單需要花多少力氣。他在 1885 年把研究結果寫成一本篇幅不長、但影響深遠的書。
這些結果畫出了今天所說的遺忘曲線。記憶在第一個小時內急遽下降，第一天持續下滑，之後下降的速度才變慢。艾賓浩斯用「節省量」——重新學習少花了多少時間——來測量，發現節省量一開始縮減得很快，之後趨於平穩。2015 年，荷蘭研究者重做了他的實驗，得到非常相似的曲線。
關鍵是，艾賓浩斯也發現了對抗遺忘的方法。他每複習一次清單，重新學習就更省力，記憶也維持得更久。把複習分散在不同時間，比全部塞進同一次練習更有效——這個發現現在被稱為間隔效應。
現代研究支持他的看法。研究顯示，分散練習、並且用自我測驗代替單純重讀的學生，在幾週甚至幾個月後記得的東西多得多。現在很多單字卡 app 會自動安排複習時間，就在一個字快要被忘記之前。
這個教訓令人振奮。遺忘是自然的，但不是最終結果。只要做簡短、時機恰當的複習，資訊就能從脆弱的短期記憶，變成維持好幾年的知識。

c.title: Fighting the Forgetting Curve
text: Few scientific graphs are as quietly discouraging as the forgetting curve. Plotted with time along the bottom and retention up the side, it begins high and plunges, flattening only after much of what was learned has slipped away. Yet the same research that revealed the curve also revealed how to bend it — a discovery with direct consequences for anyone who studies.

The curve is the legacy of Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist who, in the early 1880s, made himself the sole subject of an unusually disciplined experiment. To strip away the influence of prior knowledge and meaning, he constructed roughly 2,300 nonsense syllables — consonant-vowel-consonant combinations such as "ZUG" — and memorised lists of them to the steady beat of a metronome. He then measured how much time he "saved" when relearning each list after intervals ranging from twenty minutes to a month.

His 1885 monograph, Memory, reported that savings fell steeply within the first hour, declined further over the first day, and then eroded only gradually. Remarkably, although the data came from a single subject, the pattern has survived scrutiny: a 2015 replication by researchers in Amsterdam produced a curve strikingly close to the original.

Ebbinghaus's more practical insight concerned repetition. Distributing study sessions over time produced more durable memories than massing them together, a phenomenon now called the spacing effect. Later work added a second principle, the testing effect: actively retrieving information, as in a quiz, strengthens memory far more than passively rereading it. Combined, spaced retrieval practice ranks among the most robust findings in educational psychology.

Why should spacing help? One explanation is that allowing some forgetting to occur makes each subsequent retrieval more effortful, and this "desirable difficulty" signals to the brain that the information is worth keeping. Massed study, by contrast, feels fluent and productive, which is precisely why students overestimate how much they have learned from it.

The implication is somewhat counterintuitive. The strategies that feel most effective in the moment — rereading highlighted notes, cramming the night before — are often the least effective over weeks and months, while the approaches that feel harder pay off later. Ebbinghaus could not have imagined the flashcard apps that now schedule reviews by algorithm, but they are built on the curve he traced by hand.
tz: 很少有科學圖表像遺忘曲線這樣默默令人洩氣。以時間為橫軸、記憶保留量為縱軸畫出來，它從高處開始驟降，直到學過的東西大多溜走後才變平。然而，揭示這條曲線的同一批研究，也揭示了如何把它「扳彎」——這個發現和每一個讀書的人都直接相關。
這條曲線是赫爾曼・艾賓浩斯留下的成果。這位德國心理學家在 1880 年代初，把自己當成一場紀律異常嚴格的實驗的唯一受試者。為了剝除先前知識和字義的影響，他編了大約 2,300 個無意義音節——像 "ZUG" 這樣「子音－母音－子音」的組合——並跟著節拍器穩定的拍子背誦清單。接著他測量，在二十分鐘到一個月不等的間隔後重新學習每份清單時，能「節省」多少時間。
他在 1885 年的專著《論記憶》中指出，節省量在第一個小時內急遽下降，第一天繼續減少，之後才逐漸流失。值得注意的是，雖然資料只來自一名受試者，這個模式卻經得起檢驗：2015 年阿姆斯特丹的研究者重做實驗，得到的曲線和原版驚人地相近。
艾賓浩斯更實用的洞見和「重複」有關。把讀書時段分散在不同時間，比集中在一起能產生更持久的記憶，這個現象現在被稱為間隔效應。後來的研究又加上第二個原則——測驗效應：主動提取資訊（例如做小考），比被動重讀更能強化記憶。兩者結合的「間隔提取練習」，是教育心理學中最穩固可靠的發現之一。
為什麼間隔有幫助？一種解釋是，讓部分遺忘發生，會使每一次後續的提取更費力，而這種「值得的困難」會向大腦發出訊號：這個資訊值得保留。相較之下，集中讀書感覺流暢又有效率，這正是學生會高估自己從中學到多少的原因。
這個結論有點違反直覺。當下感覺最有效的方法——重讀畫了重點的筆記、考前一晚臨時抱佛腳——在幾週和幾個月後往往效果最差；而感覺比較吃力的方法，日後才會有回報。艾賓浩斯不可能想像得到現在用演算法安排複習的單字卡 app，但它們正是建立在他親手描繪出的那條曲線上。

topic: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs: What Do People Really Need?

a.title: What Do People Need Most?
text: What do you need to be happy? Food? Friends? A good grade? In 1943, an American psychologist named Abraham Maslow shared an idea about human needs. Today, people often draw it as a pyramid.
At the bottom are our body's needs: food, water, sleep, and warm clothes. Above them is safety — a safe home and a safe place to live.
In the middle are love and belonging. We need family and friends, and we want to be part of a group, like a class or a team.
Next is esteem. This means we want to feel proud of ourselves, and we want others to respect us.
At the top is self-actualization. This is a long word, but the idea is simple: becoming the best person you can be — for example, by growing your talents and doing what you love.

Maslow said people usually need the lower parts first. It is hard to study well when you are hungry or scared. But later researchers say life is not always like a ladder. People can need friends and food at the same time.
tz: 你需要什麼才會快樂？食物？朋友？好成績？1943 年，一位名叫亞伯拉罕・馬斯洛的美國心理學家提出了一個關於人類需求的想法。今天，人們常把它畫成一座金字塔。
最底層是身體的需求：食物、水、睡眠和保暖的衣服。再往上是安全——一個安全的家、一個安全的居住環境。
中間是愛與歸屬。我們需要家人和朋友，也想成為一個群體的一份子，像是一個班級或一支隊伍。
再往上是尊重。這是說我們想對自己感到驕傲，也希望別人尊重我們。
最頂端是自我實現。這個詞很長，但意思很簡單：成為最好的自己——例如發揮自己的才能、做自己熱愛的事。
馬斯洛說，人通常會先需要較低層的東西。肚子餓或害怕的時候，很難好好讀書。但後來的研究者說，人生不一定像爬梯子。人可以同時需要朋友和食物。

b.title: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs: A Ladder, a Pyramid, or Something Else?
text: Why do people do what they do? In 1943, the American psychologist Abraham Maslow offered an influential answer in a paper called "A Theory of Human Motivation." He argued that human needs come in levels, and that people tend to focus on higher needs only after lower ones are reasonably satisfied.

The model is usually shown as a pyramid with five layers. At the base are physiological needs such as food, water and sleep. Next come safety needs — protection, stability and freedom from fear. The third level is love and belonging, including friendship and acceptance. Above that are esteem needs: self-respect, achievement and recognition from others. At the very top sits self-actualisation, the desire to fulfil one's potential.
Interestingly, Maslow himself never drew the famous pyramid. The diagram was popularised by others, especially in management training, in the decades after his paper appeared.

The theory's appeal is easy to understand. It offers a simple explanation for everyday experience: a student who is hungry, frightened or lonely will struggle to concentrate on algebra. For this reason, many schools provide free breakfasts, counselling and clubs, recognising that learning rests on a foundation of basic well-being. Teachers who notice a tired or anxious student often look first at these lower needs.

However, research has not supported a strict order. People in difficult circumstances often value friendship and meaning highly, and needs frequently overlap rather than being met one at a time. A large 2011 study across more than 120 countries found that the needs Maslow described appear to be universal, but that people can feel satisfaction from social and self-fulfilling needs even when basic needs are not fully met.
Many psychologists therefore treat the hierarchy less as a rigid ladder and more as a helpful map — a reminder that human beings need far more than food and shelter to flourish.
tz: 人為什麼會做他們所做的事？1943 年，美國心理學家亞伯拉罕・馬斯洛在一篇名為〈人類動機理論〉的論文中提出了一個影響深遠的答案。他主張人類的需求分成不同層次，人通常要等較低層的需求大致滿足後，才會專注在較高層的需求上。
這個模型通常被畫成一座五層的金字塔。最底層是生理需求，例如食物、水和睡眠。接著是安全需求——受到保護、生活穩定、免於恐懼。第三層是愛與歸屬，包括友誼和被接納。再上面是尊重需求：自尊、成就和他人的認可。最頂端是自我實現，也就是發揮自身潛能的渴望。
有趣的是，馬斯洛本人從來沒有畫過那座有名的金字塔。這張圖是在他的論文發表後的數十年間，由其他人——尤其是在管理培訓領域——推廣開來的。
這個理論受歡迎的原因不難理解。它為日常經驗提供了簡單的解釋：一個肚子餓、害怕或孤單的學生，很難專心學代數。因此，許多學校提供免費早餐、輔導和社團，因為他們認知到學習是建立在基本身心健康的基礎上。老師注意到學生疲倦或焦慮時，常常會先關心這些較低層的需求。
然而，研究並不支持嚴格的順序。處境艱難的人往往非常重視友誼和意義，而且各種需求經常是重疊的，而不是一次滿足一個。2011 年一項涵蓋超過 120 個國家的大型研究發現，馬斯洛描述的需求似乎是普世的，但即使基本需求沒有完全被滿足，人們仍能從社交和自我實現的需求中得到滿足感。
因此，許多心理學家不把這個層次理論當成僵化的梯子，而是當成一張有用的地圖——提醒我們，人類要過得好，需要的遠不只是食物和住所。

c.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Rethinking Maslow
text: Few ideas from psychology have travelled as far as Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Introduced in his 1943 paper "A Theory of Human Motivation", it now appears in textbooks on business, nursing, education and marketing, almost always as a five-tiered pyramid. Its familiarity, however, can obscure both what Maslow actually proposed and what later research has made of it.

Maslow's central claim was that human motivation is organised around needs of differing urgency. Physiological needs come first, followed by safety, love and belonging, and esteem; only when these "deficiency needs" are adequately met, he suggested, does the drive toward self-actualisation — the realisation of one's full potential — become dominant. Crucially, he described this ordering as relative rather than absolute, noting that most people are partially satisfied at several levels simultaneously. He also admitted that the order could be reversed for some individuals.

The pyramid itself was not his. Scholars have traced the diagram to management consultants in the late 1950s and 1960s, who found in its tidy geometry an appealing teaching tool. In the process, a nuanced theory hardened into a staircase that people supposedly climb one step at a time.

Empirical tests have been mixed. Researchers have found little evidence that needs are satisfied in a fixed sequence, and critics have argued that the model reflects the individualistic values of mid-century America — placing personal fulfilment at the summit, whereas many cultures emphasise family and community. A 2011 analysis of survey data from 123 countries offered a more balanced verdict: the needs Maslow listed do appear across cultures, yet satisfaction of "higher" needs could contribute to well-being even when basic needs went unmet.

More recently, some psychologists have proposed revisions. One influential 2010 update by Douglas Kenrick and colleagues, grounded in evolutionary theory, replaced self-actualisation at the top with goals related to finding a partner and raising children. Others have suggested picturing the needs as overlapping waves rather than separate floors.

Perhaps the most enduring value of Maslow's work lies in its humane premise rather than its geometry. By insisting that psychology study healthy, growing people and not only illness, he helped inspire what later became known as positive psychology. Read in that spirit, the hierarchy is less a staircase than a reminder that people need security, connection and meaning together, not in turn.
tz: 很少有心理學概念像亞伯拉罕・馬斯洛的需求層次理論傳得這麼遠。它在 1943 年的論文〈人類動機理論〉中被提出，如今出現在商業、護理、教育和行銷的教科書裡，而且幾乎總是以五層金字塔的樣子出現。然而，它的耳熟能詳，可能反而掩蓋了馬斯洛真正提出了什麼，以及後來的研究如何看待它。
馬斯洛的核心主張是：人類動機是圍繞著緊迫程度不同的需求組織起來的。生理需求排第一，接著是安全、愛與歸屬，以及尊重；他認為，只有當這些「匱乏需求」被充分滿足時，追求自我實現——充分發揮個人潛能——的動力才會成為主導。關鍵在於，他把這個順序描述為相對的而非絕對的，並指出大多數人在好幾個層次上同時得到部分滿足。他也承認，對某些人來說順序可能會顛倒。
那座金字塔其實不是他畫的。學者追溯這張圖的來源，發現是 1950 年代末和 1960 年代的管理顧問，他們覺得這個整齊的幾何圖形是很吸引人的教學工具。在這個過程中，一個細膩的理論被固化成一座樓梯，彷彿人們應該一次爬一階。
實證檢驗的結果好壞參半。研究者幾乎找不到證據顯示需求是按固定順序被滿足的；批評者也認為，這個模型反映的是二十世紀中葉美國的個人主義價值觀——把個人成就放在頂端，而許多文化重視的是家庭和社群。2011 年一項分析 123 個國家調查資料的研究給出了較平衡的結論：馬斯洛列出的需求確實跨文化存在，但即使基本需求沒有被滿足，「較高層」需求的滿足仍能增進幸福感。
近年來，有些心理學家提出了修訂版。2010 年道格拉斯・肯瑞克等人以演化理論為基礎提出一個影響很大的更新版，把頂端的自我實現換成與尋找伴侶、養育孩子有關的目標。也有人建議把這些需求想像成彼此重疊的波浪，而不是分開的樓層。
馬斯洛的研究最持久的價值，或許在於它充滿人性的前提，而不在於那個幾何圖形。他堅持心理學應該研究健康、成長中的人，而不只是疾病，因而啟發了後來被稱為正向心理學的領域。用這種精神來讀，這個層次理論與其說是一座樓梯，不如說是一個提醒：人們需要的是安全、連結和意義同時存在，而不是一個接一個。
