topic: The Placebo Effect: When Belief Becomes Medicine
zh: 安慰劑效應：當「相信」變成了藥
discuss: Have you ever felt better just because someone said a treatment would help?
Should doctors ever give patients placebos? Why or why not?
How could the nocebo effect affect students before an exam?

a.title: The Medicine With Nothing Inside
text: Imagine you have a headache. A doctor gives you a small white pill and says, "This will help." Twenty minutes later, you feel better. But the pill was only sugar! This is called the placebo effect.
A placebo is a fake treatment. It looks like real medicine, but it has no medicine inside. Still, many people feel better after they take one.
How can this happen? When we believe something will help, our brain can change how we feel. Hope and calm can make pain feel smaller.

Doctors use placebos in tests of new medicines. One group gets the real medicine, and another group gets a placebo. The people in the test do not know which group they are in. If the real medicine works much better, scientists know it is useful.
There is also a "nocebo" effect. If people expect to feel bad, they sometimes really do feel worse! For example, some people feel sick after reading about side effects.
The placebo effect cannot cure serious illnesses, so we still need real medicine. But it shows us that our minds and bodies are closely connected.
tz: 想像你頭痛。醫生給你一顆白色小藥丸，說：「這會有幫助。」二十分鐘後，你覺得好多了。但那顆藥只是糖做的！這就叫安慰劑效應。
安慰劑是假的治療。它看起來像真的藥，但裡面沒有任何藥物。儘管如此，很多人吃了以後還是覺得好一些。
這怎麼可能？當我們相信某樣東西會有幫助，大腦可以改變我們的感受。希望和平靜能讓疼痛感覺變小。
醫生在測試新藥時會用安慰劑。一組人拿到真的藥，另一組拿到安慰劑。參加測試的人不知道自己在哪一組。如果真藥的效果好很多，科學家就知道它有用。
還有一種「反安慰劑」效應。如果人們預期會不舒服，有時候真的會覺得更糟！例如，有些人讀了副作用說明後就覺得不舒服。
安慰劑效應不能治好嚴重的疾病，所以我們還是需要真的藥。但它讓我們看到，心靈和身體是緊密相連的。

ph.ex: I always feel better after a good night's sleep.
ph.exzh: 睡個好覺後我總是感覺好一點。

ph.ex: This cake looks like a real cat!
ph.exzh: 這個蛋糕看起來像一隻真的貓！

ph.ex: Sleep and good grades are closely connected.
ph.exzh: 睡眠和好成績是緊密相連的。

b.title: The Placebo Effect: When Belief Becomes Medicine
text: In medicine, a placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient — a sugar pill, a saltwater injection, even a fake operation. Logically, it should do nothing. Yet patients who receive placebos often report real improvements, especially in symptoms such as pain, nausea and tiredness. This puzzling result is known as the placebo effect.

Scientists believe the effect comes largely from expectation. When people expect relief, the brain can release its own natural painkillers and change how strongly signals from the body are felt. The setting matters too: a confident doctor, a clinic that looks professional, or even an expensive-looking pill can strengthen the response.

Because of this, placebos play a central role in research. In a typical trial, one group receives the new drug and another receives a placebo, and ideally neither patients nor doctors know who got which. Only if the drug clearly outperforms the placebo is it considered effective.

Placebos also have a dark twin, the nocebo effect. Patients warned about possible side effects sometimes develop them even when they are taking a pill with nothing in it. In some trials, a surprising number of people taking placebos stop because of side effects they believe the pill is causing.

Perhaps most surprising, some studies have found that placebos can help even when patients are told openly that they are taking one. In a 2010 Harvard study of people with a bowel condition, those given "honest" placebos reported greater improvement than those who received no treatment. Researchers think the ritual of taking a pill may itself bring comfort.

None of this means that placebos can shrink tumours or fight infections. What they reveal instead is how closely the mind and body work together — and why the way care is delivered can matter almost as much as what is delivered.
tz: 在醫學上，安慰劑是沒有有效成分的治療——一顆糖錠、一針食鹽水，甚至是一場假手術。照理說，它應該毫無作用。然而，接受安慰劑的病人常常回報真的有改善，尤其是在疼痛、噁心和疲倦等症狀上。這個令人費解的結果被稱為安慰劑效應。
科學家認為，這個效應主要來自「預期」。當人們預期會舒緩時，大腦能釋放自己的天然止痛物質，並改變我們感受身體訊號的強度。環境也有影響：一位有自信的醫生、一間看起來很專業的診所，甚至一顆看起來很貴的藥，都能讓反應更強。
正因如此，安慰劑在研究中扮演核心角色。在典型的試驗裡，一組人服用新藥，另一組服用安慰劑，理想上病人和醫生都不知道誰拿到哪一種。只有當新藥明顯比安慰劑有效時，它才會被認為有效。
安慰劑還有一個黑暗的雙胞胎——反安慰劑效應。被告知可能有副作用的病人，有時即使吃的是什麼都沒有的藥丸，也真的出現了那些副作用。在某些試驗中，有不少服用安慰劑的人，因為他們以為是藥丸造成的副作用而退出。
也許最令人驚訝的是，有些研究發現，即使明白告訴病人他們吃的是安慰劑，安慰劑仍然有幫助。在 2010 年哈佛一項針對腸道疾病患者的研究中，服用「誠實」安慰劑的人，改善程度比完全沒接受治療的人更大。研究者認為，「吃藥」這個儀式本身可能就帶來安慰。
這些都不代表安慰劑能讓腫瘤縮小或對抗感染。它真正揭示的是心靈和身體合作得有多緊密——以及為什麼「照護的方式」幾乎和「給了什麼治療」一樣重要。

c.title: Belief, Biology and the Sugar Pill
text: Few findings in medicine are as unsettling, or as useful, as the placebo effect. A substance with no pharmacological power — sugar, starch, saline — should leave the body exactly as it found it. Yet across thousands of studies, a meaningful share of patients given such dummies report less pain, better sleep or reduced nausea. The effect is strongest for symptoms the brain itself helps to shape, and weakest for diseases that progress regardless of mood.

The phenomenon entered modern medicine dramatically in 1955, when the anaesthetist Henry Beecher published "The Powerful Placebo", estimating that about a third of patients responded to inert treatments. Later researchers argued that Beecher had overstated the case, since some of the improvement he counted was simply illness running its natural course. Even so, carefully controlled experiments have confirmed that expectation can alter brain chemistry, for instance by triggering the release of endorphins, the body's own painkillers.

This is precisely why the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial became medicine's gold standard. In such trials, neither the patients nor the doctors know who has received what, so that hope cannot quietly tip the results. If patients improve simply because they believe they are being treated, then a new drug proves its worth only by beating that belief, not by beating nothing.

The effect also has a troubling mirror image. In the nocebo effect, negative expectations produce real symptoms: participants warned about side effects frequently report them while taking inert pills. Some researchers suspect that the way risks are described on medicine packaging and in the news may quietly worsen how people feel. In some trials, a noticeable share of placebo takers drop out because of such side effects.

Recent work has complicated the old assumption that a placebo must involve deception. In "open-label" studies, patients told plainly that they were receiving sugar pills still reported benefits for conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and chronic back pain. Ritual, attention and the simple act of taking care of oneself may carry their own therapeutic weight.

None of this licenses wishful thinking: placebos do not cure cancer or clear infections. What they demonstrate is that healing is not purely mechanical. How treatment is delivered — with honesty, warmth and clear explanation — may be part of the treatment itself. Doctors who ignore this risk leaving one of their most powerful tools unused.
tz: 醫學上很少有發現，像安慰劑效應這樣既令人不安又如此有用。一種沒有藥理作用的物質——糖、澱粉、食鹽水——照理應該讓身體維持原樣。然而，在成千上萬的研究中，有相當比例服用這類「假藥」的病人回報疼痛減輕、睡得更好或噁心減少。這個效應對大腦本身參與塑造的症狀最強，對不管心情如何都會惡化的疾病則最弱。
這個現象在 1955 年戲劇性地進入現代醫學：麻醉科醫師亨利・畢傑發表〈強大的安慰劑〉，估計約三分之一的病人對無活性的治療有反應。後來的研究者認為畢傑誇大了，因為他計入的部分「改善」，其實只是疾病自然好轉。即便如此，嚴謹控制的實驗已證實，預期能改變大腦化學，例如觸發腦內啡——身體自己的止痛物質——的釋放。
這正是為什麼隨機、雙盲、安慰劑對照試驗會成為醫學的黃金標準。在這類試驗中，病人和醫生都不知道誰接受了什麼，好讓希望無法悄悄左右結果。如果病人只因為相信自己在接受治療就會好轉，那麼新藥要證明自己的價值，就必須打敗這份「相信」，而不只是打敗「什麼都沒有」。
這個效應還有一個令人困擾的鏡像。在反安慰劑效應中，負面預期會造成真實的症狀：被提醒可能有副作用的受試者，即使服用無活性的藥丸，也常常回報出現了那些副作用。有些研究者懷疑，藥品包裝和新聞描述風險的方式，可能會悄悄讓人感覺更糟。在某些試驗中，有相當比例服用安慰劑的人因為這類副作用而退出。
近年的研究動搖了「安慰劑一定要靠欺騙」這個舊觀念。在「開放標籤」研究中，病人被清楚告知吃的是糖錠，仍然在腸躁症和慢性背痛等病症上回報有幫助。儀式感、被關注，以及「照顧自己」這個單純的行為，本身可能就具有療效。
這些都不是放任一廂情願的理由：安慰劑治不了癌症，也清除不了感染。它們證明的是，療癒並不純粹是機械性的。治療如何被給予——誠實、溫暖、清楚的說明——可能本身就是治療的一部分。忽略這一點的醫生，等於讓自己最有力的工具之一閒置不用。

topic: The Sunk Cost Fallacy: Why It's So Hard to Let Go
zh: 沉沒成本謬誤：為什麼我們總是放不下？
discuss: Have you ever kept doing something only because you had already spent time or money on it?
When is it good to keep going, and when is it better to stop?
Use the question 'Would I start this today?' on one of your own hobbies or plans.

a.title: Why Is It So Hard to Stop?
text: You paid 300 dollars for a movie ticket. Thirty minutes later, you know the movie is terrible. Do you stay or leave? Many people stay. They say, "I already paid for it!"
This is called the sunk cost fallacy. A "sunk cost" is money, time, or effort that you have already spent and cannot get back. A "fallacy" is a mistake in thinking.
The money for the ticket is gone, whether you stay or leave. So the real question is: "What is the best way to use the next ninety minutes?" Staying makes you lose your time, too.

In a famous 1985 study, people imagined they had bought two ski trips for the same weekend: one for 100 dollars and one for 50 dollars. They were told they would like the cheaper trip more. But more than half of them chose the expensive trip, because they had paid more for it.
We do this in many places. We keep playing a boring game because we spent hours on it, or we finish a huge meal because we paid for it.
Next time, try asking: "If I were starting today, would I still choose this?" Forget the past, and choose what is best for your future.
tz: 你花了 300 元買電影票。三十分鐘後，你知道這部電影很難看。你要留下來還是離開？很多人會留下來。他們說：「我都已經付錢了！」
這就叫沉沒成本謬誤。「沉沒成本」是你已經花掉、拿不回來的錢、時間或心力。「謬誤」則是一種思考上的錯誤。
不管你留下還是離開，買票的錢都已經沒了。所以真正的問題是：「接下來的九十分鐘怎麼用最好？」留下來會讓你連時間也賠掉。
在 1985 年一項著名的研究中，受試者想像自己在同一個週末買了兩趟滑雪旅行：一趟 100 美元、一趟 50 美元。他們被告知自己會比較喜歡便宜的那趟。但超過一半的人選了貴的那趟，因為他們在那趟花了比較多錢。
我們在很多地方都會這樣做。我們繼續玩一款無聊的遊戲，因為已經在上面花了好幾個小時；或者把一大份餐點吃完，因為已經付了錢。
下次試著問自己：「如果我今天才開始，我還會選這個嗎？」忘掉過去，選擇對你的未來最好的事。

b.title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy: When the Past Controls the Present
text: Picture a student who has spent two years learning the violin. She no longer enjoys it and would rather join the basketball team, yet she keeps going to lessons. "I can't quit now," she says. "Think of all the time and money I've put in." Her reasoning sounds natural, but economists and psychologists see a classic error at work: the sunk cost fallacy.

A sunk cost is a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever we decide next. Strictly speaking, such costs should not affect future choices; only future costs and benefits can change the outcome. Yet people regularly let past investments drive present decisions.

In a well-known 1985 study, psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer asked people to imagine they had accidentally booked two non-refundable ski trips for the same weekend: one costing 100 dollars, the other 50. Participants were told they would enjoy the cheaper trip more. Even so, more than half chose the expensive one, apparently to avoid "wasting" the larger sum.

Why are we so reluctant to walk away? One reason is that losses feel more painful than equal gains feel pleasant, so abandoning a project feels like admitting a loss. Another is that we want to appear consistent, both to others and to ourselves.

The fallacy can be costly on a large scale. The Concorde, a supersonic passenger jet developed by Britain and France, continued to receive funding long after it was clear the project would not make money — which is why the error is sometimes called the "Concorde fallacy."

Avoiding the trap does not mean giving up whenever things get hard; persistence is often valuable. The key is to base decisions on the future rather than the past. A useful test is to ask: "If I had invested nothing so far, would I choose to start this today?"
tz: 想像一個學了兩年小提琴的學生。她已經不再喜歡拉琴，比較想加入籃球隊，卻還是繼續去上課。「我現在不能放棄，」她說，「想想我投入了多少時間和金錢。」她的理由聽起來很自然，但經濟學家和心理學家看到的是一個典型的錯誤正在作祟：沉沒成本謬誤。
沉沒成本是已經付出、不管接下來怎麼決定都收不回來的成本。嚴格來說，這類成本不應該影響未來的選擇；只有未來的成本和效益才能改變結果。然而，人們常常讓過去的投資主導現在的決定。
在 1985 年一項知名研究中，心理學家哈爾・阿克斯和凱瑟琳・布魯默請受試者想像，自己不小心在同一個週末訂了兩趟不能退款的滑雪旅行：一趟 100 美元，另一趟 50 美元。受試者被告知他們會比較喜歡便宜的那趟。即便如此，超過一半的人還是選了貴的那趟，顯然是為了避免「浪費」比較大的那筆錢。
為什麼我們這麼不願意放手？原因之一是，損失帶來的痛苦，比同等收穫帶來的快樂更強烈，所以放棄一個計畫感覺就像承認自己虧了。另一個原因是，我們希望在別人和自己眼中顯得前後一致。
這種謬誤在大規模時可能代價高昂。協和號是英國和法國共同研發的超音速客機，即使早已清楚這個計畫不會賺錢，它仍持續獲得資金——這就是為什麼這種錯誤有時被稱為「協和謬誤」。
避開這個陷阱，並不代表遇到困難就放棄；堅持往往是有價值的。關鍵在於根據未來、而不是過去來做決定。一個有用的檢驗是問自己：「如果到目前為止我什麼都沒投入，我今天還會選擇開始做這件事嗎？」

c.title: Sunk Costs and the Psychology of Not Letting Go
text: Economics offers a deceptively simple rule for decision-making: ignore what cannot be changed. Money already spent, hours already invested and effort already expended are "sunk"; they are gone regardless of what we do next, and so they should carry no weight in choosing what to do now. Human beings, however, find this rule remarkably hard to follow.

The sunk cost fallacy describes our tendency to continue an endeavour because of what we have already put into it rather than what we expect to get out of it. A diner who forces down an unpleasant meal "because it was expensive", a company that pours money into a failing product, a government that prolongs a costly project to justify earlier spending — all are reasoning backward from the past instead of forward from the present.

Psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer documented the effect in a series of studies published in 1985. In one field experiment, theatre-goers who had been randomly charged full price for season tickets attended more performances in the first half of the season than those who had received discounts, even though the plays were identical. Having paid more, they seemed determined to "get their money's worth." The difference faded later in the season, suggesting that the pull of a sunk cost weakens over time.

Several mechanisms appear to drive this behaviour. Loss aversion, the finding that losses loom larger than equivalent gains, makes abandoning an investment feel like accepting a painful loss. A desire for self-justification also plays a role: walking away can feel like admitting that the original decision was a mistake. Social pressure adds a further layer, since persisting can look like commitment while quitting can look like weakness.

Interestingly, the picture is not entirely one-sided. Some researchers note that what looks irrational in a laboratory may sometimes be sensible in real life — for example, when honouring past commitments protects a person's reputation for reliability. Persistence, too, is often how difficult but worthwhile goals are achieved. The challenge lies in telling the two apart.

The practical lesson, then, is not "always quit" but "decide afresh." Asking whether you would begin a project today, knowing what you now know, strips away the emotional weight of the past and leaves only the question that matters: what course of action offers the best future from here?
tz: 經濟學提供了一條看似簡單的決策規則：忽略無法改變的事。已經花掉的錢、已經投入的時數、已經耗費的心力都是「沉沒」的；不管我們接下來怎麼做，它們都已經回不來了，因此在決定現在該怎麼做時，它們不該占任何分量。然而，人類發現這條規則出奇地難以遵守。
沉沒成本謬誤描述的是我們傾向於因為已經投入了多少，而不是預期能得到多少，就繼續一件事。勉強吃完難吃餐點「因為它很貴」的用餐者、把錢不斷砸進失敗產品的公司、為了替先前的支出辯護而延長昂貴計畫的政府——全都是從過去往回推理，而不是從現在往前看。
心理學家哈爾・阿克斯和凱瑟琳・布魯默在 1985 年發表的一系列研究中記錄了這個效應。在一項實地實驗中，被隨機收取全額季票費用的劇院觀眾，在演出季上半段看戲的場次，比拿到折扣的觀眾多，儘管演出完全相同。付了比較多錢的人，似乎決心要「把錢看回本」。這個差距到演出季後半段就消失了，顯示沉沒成本的拉力會隨時間減弱。
有幾種機制似乎在驅動這種行為。損失規避——也就是損失看起來比同等收穫更巨大的發現——讓放棄一項投資感覺像是接受痛苦的損失。自我辯護的欲望也扮演了角色：放手可能感覺像是承認當初的決定是錯的。社會壓力又多加了一層，因為堅持下去看起來像是有承諾，而放棄則看起來像是軟弱。
有趣的是，事情並非完全一面倒。有些研究者指出，在實驗室裡看似不理性的行為，在現實生活中有時可能是明智的——例如，信守過去的承諾能保護一個人「可靠」的名聲。堅持，也往往是達成困難但值得的目標的方法。難處在於如何分辨這兩者。
那麼，實際的教訓並不是「永遠放棄」，而是「重新決定」。問自己：以我現在知道的一切，今天還會不會開始這個計畫？這能剝除過去帶來的情緒重量，只留下真正重要的問題：從現在起，哪一條路能帶來最好的未來？

topic: The Tragedy of the Commons: When Sharing Goes Wrong
zh: 公地悲劇：大家共用的東西為什麼會被用壞？

a.title: Too Many Cows on One Field
text: Imagine a big green field in a village. Everyone in the village can use it. Each family puts some cows on the field to eat the grass.
One farmer thinks, "If I add one more cow, I will get more milk and money." This sounds smart. But every farmer has the same idea, so soon there are too many cows.
The cows eat all the grass, and it cannot grow back. In the end, there is no food for any cow, and everyone loses.

This story is called the tragedy of the commons. A "commons" is something that many people share, like a field, the ocean, or clean air. In 1968, an American scientist named Garrett Hardin made the idea famous.
We can see it today. When too many boats catch fish in the same sea, the fish disappear. When people throw trash in a park, the park becomes dirty for everyone.
But there is hope. A scientist named Elinor Ostrom showed that many communities make fair rules together and take good care of what they share. In 2009, she won a Nobel Prize for this work.

牛把草全吃光了，草也長不回來。最後，沒有任何一頭牛有東西吃，每個人都損失了。
這個故事叫做公地悲劇。「公地」是很多人共用的東西，像是草地、海洋或乾淨的空氣。1968 年，一位名叫蓋瑞特・哈丁的美國科學家讓這個概念變得有名。
今天我們也看得到這種事。當太多船在同一片海捕魚，魚就消失了。當人們在公園亂丟垃圾，公園就對每個人來說都變髒了。
但還是有希望的。一位名叫伊莉諾・歐斯壯的科學家證明，許多社群會一起訂定公平的規則，好好照顧大家共用的東西。2009 年，她因為這項研究獲得了諾貝爾獎。

b.title: The Tragedy of the Commons: When Sharing Goes Wrong
text: In 1968, the American ecologist Garrett Hardin published a short essay in the journal Science that would become one of the most cited articles of its kind. Its title, "The Tragedy of the Commons," named a problem that appears wherever people share a limited resource.

Hardin borrowed an example from the nineteenth-century writer William Forster Lloyd. Picture a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding another animal, while the cost — slightly less grass for everyone — is shared by the whole group. From each individual's point of view, adding animals makes sense. But when everyone follows the same logic, the pasture is overgrazed and eventually ruined. The "tragedy" is that sensible individual choices can produce a result that nobody wants.

Modern examples are easy to find. Fish stocks in many oceans have collapsed because of overfishing; the cod fishery off Newfoundland, Canada, was closed in 1992 after centuries of plenty. Traffic jams, crowded national parks and the carbon dioxide released into our shared atmosphere follow a similar pattern.
Hardin himself was pessimistic. He doubted that people would limit themselves voluntarily, and he believed the only solutions were government control or dividing the commons into private property.

Later research told a more hopeful story. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom studied fisheries, forests and irrigation systems around the world and found that local communities often manage shared resources successfully for generations. They do so by setting clear rules, monitoring use and applying fair penalties to those who break the rules. In 2009, her work earned her the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, making her the first woman to receive it.
The tragedy of the commons, then, is a warning rather than a fate. Shared resources can be destroyed — but with trust and good rules, they can also be protected.
tz: 1968 年，美國生態學家蓋瑞特・哈丁在《科學》期刊發表了一篇短文，後來成為同類文章中被引用最多的文章之一。它的標題〈公地悲劇〉，點出了一個只要有人共用有限資源就會出現的問題。
哈丁借用了十九世紀作家威廉・佛斯特・洛伊德的例子。想像一片對所有牧人開放的牧場。每個牧人多放一頭牲畜，就能得到全部的好處，而代價——每個人的草都少了一點——則由整個群體分攤。從每個人的角度來看，多放牲畜是合理的。但當每個人都照同樣的邏輯做，牧場就會被過度放牧，最終毀掉。「悲劇」在於：每個人合理的選擇，可能產生一個沒有人想要的結果。
現代的例子俯拾皆是。許多海洋的魚群因為過度捕撈而崩潰；加拿大紐芬蘭外海的鱈魚漁場，在漁產豐富了好幾個世紀之後，於 1992 年被迫關閉。塞車、擁擠的國家公園，以及排放到我們共享大氣中的二氧化碳，都遵循類似的模式。
哈丁本人很悲觀。他懷疑人們會自願節制，並認為唯一的解決方法是由政府控管，或是把公地分割成私人財產。
後來的研究則講述了一個比較有希望的故事。政治學家伊莉諾・歐斯壯研究了世界各地的漁場、森林和灌溉系統，發現地方社群常常能成功管理共享資源好幾個世代。他們的做法是訂定清楚的規則、監督使用情況，並對違規的人施以公平的處罰。2009 年，她的研究為她贏得諾貝爾經濟學獎，使她成為第一位獲得這個獎項的女性。
所以，公地悲劇是一個警告，而不是注定的命運。共享資源可能被摧毀——但只要有信任和好的規則，它們也能被保護。

c.title: Beyond the Tragedy: Rethinking the Commons
text: Few essays have shaped environmental thinking as profoundly as Garrett Hardin's "The Tragedy of the Commons", published in Science in 1968. Its central image — a pasture open to all, ruined because each herder rationally adds one more animal — offered a stark explanation for overfishing, pollution and population growth. The logic seemed airtight: when benefits are private but costs are shared, individuals have every incentive to overuse a common resource.

Hardin drew two prescriptions from this logic. Either the commons must be placed under the coercive control of the state, or it must be divided into private property whose owners bear the full consequences of their decisions. Appeals to conscience, he argued, were futile, since those who restrained themselves would simply be outcompeted by those who did not.

The diagnosis remains relevant. The collapse of the northern cod off Newfoundland, which forced Canada to impose a moratorium in 1992 and cost tens of thousands of jobs, is often cited as a textbook case. At a global scale, the atmosphere functions as a commons into which every nation can emit carbon while bearing only a fraction of the resulting harm.

Yet Hardin's account has been heavily criticised, most influentially by the political scientist Elinor Ostrom. Drawing on fieldwork from Swiss alpine meadows to Japanese forests and Philippine irrigation systems, she documented communities that had sustained shared resources for centuries without either privatisation or top-down control. Her findings suggested that ordinary people were far more capable of cooperation than Hardin had assumed.

Ostrom identified recurring "design principles" behind these successes: clearly defined boundaries, rules suited to local conditions, participation of users in making those rules, effective monitoring, graduated sanctions for violators and accessible ways to resolve conflicts. Her work earned her the 2009 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, the first awarded to a woman. Critics also noted that Hardin had confused a genuine commons, governed by a community, with an unregulated "open-access" resource that no one manages at all.

The distinction matters. The tragedy Hardin described is real, but it is not inevitable; it is most likely where trust, communication and enforceable rules are absent. The lesson for global challenges such as climate change is therefore neither despair nor complacency, but the harder task of building institutions capable of cooperation at an unprecedented scale.
tz: 很少有文章像蓋瑞特・哈丁 1968 年發表在《科學》期刊上的〈公地悲劇〉這樣，深深影響了環境思想。它的核心意象——一片對所有人開放的牧場，因為每個牧人都理性地多放一頭牲畜而被毀——為過度捕撈、污染和人口成長提供了一個鮮明的解釋。這套邏輯看似天衣無縫：當好處歸個人、代價卻由大家分攤時，每個人都有充分的誘因過度使用共有資源。
哈丁從這套邏輯得出兩帖藥方。要嘛把公地交由國家強制控管，要嘛把它分割成私人財產，讓所有者承擔自己決定的全部後果。他主張，訴諸良知是徒勞的，因為那些自我節制的人，只會被不節制的人比下去。

然而，哈丁的論述受到大量批評，其中影響最大的是政治學家伊莉諾・歐斯壯。她根據從瑞士高山草原到日本森林、再到菲律賓灌溉系統的田野調查，記錄了許多社群在既沒有私有化、也沒有由上而下控管的情況下，維持共享資源長達數百年。她的發現顯示，一般人合作的能力遠比哈丁假設的強得多。
歐斯壯歸納出這些成功案例背後反覆出現的「設計原則」：清楚界定的邊界、適合在地條件的規則、使用者參與訂定規則、有效的監督、對違規者的漸進式制裁，以及容易取得的衝突解決方式。她的研究為她贏得 2009 年諾貝爾經濟學獎，是第一位獲獎的女性。批評者也指出，哈丁把由社群治理的真正公地，和沒有人管理、不受規範的「開放取用」資源混為一談。
這個區別很重要。哈丁描述的悲劇是真實的，但並非無可避免；它最可能發生在缺乏信任、溝通和可執行規則的地方。因此，對氣候變遷這類全球挑戰而言，該得到的教訓既不是絕望、也不是自滿，而是更艱難的任務：建立能在前所未有的規模上促成合作的制度。

a.title: Why the First Number Sticks
text: You see a jacket in a shop. The tag says, "Was 3,000 dollars — now only 1,500!" You think, "What a great deal!" But is it? Maybe the jacket was never worth 3,000 dollars.
This is the anchoring effect. An anchor is a heavy object that stops a ship from moving. In our minds, the first number we see can work like an anchor. It holds our thinking in one place.

In 1974, two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, did a famous test. People spun a wheel with numbers on it. The wheel always stopped at 10 or 65. Then people guessed what percent of the countries in the United Nations were in Africa.

The results were surprising. People who saw 10 guessed about 25 percent. People who saw 65 guessed about 45 percent. The number on the wheel had nothing to do with the question, but it still changed their answers!
Shops, sellers, and even friends use anchors. When you buy something, think about what it is really worth to you — not just the first number you see.
tz: 你在店裡看到一件夾克。標籤上寫著：「原價 3,000 元——現在只要 1,500！」你心想：「太划算了！」但真的是這樣嗎？也許這件夾克從來就不值 3,000 元。
這就是錨定效應。錨是一種能讓船停住不動的重物。在我們的腦袋裡，看到的第一個數字就像一個錨，把我們的想法固定在某個地方。
1974 年，兩位心理學家阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼做了一個有名的實驗。受試者轉動一個寫著數字的轉盤，轉盤總是停在 10 或 65。接著，受試者要猜聯合國的會員國中，有百分之多少在非洲。
結果令人驚訝。看到 10 的人猜大約 25%；看到 65 的人猜大約 45%。轉盤上的數字和問題毫無關係，卻還是改變了他們的答案！
商店、賣家，甚至朋友都會用「錨」。買東西時，想想它對你真正值多少——而不只是看到的第一個數字。

b.title: The Anchoring Effect: How First Numbers Bend Our Judgement
text: Ask a friend whether the Great Wall of China is longer or shorter than 100 kilometres, and then ask how long they think it is. Ask another friend the same question with 50,000 kilometres instead. Their estimates will probably be very different, even though the first number was just a suggestion. This tendency to rely too heavily on an initial value is called the anchoring effect.

In a classic 1974 study, the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman asked participants to spin a wheel of fortune that had been secretly set to stop at either 10 or 65. Participants then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. The median estimate was 25 percent for those who saw 10 and 45 percent for those who saw 65 — although everyone believed the wheel was random.

Why are we so easily anchored? One explanation is that we start from the anchor and adjust, but stop adjusting too early. Another is that the anchor makes information consistent with it come to mind more easily. Either way, the first number shapes where we end up.

Anchoring has real consequences. In negotiations, the first offer often influences the final price. Shops display high "original prices" so that discounts look generous. Studies have even found that suggested numbers can affect the decisions of experienced professionals, such as judges deciding sentences and estate agents valuing homes.

The effect is hard to escape, but not impossible. Experts recommend forming your own estimate before you hear anyone else's, researching independent information, and deliberately considering reasons why the anchor might be wrong.
The next time a number arrives first, treat it as a starting point to question, not a fact to accept. A little doubt at the right moment can save you money — and help you think more clearly.

在 1974 年一項經典研究中，心理學家阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼請受試者轉動一個幸運轉盤——它被偷偷設定成只會停在 10 或 65。接著受試者估計聯合國會員國中非洲國家所占的百分比。看到 10 的人，估計的中位數是 25%；看到 65 的人則是 45%——儘管每個人都以為轉盤是隨機的。
我們為什麼這麼容易被錨定？一種解釋是，我們從錨出發再做調整，卻太早停止調整。另一種解釋是，錨會讓和它一致的資訊更容易浮現在腦海中。不管是哪一種，第一個數字都會影響我們最後的答案。
錨定效應有真實的後果。在談判中，第一個出價常常會影響最後的價格。商店標示很高的「原價」，好讓折扣看起來很大方。研究甚至發現，被提示的數字會影響經驗豐富的專業人士的決定，例如法官量刑、房仲估價。
這個效應很難擺脫，但並非不可能。專家建議：在聽到別人的數字之前先形成自己的估計、查找獨立的資訊，並刻意想想這個錨可能錯在哪裡。
下次當一個數字先出現時，把它當成一個要質疑的起點，而不是一個要接受的事實。在對的時刻多一點懷疑，能幫你省錢——也能幫你想得更清楚。

c.title: The Stubborn Power of First Numbers
text: Rational decision-making assumes that irrelevant information is ignored. The anchoring effect shows how poorly that assumption describes human judgement. When people make numerical estimates, an initial value — even one they know to be arbitrary — exerts a measurable pull on their final answer, drawing it toward the anchor.

The phenomenon was established in Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman's influential 1974 paper on judgement under uncertainty. In their best-known demonstration, a rigged wheel of fortune produced either 10 or 65 before participants estimated the proportion of African nations in the United Nations. Median answers of 25 and 45 percent respectively revealed that a number generated by apparent chance, in full view of the participants, could shift estimates substantially.

Subsequent studies have shown that anchors need not even be plausible. In one experiment, people asked whether Mahatma Gandhi died before or after the age of 140 subsequently gave higher estimates of his actual age at death than those given a much lower anchor. Another line of research reported that writing down the last two digits of one's social security number influenced how much participants were willing to pay for ordinary goods, although a large recent replication found that this particular effect was considerably weaker than originally reported.

Two mechanisms are commonly proposed. The first, which Tversky and Kahneman emphasised, is insufficient adjustment: people begin at the anchor and move away from it, but stop too soon. The second, selective accessibility, holds that considering the anchor brings to mind evidence consistent with it, which then biases the estimate. The two accounts are not mutually exclusive, and both may operate in different situations.

Expertise offers surprisingly limited protection. Experienced estate agents' valuations of houses have been shown to shift with the listing price they were given, and studies with legal professionals suggest that sentencing demands, even arbitrary ones, can influence judicial decisions. In negotiations, whoever makes the first offer often gains an advantage for the same reason.

Debiasing is difficult but possible. Strategies that encourage people to "consider the opposite" — to generate reasons why the anchor might be inappropriate — reduce the effect, as does forming an independent estimate before exposure to any anchor. The broader lesson is humbling: the order in which information arrives can matter almost as much as the information itself.

這個現象是在阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼 1974 年那篇關於不確定情況下判斷的重要論文中確立的。在他們最有名的示範中，一個被動了手腳的幸運轉盤會轉出 10 或 65，接著受試者估計聯合國中非洲國家所占的比例。中位數答案分別是 25% 和 45%，顯示一個在受試者眼前、看似隨機產生的數字，就能大幅改變估計。

a.title: Would You Follow the Group?
text: Look at a line on a card. Then look at three other lines and choose the one that is the same length. Easy, right? Now imagine that everyone around you gives the same wrong answer. What would you say?

In the 1950s, an American psychologist named Solomon Asch tested this. In each group, only one person was a real participant. The others were actors who had been told to give wrong answers on purpose.

The task was very easy. When people did it alone, they almost never made mistakes. But in the group, the real participants often followed the others. About one third of their answers agreed with the wrong group answer. About three out of four people went along with the group at least once.
Why? Some people did not want to look strange. Others started to doubt their own eyes.
But Asch found something hopeful. When just one other person gave the right answer, the real participants were much less likely to follow the wrong group. One friend can give us courage.
So the next time everyone seems to agree, remember: you are allowed to think for yourself — and your honest answer might help someone else be brave, too.
tz: 看一看卡片上的一條線。再看另外三條線，選出和它一樣長的那條。很簡單，對吧？現在想像你身邊的每個人都給了同一個錯誤答案。你會怎麼說？
1950 年代，一位名叫所羅門・阿希的美國心理學家測試了這個情況。在每一組裡，只有一個人是真正的受試者，其他人都是演員，事先被告知要故意說錯答案。
這個任務非常簡單。人們自己做的時候，幾乎從來不會出錯。但在團體裡，真正的受試者常常跟著其他人走。他們大約三分之一的答案和錯誤的團體答案一樣。大約每四個人中有三個人，至少有一次跟著團體一起錯。
為什麼？有些人不想看起來很奇怪。有些人則開始懷疑自己的眼睛。
不過阿希也發現了一件令人振奮的事。只要有另外一個人說出正確答案，真正的受試者跟著錯誤團體走的可能性就大幅降低。一個朋友就能給我們勇氣。
所以下次當大家似乎都同意時，記得：你可以自己思考——而你誠實的答案，也可能幫助別人變得勇敢。

b.title: The Asch Experiments: The Pull of the Crowd
text: Most of us like to think we would stand firm if a group got something obviously wrong. In the early 1950s, the American psychologist Solomon Asch designed a set of experiments to test that belief, and the results have been discussed ever since.

Participants were told they were taking part in a study of visual perception. Seated around a table with about seven others, they were shown a line and asked which of three comparison lines matched it in length. The task was easy: people tested alone almost never made mistakes. But the others at the table were actors, instructed to give the same wrong answer on certain rounds. The real participant always answered near the end.

Across these critical rounds, about a third of the participants' answers agreed with the incorrect majority. Around three-quarters of participants conformed at least once, while roughly a quarter never did. In interviews afterwards, some said they had gone along to avoid seeming odd; others said they had begun to doubt their own judgement.

Asch also discovered what weakens conformity. When just one actor gave the correct answer, conformity dropped sharply. When participants could write their answers privately instead of saying them aloud, it fell too.

Later studies in many countries found similar effects, although the strength varied over time and across cultures. Researchers have also pointed out that Asch's participants were not mindless: most answers were still independent, and many who conformed felt clearly uncomfortable. Some critics also argue that the experiments reflected the cautious mood of 1950s America, when standing out could carry real risks.

The experiments remind us that social pressure is powerful — and that even a single voice of dissent can make it easier for others to speak honestly. In classrooms, meetings and online discussions, that voice may sometimes need to be yours.

c.title: Independence and Conformity: Reconsidering Asch
text: Solomon Asch's line-judgment studies, conducted in the early 1950s, are among the most cited experiments in social psychology, usually summarised as proof of human conformity. Asch himself, however, set out with a different expectation. Sceptical of earlier research suggesting that people were easily swayed by suggestion, he designed a task so unambiguous that he anticipated considerable independence. The results only partly confirmed that hope.

In the standard procedure, a lone participant joined a group of confederates who, on twelve of eighteen trials, unanimously chose an obviously incorrect comparison line. Control participants judging alone erred less than one percent of the time. Under group pressure, roughly 37 percent of critical responses matched the erroneous majority. Yet the distribution was striking: about a quarter of participants never yielded, while a small minority conformed on most trials.

Variations clarified the mechanisms. Conformity rose as the majority grew from one to three confederates but changed little beyond that. Most dramatically, the presence of a single dissenting ally — even one who gave a different wrong answer — reduced conformity substantially, suggesting that the power of the majority depended heavily on its unanimity. Allowing participants to respond in writing also lowered conformity, pointing to the role of public exposure.

Post-experimental interviews revealed varied motives. Some conformers reported that they knew the majority was wrong but did not wish to stand out; others came to doubt their own perception; a few claimed to have actually seen the lines as the group did. These accounts anticipated a distinction later formalised by psychologists between normative influence, driven by the desire for acceptance, and informational influence, driven by uncertainty about what is correct.

Replications have qualified the picture further. A 1996 meta-analysis by Rod Bond and Peter Smith found that conformity in Asch-type studies had declined in the United States since the 1950s and tended to be higher in more collectivist cultures. Some scholars have also argued that textbooks overstate Asch's findings, neglecting the fact that roughly two-thirds of all responses resisted the majority.

The enduring lesson may therefore concern both vulnerability and resilience. Groups can bend individual judgement, but unanimity is fragile, and a single honest dissenter can free others to report what they see. In that sense, Asch's experiments are as much about the value of independent voices as about the pressure to conform.
tz: 所羅門・阿希在 1950 年代初期進行的線段判斷研究，是社會心理學中被引用最多的實驗之一，通常被總結為人類從眾的證據。然而，阿希本人一開始的預期並不一樣。他懷疑早期那些顯示人很容易受暗示左右的研究，於是設計了一個毫不含糊的任務，預期會看到相當多的獨立判斷。結果只部分印證了他的期望。
在標準程序中，一位單獨的受試者加入一群實驗同謀，這些同謀在十八次試驗中有十二次一致選擇明顯錯誤的比較線。單獨判斷的對照組，出錯率不到百分之一。在團體壓力下，大約 37% 的關鍵回答和錯誤的多數一致。然而，分布情形很引人注目：大約四分之一的受試者從未屈服，而只有少數人在大多數試驗中從眾。
各種變化版本釐清了背後的機制。當多數人從一位同謀增加到三位時，從眾率上升，但超過三位之後就變化不大。最戲劇性的是，只要有一位持不同意見的盟友——即使他給的是另一個錯誤答案——從眾就大幅減少，顯示多數人的力量很大程度取決於「全體一致」。讓受試者以書面作答也會降低從眾，指出了公開曝光所扮演的角色。
實驗後的訪談揭露了各種不同的動機。有些從眾者表示他們知道多數人是錯的，但不想顯得突兀；有些人則逐漸懷疑起自己的知覺；少數人甚至聲稱自己真的看到和團體一樣的結果。這些說法預示了心理學家後來正式提出的區分：由渴望被接納所驅動的「規範性影響」，以及由不確定什麼是對的所驅動的「資訊性影響」。
重複研究讓這個圖像更加修正。羅德・龐德和彼得・史密斯 1996 年的統合分析發現，美國在阿希式研究中的從眾程度自 1950 年代以來已經下降，而且在比較集體主義的文化中往往比較高。也有學者主張，教科書誇大了阿希的發現，忽略了大約三分之二的回答其實抵抗了多數。
因此，這些實驗留下的教訓，可能同時關乎脆弱與韌性。團體能扭曲個人的判斷，但全體一致是很脆弱的，一個誠實的異議者就能讓其他人自由說出自己看到的。從這個意義上說，阿希的實驗談的不只是從眾的壓力，也同樣是獨立聲音的價值。

topic: The Availability Heuristic: Why Rare Dangers Feel Common
zh: 可得性捷思：為什麼罕見的危險感覺很常見？
src: Tversky & Kahneman (1973) · Schwarz et al. (1991) · Gigerenzer (2006)
discuss: Which dangers do you worry about most? Are they really the most common?
How does the news affect what we think is common?
What can you do before believing that something is 'happening everywhere'?

a.title: What Comes to Mind First
text: Which is more dangerous: flying in a plane or riding in a car? Many people say flying. They remember scary news about plane crashes. But in most countries, car trips are far more dangerous than plane trips.
This mistake is called the availability heuristic. A "heuristic" is a mental shortcut — a quick way of thinking. When something comes to mind easily, we think it must happen often.
In 1973, two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, tested this. They asked people: "Are there more English words that start with the letter K, or more words with K as the third letter?"

Most people said words that start with K. It is easy to think of words like "kite" and "king." But in fact, words with K as the third letter, like "make" and "bike," are about twice as common. They are just harder to think of.
The news can make this bias stronger. Rare events, like shark attacks, are often shown again and again, so they feel common. Everyday dangers, like not wearing a seat belt, seldom make big news.
So before you decide how likely something is, ask: "Do I remember it because it is common, or because it is easy to remember?"
tz: 哪一個比較危險：搭飛機還是坐汽車？很多人會說搭飛機。他們記得那些關於墜機的可怕新聞。但在大多數國家，坐車其實比搭飛機危險得多。
這種錯誤叫做可得性捷思。「捷思」是一種思考的捷徑——一種快速的思考方式。當某件事很容易浮現在腦海，我們就以為它一定很常發生。
1973 年，兩位心理學家阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼測試了這個現象。他們問受試者：「英文裡是以字母 K 開頭的字比較多，還是第三個字母是 K 的字比較多？」
大多數人說以 K 開頭的字比較多。像 kite、king 這樣的字很容易想到。但事實上，第三個字母是 K 的字，例如 make 和 bike，大約多了一倍。它們只是比較難想到而已。
新聞可能讓這種偏誤更嚴重。罕見的事件，例如鯊魚攻擊，常常一再被報導，所以感覺很常見。日常的危險，例如不繫安全帶，卻很少成為大新聞。
所以在判斷某件事有多可能發生之前，問問自己：「我記得它，是因為它很常見，還是因為它很好記？」

b.title: The Availability Heuristic: When Memory Misleads Judgement
text: How likely are you to be struck by lightning, attacked by a shark or win the lottery? Most people answer such questions not by consulting statistics but by asking themselves, often without realising it, how easily examples come to mind. Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman called this mental shortcut the availability heuristic.

In a famous 1973 experiment, they asked participants whether the letter K was more likely to appear as the first letter of English words or as the third. Most chose the first position, because words beginning with K — "kitchen," "kind," "key" — are easy to retrieve from memory. In fact, K appears roughly twice as often in the third position, as in "make" or "ask." The ease of recall had been mistaken for frequency.

Shortcuts like this are not foolish. In everyday life, things that come to mind easily often are common, so the heuristic usually works reasonably well. The trouble begins when ease of recall is driven by something other than frequency — such as how recent, vivid or emotional an event was.

Media coverage is a major source of distortion. Dramatic but rare events, such as plane crashes or terrorist attacks, receive intense attention, while common risks like heart disease or road accidents rarely become headlines. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, many Americans chose to drive instead of fly; researchers later estimated that the extra road traffic led to around 1,600 additional deaths in the following year.
To make better judgements, it helps to check actual data rather than relying on what we remember, and to ask whether a striking example is typical or simply memorable.
Our memories are wonderful tools, but they were not designed to work like statistics books. Knowing this can help us worry less about rare dangers and pay more attention to common ones.
tz: 你被雷打到、被鯊魚攻擊或中樂透的機率有多高？大多數人回答這類問題時，不是去查統計數據，而是——常常在不知不覺中——問自己例子有多容易浮現在腦海。心理學家阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼把這種思考捷徑稱為可得性捷思。
在 1973 年一個著名的實驗中，他們問受試者：字母 K 比較常出現在英文單字的第一個字母，還是第三個字母？大多數人選了第一個，因為以 K 開頭的字——kitchen、kind、key——很容易從記憶中提取。事實上，K 出現在第三個位置的次數大約多一倍，例如 make 或 ask。人們把「容易想起」誤當成了「出現頻率」。
這樣的捷徑並不愚蠢。在日常生活中，容易想到的事情往往確實很常見，所以這個捷思通常還算好用。問題在於，當「容易想起」是由頻率以外的因素造成時——例如事件有多新、多鮮明或多情緒化——就會出錯。
媒體報導是一個主要的扭曲來源。戲劇性但罕見的事件，例如墜機或恐怖攻擊，會受到大量關注；而心臟病或交通事故這類常見的風險，卻很少登上頭條。2001 年 9 月 11 日的攻擊事件後，許多美國人選擇開車而不搭飛機；研究者後來估計，多出來的道路交通在接下來一年造成了大約 1,600 人額外死亡。

c.title: Availability: Judging by What Comes to Mind
text: People rarely estimate frequencies or probabilities by calculation. Instead, as Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman argued in 1973, they often substitute an easier question — how readily do instances come to mind? — for the harder one they were asked. This substitution, the availability heuristic, is efficient and frequently accurate, because common events usually are easier to recall. But availability is shaped by many forces besides frequency, and where those forces diverge from reality, judgement goes astray.

The original demonstrations were elegant. Asked whether English contains more words beginning with K or more with K in the third position, most participants chose the former, though the latter are roughly twice as common; first letters simply provide a better retrieval cue. In another study, participants heard lists of names in which famous women and less famous men were mixed together, or vice versa. They later judged the gender with more famous names to be more numerous, even when it was actually less frequent.

Subsequent research identified a subtle refinement. In a 1991 study led by Norbert Schwarz, participants asked to recall twelve examples of their own assertive behaviour rated themselves as less assertive than those asked to recall six. Generating twelve examples was difficult, and that experienced difficulty was taken as evidence that such behaviour was rare. What matters, then, is not only what comes to mind but how easily it does so.

The heuristic helps explain distorted public perceptions of risk. Vivid, dramatic and heavily reported hazards — aircraft disasters, shark attacks, terrorism — tend to be overestimated, while chronic, mundane killers such as diabetes or road accidents are underestimated. After the September 11 attacks, a shift from flying to driving in the United States has been estimated to have caused around 1,600 extra road deaths over the following year, a toll that exceeded the number of people killed on board the hijacked planes.

Availability also interacts with what has been called an availability cascade, in which a striking story generates media coverage, public concern and further coverage, until perceived importance far outstrips actual risk. Policies may then follow the story rather than the statistics.

The remedy is not to distrust memory entirely but to recognise its biases. Consulting base rates, asking whether an example is representative or merely memorable, and noticing when emotion is doing the estimating can all bring judgement closer to the evidence.
tz: 人們很少用計算來估計頻率或機率。相反地，正如阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼在 1973 年所主張的，人們常常把被問到的難題，替換成一個比較簡單的問題——例子有多容易浮現在腦海？這種替換就是可得性捷思，它很有效率，也常常很準確，因為常見的事件通常比較容易想起。但「可得性」受到頻率以外許多因素的影響，當這些因素偏離現實時，判斷就會走偏。
最初的示範相當巧妙。被問到英文中以 K 開頭的字比較多、還是第三個字母是 K 的字比較多時，大多數受試者選了前者，但後者其實大約多一倍；只是第一個字母是更好的提取線索。在另一項研究中，受試者聽到一串名字，裡面混合了有名的女性和比較不出名的男性，或者反過來。他們之後會認為有名人名字較多的那個性別人數比較多，即使它其實比較少。
後續研究發現了一個細微的修正。在 1991 年由諾伯特・施瓦茨主持的研究中，被要求回想十二個自己果斷行為例子的受試者，評價自己的果斷程度，比被要求回想六個例子的人還低。想出十二個例子很困難，而這種感受到的困難，被當成這類行為很少見的證據。所以，重要的不只是想起了什麼，還有想起來有多容易。
這個捷思有助於解釋大眾對風險的扭曲認知。鮮明、戲劇化、大量報導的危險——空難、鯊魚攻擊、恐怖主義——往往被高估；而糖尿病或交通事故這類慢性、平凡的殺手則被低估。九一一攻擊之後，美國人從搭飛機轉為開車，據估計在接下來一年多造成了約 1,600 人的道路死亡，這個數字超過了被劫持飛機上的罹難人數。
可得性也會和所謂的「可得性連鎖反應」交互作用：一個引人注目的故事引發媒體報導、大眾關注和更多報導，直到人們感受到的重要性遠遠超過實際風險。政策接著可能跟著故事走，而不是跟著統計數據走。
解決之道不是完全不信任記憶，而是認清它的偏誤。查閱基本比率、問問一個例子是具代表性的還是只是好記，以及察覺什麼時候是情緒在幫我們估計——這些都能讓判斷更接近證據。

topic: Broken Windows Theory: Can Small Disorder Lead to Big Problems?
zh: 破窗理論：一扇破窗，真的會引來更多問題嗎？
src: Wilson & Kelling (1982) · Keizer, Lindenberg & Steg (2008) · Braga, Welsh & Schnell (2015)

a.title: Can One Broken Window Lead to More Trouble?
text: Imagine a street with one broken window. Nobody fixes it. Soon, more windows are broken. Then people start to throw rubbish on the ground and paint on the walls. Why does one small problem grow?

In 1982, two American thinkers, James Q. Wilson and George Kelling, wrote about this idea. They called it the broken windows theory. They said that small signs of disorder, like broken windows or rubbish, send a message: "Nobody cares here." This message may lead to bigger problems, even crime.

In 2008, researchers in the Netherlands tested a similar idea. They put paper flyers on bicycles parked near a wall. When the wall was clean, about one third of the riders threw the flyer on the ground. When the wall was covered in graffiti, more than two thirds did.

In the 1990s, New York City used the theory. Police paid attention to small problems, and crime fell a lot. But crime also fell in many other cities that did not do this. Some people also felt the police treated them unfairly. So experts still argue about how well it works.
Still, the main idea is useful. When we take care of small things, like picking up rubbish or fixing what is broken, we show that we care about our home, our school and our town.
tz: 想像一條街上有一扇破掉的窗戶，沒有人去修。很快地，更多窗戶被打破了。接著，人們開始把垃圾丟在地上、在牆上亂畫。為什麼一個小問題會越變越大？
1982 年，兩位美國學者詹姆斯・Q・威爾遜和喬治・凱林寫到了這個想法，他們稱之為破窗理論。他們說，失序的小跡象，像是破窗或垃圾，會傳達一個訊息：「這裡沒人在乎。」這個訊息可能會導致更大的問題，甚至是犯罪。
2008 年，荷蘭的研究者測試了一個類似的想法。他們把紙傳單放在停在一面牆旁邊的腳踏車上。當牆面很乾淨時，大約三分之一的騎士把傳單丟在地上；當牆上滿是塗鴉時，超過三分之二的人這麼做。
1990 年代，紐約市運用了這個理論。警察特別注意小問題，犯罪率也大幅下降。但許多沒有這麼做的城市，犯罪率也下降了。有些人也覺得警察對待他們不公平。所以專家們至今仍在爭論它到底有多有效。
不過，它的主要想法還是很有用。當我們照顧好小事情，像是撿起垃圾或修好壞掉的東西，就是在表示我們在乎自己的家、學校和城鎮。

b.title: Broken Windows: Disorder, Crime and Controversy
text: In 1982, the social scientists James Q. Wilson and George Kelling published an article in The Atlantic magazine titled "Broken Windows". Their argument was simple. If a broken window in a building is left unrepaired, the rest of the windows will soon be broken too, because the damage signals that no one is in charge. Small signs of disorder, such as litter, graffiti and public drinking, may encourage more serious crime.

The authors drew on an experiment by the psychologist Philip Zimbardo in 1969. He left a car with its hood up and no licence plates on a street in the Bronx, New York, and another in Palo Alto, California. The Bronx car was stripped within days. The Palo Alto car was left untouched for over a week — until Zimbardo smashed part of it with a hammer, after which passers-by soon joined in.

Later experiments supported part of the idea. In 2008, Kees Keizer and colleagues in the Netherlands found that people were far more likely to drop litter or break rules when they saw signs that others had already broken them.

The theory became famous in the 1990s, when New York City police began cracking down on minor offences such as fare dodging, and serious crime fell sharply. Yet critics pointed out that crime also dropped in cities that used very different methods, suggesting that factors such as the economy and changes in drug markets also played a part. Aggressive policing of small offences was also accused of targeting poor and minority communities.

Today many researchers draw a distinction. Fixing the physical environment — cleaning up empty lots, repairing buildings — appears to reduce some crime, while simply arresting more people for minor offences is far more controversial. The lesson may be that a neighbourhood feels safer when people can see that someone cares for it.
tz: 1982 年，社會科學家詹姆斯・Q・威爾遜和喬治・凱林在《大西洋》雜誌上發表了一篇題為〈破窗〉的文章。他們的論點很簡單：如果一棟建築的一扇破窗沒有修理，其他窗戶很快也會被打破，因為這樣的損壞傳達出「沒有人在管」的訊號。失序的小跡象，例如垃圾、塗鴉和在公共場所喝酒，可能會助長更嚴重的犯罪。
兩位作者引用了心理學家菲利普・津巴多在 1969 年做的一項實驗。他把一輛打開引擎蓋、沒有車牌的車停在紐約布朗克斯區的街上，另一輛則停在加州的帕羅奧圖。布朗克斯的那輛車在幾天內就被拆光了。帕羅奧圖的那輛車則一個多星期都沒人碰——直到津巴多自己用鐵鎚砸壞了一部分，之後路過的人很快就加入破壞。
後來的實驗支持了這個想法的一部分。2008 年，荷蘭的基斯・凱澤和同事發現，當人們看到別人已經違反規定的跡象時，他們亂丟垃圾或違反規定的可能性會高出許多。
這個理論在 1990 年代聲名大噪，當時紐約市警方開始嚴格取締逃票等輕微違法行為，重大犯罪也大幅下降。然而批評者指出，採用完全不同方法的城市，犯罪率也下降了，這表示經濟、毒品市場的變化等因素也有影響。強硬取締輕微違法的做法，也被指控針對貧窮與少數族裔社區。
如今許多研究者會做出區分。改善實體環境——清理空地、修繕建築——似乎能減少部分犯罪；而只是因為輕微違法就逮捕更多人，則爭議大得多。其中的教訓或許是：當人們看得出有人在照顧一個社區時，那裡就會讓人覺得比較安全。

c.title: Broken Windows: The Rise and Reassessment of a Policing Idea
text: Few ideas in criminology have travelled as far from the page to the street as the broken windows theory. Proposed by James Q. Wilson and George Kelling in a 1982 essay in The Atlantic, it held that visible disorder — an unrepaired window, litter, aggressive begging — signals that a neighbourhood is uncontrolled, drawing in offenders and driving law-abiding residents indoors. Left unchecked, the authors argued, minor disorder could spiral into serious crime.

The essay cited Philip Zimbardo's 1969 demonstration in which an abandoned car in the Bronx was quickly vandalised, while an identical car in affluent Palo Alto sat untouched for over a week until Zimbardo himself damaged it, whereupon passers-by joined in. The anecdote was vivid, but it was a single, informal demonstration rather than a controlled study.

Firmer evidence for the psychological mechanism came later. In a series of field experiments published in Science in 2008, Kees Keizer, Siegwart Lindenberg and Linda Steg found that when people saw evidence that a norm had been violated — graffiti on a wall despite a ban, for instance — they were substantially more likely to violate other norms, such as littering. Disorder, it seemed, spread not only within one type of behaviour but across types.

The policy history is more contested. During the 1990s, New York City under Police Commissioner William Bratton emphasised enforcement against minor offences such as fare evasion, and serious crime fell dramatically. Supporters credited the strategy. Sceptics noted that crime declined in many American cities with very different policing, and pointed to factors including economic growth, a waning crack-cocaine epidemic and increased police numbers. Disentangling these causes has proved extremely difficult.

A 2015 meta-analysis by Anthony Braga, Brandon Welsh and Cory Schnell offered a nuanced verdict. Strategies that addressed disorder produced modest reductions in crime, but the benefits came mainly from community problem-solving approaches, not from aggressive tactics centred on mass arrests. Meanwhile, practices associated with "zero tolerance", including the later surge in stop-and-frisk encounters in New York, attracted sustained criticism for disproportionately targeting Black and Latino residents and damaging trust in the police.

The theory's most durable insight may therefore be environmental rather than punitive. Experiments in which vacant lots were cleaned and planted have been followed by reductions in some violent crime, suggesting that repairing places, not merely policing people, can communicate the message Wilson and Kelling had in mind: someone here is paying attention.
tz: 在犯罪學中，很少有哪個想法能像破窗理論這樣，從紙上一路走到街頭。它由詹姆斯・Q・威爾遜和喬治・凱林在 1982 年《大西洋》雜誌的一篇文章中提出，主張看得見的失序——沒修的窗戶、垃圾、強行乞討——傳達出一個社區失去控制的訊號，會把犯罪者吸引進來，並把守法的居民趕回室內。兩位作者主張，如果放任不管，輕微的失序可能會急遽惡化成嚴重犯罪。
這篇文章引用了菲利普・津巴多在 1969 年的示範：一輛被丟棄在布朗克斯區的車很快就遭到破壞，而停在富裕的帕羅奧圖、一模一樣的車則一個多星期都沒人碰，直到津巴多自己動手破壞它，路人才隨即加入。這段軼事很生動，但它只是一次非正式的示範，而不是受控制的研究。
關於心理機制更扎實的證據後來才出現。基斯・凱澤、齊格瓦特・林登貝格和琳達・斯特格在 2008 年發表於《科學》期刊的一系列田野實驗中發現，當人們看到某條規範已經被違反的證據時——例如明明禁止卻還是出現在牆上的塗鴉——他們違反其他規範（例如亂丟垃圾）的可能性就會大幅提高。看來，失序不只會在同一種行為中擴散，還會跨越不同種類的行為。
政策上的歷史就更有爭議了。1990 年代，在警察局長威廉・布拉頓的領導下，紐約市著重取締逃票等輕微違法行為，重大犯罪也大幅下降。支持者把功勞歸給這項策略。懷疑者則指出，許多採取完全不同警務方式的美國城市，犯罪率也下降了，並點出經濟成長、快克古柯鹼氾濫退燒以及警力增加等因素。要釐清這些原因，結果證明極為困難。
安東尼・布拉加、布蘭登・威爾許和柯瑞・施奈爾 2015 年的統合分析給出了一個細緻的結論。處理失序的策略確實讓犯罪小幅減少，但效益主要來自社區共同解決問題的做法，而不是以大量逮捕為核心的強硬手段。同時，與「零容忍」相關的做法，包括紐約後來激增的「攔停搜身」，長期受到批評，被指不成比例地針對黑人與拉丁裔居民，並損害民眾對警察的信任。
因此，這個理論最持久的洞見，可能在於環境而不是懲罰。在一些實驗中，空地被清理並種上植物之後，部分暴力犯罪隨之減少，這顯示修復地方——而不只是管束人——也能傳達威爾遜和凱林心中想傳達的訊息：這裡有人在注意。

a.title: When Thoughts and Actions Don't Match
text: Imagine you believe junk food is bad for you, but you just ate three bags of chips. How do you feel? A little uncomfortable, maybe. Psychologists call this feeling cognitive dissonance. It happens when our beliefs and our actions do not match.

The idea came from an American psychologist named Leon Festinger in 1957. He said people do not like this feeling, so they try to make it go away. Often, they change what they think instead of what they do.

In a famous study in 1959, Festinger and James Carlsmith asked students to do a very boring task for an hour. Then the students were paid to tell the next person that the task was fun. Some got one dollar. Others got twenty dollars.

Later, the students said how much they had enjoyed the task. Surprisingly, the one-dollar group said they liked it more. Why? The twenty-dollar group had a good reason to lie: money. The one-dollar group did not, so they told themselves the task was not so bad after all.
There is an old story about this, too. A fox cannot reach some grapes, so he says, "They are probably sour anyway."
Dissonance can be useful when it pushes us to change bad habits. But we should watch out for easy excuses that only make us feel better.
tz: 想像一下，你相信垃圾食物對身體不好，但你剛剛吃了三包洋芋片。你感覺如何？大概有點不舒服吧。心理學家把這種感覺叫做認知失調。當我們的信念和行為不一致時，它就會出現。
這個想法來自一位名叫利昂・費斯汀格的美國心理學家，時間是 1957 年。他說人們不喜歡這種感覺，所以會想辦法讓它消失。很多時候，人們改變的是自己的想法，而不是自己的行為。
在 1959 年一項著名的研究中，費斯汀格和詹姆斯・卡爾史密斯請學生做一件非常無聊的任務，做一個小時。接著，學生拿錢去告訴下一個人這個任務很好玩。有些人拿到一美元，其他人拿到二十美元。
之後，學生們說出自己有多喜歡這個任務。令人驚訝的是，拿一美元的那組說他們比較喜歡。為什麼？拿二十美元的那組有個說謊的好理由：錢。拿一美元的那組沒有，所以他們告訴自己，這個任務終究也沒那麼糟。
有一個古老的故事也在講這件事。一隻狐狸搆不到一串葡萄，於是牠說：「反正那些葡萄大概是酸的。」
當認知失調推動我們改掉壞習慣時，它是有用的。但我們要小心那些只會讓自己好過一點的輕鬆藉口。

b.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why We Explain Away Our Choices
text: Most people like to see themselves as reasonable and consistent. So what happens when we act against our own beliefs — say, by smoking while knowing it is harmful? According to the American psychologist Leon Festinger, we feel an unpleasant tension he called cognitive dissonance. In his 1957 book, he argued that people are strongly motivated to reduce this tension, often by adjusting their beliefs rather than their behaviour.

Festinger had seen the idea in action. In 1954, he and two colleagues secretly joined a small group whose leader predicted that a great flood would destroy much of the world on a certain date. When the date passed without disaster, some members did not give up their belief. Instead, they decided their faith had saved the world and began trying harder to win new followers. The researchers described the case in the 1956 book When Prophecy Fails.

The best-known experiment came in 1959. Festinger and James Carlsmith had students perform dull tasks, such as turning pegs, for an hour. Each student was then paid either one dollar or twenty dollars to tell a waiting participant that the tasks had been enjoyable. Afterwards, those paid one dollar rated the tasks as more enjoyable than those paid twenty. With a large reward, lying was easy to justify. With a tiny one, students resolved the conflict by deciding the task had not been so bad.
Dissonance also appears after difficult decisions. Having chosen one option, people tend to rate it more highly and the rejected option lower, which helps them feel they chose well.

Not everyone accepted Festinger's explanation. In 1967, Daryl Bem suggested that people simply observe their own behaviour and infer their attitudes from it, without any inner tension. Debate between the two views continued for years.
Whatever its exact cause, the theory offers a useful warning: when we hear ourselves inventing excuses, it may be a sign that our actions, not our beliefs, need to change.
tz: 大多數人都喜歡把自己看成講道理、言行一致的人。那麼，當我們的行為違背自己的信念時——例如明知抽菸有害卻還在抽——會發生什麼事？根據美國心理學家利昂・費斯汀格的說法，我們會感到一種不愉快的緊張，他稱之為認知失調。在他 1957 年的著作中，他主張人們有強烈的動機去減少這種緊張，而且常常是靠調整自己的信念，而不是改變行為。
費斯汀格曾親眼看到這個想法如何運作。1954 年，他和兩位同事祕密加入一個小團體，團體的領袖預言一場大洪水會在某一天毀滅世界的大部分地區。當那一天過去、災難並沒有發生時，有些成員並沒有放棄他們的信念。相反地，他們認定是自己的信仰拯救了世界，並開始更努力地招募新信徒。研究者在 1956 年的《當預言失靈》一書中描述了這個案例。
最有名的實驗出現在 1959 年。費斯汀格和詹姆斯・卡爾史密斯讓學生做枯燥的任務，例如轉動木栓，做一個小時。接著每位學生拿到一美元或二十美元，去告訴一位等待中的受試者這些任務很有趣。之後，拿一美元的人對任務的評價比拿二十美元的人更有趣。報酬很高時，說謊很容易找到理由；報酬很少時，學生就以「這個任務其實沒那麼糟」來化解內心的衝突。
做完困難的決定後也會出現認知失調。選了一個選項之後，人們往往會把它評得更高，把被放棄的選項評得更低，這能幫助他們覺得自己選對了。
並不是每個人都接受費斯汀格的解釋。1967 年，達里爾・貝姆提出，人們只是觀察自己的行為，並從中推斷自己的態度，根本不需要任何內在的緊張。這兩種觀點之間的爭論持續了好幾年。
不論確切的原因是什麼，這個理論都提供了一個有用的警告：當我們聽見自己在編藉口時，也許代表需要改變的是我們的行為，而不是信念。

c.title: Cognitive Dissonance and the Art of Self-Justification
text: In Aesop's fable, a fox who cannot reach a bunch of grapes concludes that they were probably sour. The fox does not change his situation; he changes his opinion. In 1957, the social psychologist Leon Festinger turned this ancient insight into a formal theory. Cognitive dissonance, he proposed, is the uncomfortable state produced when a person holds two cognitions — beliefs, attitudes or knowledge of one's own behaviour — that are psychologically inconsistent. Because the state is aversive, people are driven to reduce it.

Reduction can take several forms. One may change the behaviour, add new justifying beliefs, or downplay the importance of the conflict. A smoker, for instance, might quit, decide that the evidence is exaggerated, or reason that life is short anyway. Festinger's crucial insight was that when behaviour is hard to undo, belief is often what yields.

The classic demonstration, by Festinger and James Carlsmith in 1959, involved what is now called induced compliance. Students who had completed tedious tasks were paid either one dollar or twenty dollars to tell a waiting participant that the tasks were interesting. Those paid one dollar later reported enjoying the tasks more. Twenty dollars provided sufficient external justification for the lie; one dollar did not, so the students closed the gap internally. Later studies extended the theory to effort justification, in which people value groups more after a severe initiation, and to post-decision dissonance, in which people come to value chosen options more highly.

The theory was enormously productive, but it also attracted serious critics. Daryl Bem's self-perception theory proposed that people infer their attitudes from their behaviour much as an outside observer would, with no need for inner discomfort. Subsequent experiments suggested that both processes operate in different circumstances. More recently, large replication efforts have produced weaker results for some classic paradigms than the original studies reported, prompting researchers to reconsider how robust the effects are.

Even so, the idea has proven useful in explaining puzzling behaviour, from investors who refuse to sell failing shares to leaders who defend policies long after evidence has turned against them. Its most practical lesson concerns self-awareness. The discomfort of dissonance can be a valuable signal; the danger lies in silencing it too quickly with convenient stories.

As the psychologists Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson observed in their popular book on the subject, self-justification is not the same as lying to others; it is more dangerous, because we believe it ourselves.
tz: 在伊索寓言裡，一隻搆不到葡萄的狐狸斷定那些葡萄大概是酸的。狐狸沒有改變自己的處境，而是改變了自己的看法。1957 年，社會心理學家利昂・費斯汀格把這個古老的洞見變成了一套正式的理論。他提出，認知失調是一種不舒服的狀態：當一個人同時抱持兩種在心理上互相矛盾的認知——信念、態度，或對自己行為的了解——時就會產生。因為這種狀態令人厭惡，人們會被驅使去減少它。
減少失調的方式有好幾種。人可以改變行為、加上新的合理化信念，或是淡化衝突的重要性。例如，一個抽菸的人可能會戒菸、認定那些證據太誇大，或告訴自己反正人生苦短。費斯汀格關鍵的洞見是：當行為很難挽回時，讓步的往往是信念。

最經典的示範是費斯汀格和詹姆斯・卡爾史密斯在 1959 年做的，也就是現在所說的「誘導順從」。做完冗長乏味任務的學生，拿到一美元或二十美元，去告訴一位等待中的受試者這些任務很有趣。拿一美元的人事後表示自己比較喜歡那些任務。二十美元為謊言提供了足夠的外在理由；一美元則不夠，所以學生只好在內心把落差補起來。後來的研究把這個理論延伸到「努力合理化」——人們在經歷嚴苛的入會儀式後會更重視那個團體——以及「決策後失調」——人們會逐漸更看重自己選擇的選項。
這個理論催生了大量研究，但也引來嚴厲的批評。達里爾・貝姆的「自我知覺理論」主張，人們就像局外的觀察者一樣，從自己的行為推斷自己的態度，根本不需要內在的不適感。後續實驗顯示，這兩種歷程在不同情況下都會運作。近年來，大型的重複驗證研究對某些經典實驗典範得到的結果比原始研究弱，促使研究者重新思考這些效應到底有多穩固。
即便如此，這個概念在解釋令人費解的行為上一直很有用：從拒絕賣掉虧損股票的投資人，到在證據早已不利之後仍為政策辯護的領導者。它最實際的教訓和自我覺察有關。失調帶來的不適可以是一個寶貴的訊號；危險在於太快用方便的說法讓它安靜下來。
正如心理學家卡蘿・塔芙瑞斯和艾略特・亞隆森在他們討論這個主題的暢銷書中所指出的：自我合理化和對別人說謊不一樣；它更危險，因為我們自己也相信了。

a.title: Lost in the Moment
text: Have you ever been so busy drawing, playing a game, or practising an instrument that you forgot what time it was? Hours felt like minutes. You were not bored, and you were not worried. You were in "flow."

The word was made popular by a psychologist named Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. (His name is hard to say: "ME-high CHEEK-sent-me-high-ee.") He was born in 1934 and later worked in the United States. He talked to many people — artists, rock climbers, chess players, and surgeons — about the times they felt happiest.
Many of them described the same feeling. They were completely focused. They knew exactly what to do next, and they forgot about themselves and their problems.
Csikszentmihalyi found that flow usually happens when a task is just right: not too easy and not too hard. If it is too easy, we get bored. If it is too hard, we get worried.
Clear goals also help. So does quick feedback — for example, seeing your score go up in a game or hearing that a song sounds right.
You can find flow in many places, even in homework! Choose a task with a little challenge, put your phone away, and give it your full attention.

這個詞是由一位名叫米哈里・契克森米哈伊的心理學家推廣開來的。（他的名字很難唸：「ME-high CHEEK-sent-me-high-ee」。）他生於 1934 年，後來在美國工作。他訪問了很多人——藝術家、攀岩者、棋手和外科醫生——問他們最快樂的時刻。
他們之中有很多人描述了同樣的感覺：完全專注、清楚知道下一步該做什麼，而且忘了自己和自己的煩惱。
契克森米哈伊發現，心流通常發生在任務「剛剛好」的時候：不會太簡單，也不會太難。太簡單，我們會覺得無聊；太難，我們會擔心。
清楚的目標也有幫助。快速的回饋也是——例如在遊戲裡看到分數往上跳，或聽到一首歌彈得對了。
你可以在很多地方找到心流，甚至是寫功課的時候！選一個有點挑戰性的任務，把手機收起來，然後全心投入。

b.title: Flow: The Science of Being Completely Absorbed
text: A climber on a difficult wall, a pianist deep in a sonata, a coder solving a tricky bug — each may describe the same experience: total absorption, a sense of control, and the feeling that time has bent. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called this state "flow," and he spent much of his career trying to understand it.

Born in 1934, Csikszentmihalyi became curious about happiness after witnessing the suffering of the Second World War as a child. In the 1960s and 1970s he interviewed artists, athletes, chess players and surgeons, and later used a method in which participants carried pagers that beeped at random times, prompting them to record what they were doing and how they felt. His 1990 book, Flow, brought the idea to a wide audience.

Several conditions tend to produce flow. The activity should have clear goals and provide immediate feedback. Most importantly, the challenge must match the person's skills. When a task is too easy relative to our abilities, we feel bored; when it is far too hard, we feel anxious. Flow appears in the narrow channel between the two, and as skills grow, the challenge must grow too.

During flow, people often lose self-consciousness — they stop worrying about how they look to others — and their sense of time changes. Many describe the activity as rewarding in itself, regardless of any prize or praise.

Researchers have linked frequent flow experiences with greater wellbeing and engagement, though cause and effect are hard to separate. Flow is also not always positive: people can experience it while gambling or playing video games for unhealthy lengths of time.

For students, the practical lesson is to seek tasks slightly beyond their current ability, remove distractions, and set clear goals. Learning feels hardest when it is either trivially easy or hopelessly difficult — and most satisfying in between.
tz: 攀爬困難岩壁的攀岩者、沉浸在奏鳴曲中的鋼琴家、正在解一個棘手錯誤的程式設計師——他們可能都會描述同一種經驗：完全投入、掌控感，以及時間彷彿被扭曲的感覺。心理學家米哈里・契克森米哈伊把這種狀態稱為「心流」，並花了大半生試圖理解它。
契克森米哈伊生於 1934 年，小時候目睹二次世界大戰的苦難後，開始對「幸福」感到好奇。1960 和 1970 年代，他訪問了藝術家、運動員、棋手和外科醫生；後來又使用一種方法：讓受試者隨身攜帶呼叫器，在隨機時間響起，提醒他們記錄當下在做什麼、感覺如何。他 1990 年的著作《心流》讓這個概念廣為人知。
有幾個條件容易產生心流。活動要有清楚的目標，並提供立即的回饋。最重要的是，挑戰必須和個人的技能相當。當任務相對於能力太簡單，我們會覺得無聊；太難時，則會感到焦慮。心流出現在兩者之間那條狹窄的通道裡，而且隨著技能成長，挑戰也必須跟著提高。

研究者把經常經歷心流和較高的幸福感、投入程度連結在一起，不過因果關係很難區分。心流也不一定都是正面的：人們在賭博或長時間打電玩到不健康的程度時，也可能經歷心流。
對學生來說，實用的教訓是：找略高於目前能力的任務、排除讓人分心的事物、設定清楚的目標。學習在太簡單或難到沒希望時感覺最辛苦——在兩者之間時最令人滿足。

c.title: The Optimal Experience: Flow and Its Limits
text: What makes an experience deeply satisfying? For centuries philosophers answered in terms of virtue or pleasure. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi took a more empirical route. Beginning in the 1960s, he asked painters, rock climbers, dancers, chess masters and surgeons to describe moments when their work felt most rewarding, and he was struck by how similar their accounts were across very different activities.

He called the shared state "flow", borrowing a metaphor several interviewees used: the sense of being carried along by a current. Its hallmarks include intense concentration on the present moment, a merging of action and awareness, a loss of reflective self-consciousness, a sense of control, a distorted perception of time, and the experience of the activity as intrinsically rewarding — what he termed "autotelic".

To study flow outside interviews, Csikszentmihalyi and colleagues developed the experience sampling method. Participants carried pagers that signalled them at random moments throughout the day, at which point they recorded their activity, their level of challenge and skill, and their mood. The data suggested that flow was most likely when both challenge and skill were relatively high and roughly balanced; low challenge with high skill tended to produce relaxation or boredom, and high challenge with low skill produced anxiety.

The model has proved influential in education, sport, game design and workplace research. Video game designers, for instance, adjust difficulty dynamically to keep players in the channel between frustration and tedium — an application of Csikszentmihalyi's insight that also explains why some games are so hard to put down.

That last observation hints at the theory's limits. Flow is morally neutral: a person can be absorbed in gambling, compulsive gaming or harmful work as completely as in composing music. Moreover, measuring flow relies heavily on self-report, and while studies associate frequent flow with wellbeing, the direction of causation remains uncertain. Some researchers have also questioned whether a single "flow state" exists, or whether the label groups together several related experiences.

Csikszentmihalyi, who died in 2021, argued that the quality of life depends less on circumstances than on how attention is invested. Whatever its scientific limits, the idea offers a practical heuristic for learners: choose challenges just beyond your current skill, define clear goals, seek prompt feedback and protect your attention from interruption. Over time, such deliberate choices can turn ordinary tasks into sources of satisfaction.
tz: 是什麼讓一段經驗深深令人滿足？幾個世紀以來，哲學家用美德或快樂來回答。心理學家米哈里・契克森米哈伊走了一條比較實證的路。從 1960 年代起，他請畫家、攀岩者、舞者、西洋棋大師和外科醫生描述工作最有收穫的時刻，並驚訝地發現，在截然不同的活動中，他們的描述竟如此相似。
他把這種共同的狀態稱為「心流」，借用了幾位受訪者使用的比喻：被一股水流帶著走的感覺。它的特徵包括：高度專注於當下、行動和意識融為一體、失去反思性的自我意識、掌控感、對時間的感知改變，以及覺得活動本身就有內在的回報——他稱之為「自成目的」（autotelic）。
為了在訪談之外研究心流，契克森米哈伊和同事發展出經驗取樣法。受試者攜帶呼叫器，一天中會在隨機時刻收到訊號，這時他們要記錄自己正在做的活動、挑戰和技能的程度，以及當下的心情。資料顯示，當挑戰和技能都相對較高、而且大致平衡時，最容易出現心流；低挑戰配上高技能往往產生放鬆或無聊，高挑戰配上低技能則產生焦慮。
這個模型在教育、運動、遊戲設計和職場研究中都很有影響力。例如，電玩設計師會動態調整難度，讓玩家停留在挫折與乏味之間的通道裡——這是契克森米哈伊洞見的應用，也解釋了為什麼有些遊戲讓人放不下。
最後這一點暗示了這個理論的局限。心流在道德上是中性的：一個人可以像作曲時一樣，完全沉浸在賭博、強迫性的打電玩或有害的工作中。此外，測量心流高度依賴自我報告；雖然研究把經常經歷心流和幸福感連結在一起，因果方向仍不確定。也有研究者質疑是否真的存在單一的「心流狀態」，還是這個標籤其實把幾種相關的經驗歸在一起。
契克森米哈伊於 2021 年過世，他主張生活品質與其說取決於環境，不如說取決於我們如何投注注意力。不管它在科學上有什麼局限，這個概念為學習者提供了一個實用的經驗法則：選擇略高於目前技能的挑戰、設定清楚的目標、尋求即時回饋，並保護自己的注意力不被打斷。久而久之，這些刻意的選擇能把平凡的任務變成滿足感的來源。

a.title: Same Facts, Different Words
text: Which meat would you buy: one that is "75% lean" or one that is "25% fat"? Most people choose the first one. But wait — they are exactly the same! Only the words are different.
This is called the framing effect. A frame is the way information is shown to us. When the same facts are described in different ways, we often make different choices.
In 1981, two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, did a famous study. They asked people to imagine that a disease would kill 600 people. Then they described two plans to deal with it.

Some people heard: "Plan A will save 200 people." Most of them chose Plan A. Other people heard: "With Plan A, 400 people will die." Most of them chose the other plan instead. But both sentences mean the same thing!
Why does this happen? Words like "save" and "win" make us feel safe. Words like "die" and "lose" make us feel afraid. Our feelings change our choices.

Shops and advertisers know this very well. A sign may say "90% of customers are happy" instead of "10% are unhappy." When you see numbers, try to turn them around in your head. Then you can see the whole picture.
tz: 你會買哪一種肉：「75% 瘦肉」的，還是「25% 脂肪」的？大多數人會選第一種。但等一下——它們完全一樣！只是用字不同而已。
這叫做框架效應。框架就是資訊呈現給我們的方式。當同樣的事實用不同的方式描述時，我們常常會做出不同的選擇。
1981 年，兩位心理學家阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼做了一項著名的研究。他們請人們想像有一種疾病會害死 600 人，接著描述兩個應對的方案。
有些人聽到的是：「方案 A 會救活 200 人。」他們大多選了方案 A。另一些人聽到的是：「採用方案 A，會有 400 人死亡。」他們大多改選了另一個方案。但這兩句話的意思是一樣的！
為什麼會這樣？「救」和「贏」這類字眼讓我們覺得安全；「死」和「輸」這類字眼讓我們感到害怕。我們的感覺改變了我們的選擇。
商店和廣告商都很清楚這一點。一個標示可能會寫「90% 的顧客很滿意」，而不是「10% 的顧客不滿意」。當你看到數字時，試著在腦中把它反過來想。這樣你就能看到全貌。

b.title: The Framing Effect: How Words Shape Our Choices
text: A doctor tells you that a surgery has a 90 percent survival rate. Another doctor says the same surgery has a 10 percent death rate. The facts are identical, yet many people feel far more comfortable with the first description. This is the framing effect: our decisions can change depending on how the same information is presented.

The best-known demonstration comes from a 1981 study by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman. Participants imagined that an unusual disease was expected to kill 600 people and had to choose between two programmes. In one version, they read that Programme A would save 200 people for sure, while Programme B offered a one-third chance of saving all 600 and a two-thirds chance of saving no one. About 72 percent chose the certain option.

Another group saw the same choices described in terms of deaths: under one programme 400 people would die for certain, while the other offered a one-third chance that nobody would die. This time, about 78 percent chose the risky option. Simply changing "saved" to "die" reversed people's preferences.

Kahneman and Tversky explained this using prospect theory. People tend to avoid risks when choices are framed as gains, but take risks to avoid losses. Framing effects have since been found in many areas. In a 1982 study, even doctors were influenced by whether surgery was described in terms of survival or death. Advertisers, politicians and even public health campaigns use the same insight every day.

Framing is not always a trick. Every message has to be described somehow, and no frame is completely neutral. But knowing about the effect can protect us. When you meet an impressive figure, try reframing it: "95 percent fat-free" also means "5 percent fat". If your opinion changes, the words, not the facts, were doing the work.
tz: 一位醫生告訴你，某項手術的存活率是 90%。另一位醫生說，同一項手術的死亡率是 10%。事實完全相同，但許多人對第一種說法感到安心得多。這就是框架效應：同樣的資訊，因為呈現方式不同，我們的決定就可能改變。
最有名的示範來自阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼 1981 年的研究。受試者想像有一種不尋常的疾病預計會害死 600 人，必須在兩個方案中選一個。在其中一個版本中，他們讀到方案 A 一定能救活 200 人，而方案 B 有三分之一的機率救活全部 600 人、三分之二的機率一個人也救不了。大約 72% 的人選擇了確定的方案。
另一組人看到的是同樣的選項，但改用死亡人數來描述：採用其中一個方案，確定會有 400 人死亡；另一個方案則有三分之一的機率沒有人會死。這一次，大約 78% 的人選了有風險的方案。只是把「救活」換成「死亡」，就讓人們的偏好整個反轉。
康納曼和特沃斯基用「展望理論」來解釋這個現象。當選擇被描述成「獲得」時，人們傾向於避開風險；但為了避免「損失」，人們卻願意冒險。從那之後，許多領域都發現了框架效應。在 1982 年的一項研究中，連醫生都會受到手術被描述成「存活」還是「死亡」的影響。廣告商、政治人物，甚至公共衛生宣導，每天都在運用同樣的道理。
框架並不一定是詭計。每一則訊息都必須用某種方式來描述，沒有哪一種框架是完全中立的。但了解這個效應可以保護我們。當你看到一個很亮眼的數字時，試著換個框架想想：「95% 不含脂肪」也代表「含 5% 脂肪」。如果你的看法因此改變，那麼發揮作用的就是用字，而不是事實。

c.title: Framing: Why Logically Equivalent Choices Feel Different
text: Classical economics assumes that a rational decision-maker cares about outcomes, not about how those outcomes are described. Yet a large body of research shows that logically equivalent descriptions can produce systematically different choices. This phenomenon, the framing effect, was given its most famous demonstration in 1981 by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, in a study now known as the "Asian disease problem".

Participants were told to imagine that a disease was expected to kill 600 people. When the alternatives were framed in terms of lives saved — one programme would save 200 people for certain, another offered a one-third probability of saving everyone — 72 percent preferred the certain option. When the identical alternatives were framed in terms of lives lost, 78 percent preferred the gamble. Preferences flipped although nothing of substance had changed.

The authors interpreted these results through prospect theory, which they had published two years earlier. People evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point rather than in absolute terms, are generally risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses, and feel losses more intensely than equivalent gains. A frame works by shifting the reference point, turning the same outcome from a gain into a loss.

Later researchers distinguished several types of framing. In attribute framing, a single feature is described positively or negatively, as when consumers rate beef labelled "75 percent lean" more favourably than beef labelled "25 percent fat". In goal framing, messages stress either the benefits of acting or the costs of failing to act. Each type seems to work through somewhat different mechanisms.

Framing effects are robust but not unlimited. Some studies suggest they become weaker when people think more carefully or must explain their reasoning, though even experts are not immune: in one 1982 study, physicians were swayed by whether surgical outcomes were described as survival or mortality. Intriguingly, a 2012 study by Boaz Keysar and colleagues found that the effect shrank when people considered the disease problem in a foreign language, perhaps because a less familiar language creates emotional distance and encourages more deliberate thought.

Because every message must be expressed in some form, there is no such thing as a frame-free presentation. The ethical question, then, is not whether communicators frame information but how. A doctor who presents both survival and mortality figures, or a journalist who reports both absolute and relative risks, is helping the audience see past the frame to the facts beneath it.
tz: 古典經濟學假設，理性的決策者在乎的是結果，而不是那些結果怎麼被描述。然而大量研究顯示，邏輯上等值的描述，可能會產生有系統的不同選擇。這個現象就是框架效應，它最有名的示範是阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼在 1981 年所做、如今被稱為「亞洲疾病問題」的研究。
受試者被要求想像有一種疾病預計會害死 600 人。當選項以「救活的人數」來描述時——一個方案確定能救活 200 人，另一個方案有三分之一的機率救活所有人——72% 的人偏好確定的選項。當完全相同的選項改以「失去的人命」來描述時，78% 的人偏好賭一把。雖然實質內容一點都沒變，偏好卻翻轉了。
兩位作者用他們兩年前發表的展望理論來解讀這些結果。人們是相對於某個參考點、而不是以絕對的角度來評估結果；面對獲得時通常規避風險，面對損失時則追求風險；而且對損失的感受比同等的獲得更強烈。框架的作用就是移動參考點，把同一個結果從「獲得」變成「損失」。
後來的研究者區分出好幾種框架。在「屬性框架」中，單一特徵被以正面或負面的方式描述，例如消費者對標示「75% 瘦肉」的牛肉評價，比標示「25% 脂肪」的牛肉更好。在「目標框架」中，訊息強調的是採取行動的好處，或是不行動的代價。每一種框架似乎都透過略有不同的機制運作。
框架效應很穩固，但並非沒有極限。有些研究指出，當人們想得更仔細，或必須說明自己的理由時，效應會變弱；不過即使是專家也無法免疫：在 1982 年的一項研究中，醫師也會因為手術結果被描述成「存活」還是「死亡」而動搖。有趣的是，博阿茲・凱薩和同事 2012 年的研究發現，當人們用外語來思考疾病問題時，效應會縮小，或許是因為不那麼熟悉的語言製造了情緒上的距離，促使人更審慎地思考。
因為每一則訊息都必須以某種形式表達，所以根本沒有「不帶框架」的呈現方式。因此，倫理上的問題不在於傳達者有沒有替資訊加上框架，而在於怎麼加。一位同時提供存活率和死亡率的醫生，或一位同時報導絕對風險和相對風險的記者，就是在幫助閱聽人看穿框架，看到底下的事實。

topic: The Gambler's Fallacy: Why Chance Has No Memory
zh: 賭徒謬誤：連輸五次，下一次就一定會贏嗎？
src: Tversky & Kahneman (1971) · Chen, Moskowitz & Shue (2016) · Miller & Sanjurjo (2018)
discuss: Have you ever felt that you were "due" for good luck? Why?
Why do you think random streaks feel so meaningful?
Can you think of a situation where the past really does change the chances?

a.title: Is a Coin Ever "Due"?
text: You flip a coin five times, and it lands on heads every time. What will happen next? Many people feel that tails is "due" — that it has to come soon. But the coin does not remember anything. The chance of tails is still one in two.
This mistake is called the gambler's fallacy. A fallacy is a wrong way of thinking. People believe that if something happens many times, the opposite is more likely to happen next.

The most famous example happened in 1913 at a casino in Monte Carlo. In a game of roulette, the ball landed on black again and again — 26 times in a row! As the blacks kept coming, players bet more and more money on red. They were sure red had to come. They lost millions.
Why do we think this way? Our brains love patterns. We expect a short line of results to look balanced, like a long one. But a small number of coin flips can easily look strange.
Remember: the gambler's fallacy is only a mistake when each event is independent, which means it does not change the next one. A coin, a dice roll and a roulette wheel are all like this.
So next time someone says, "I've lost five times, so I'm sure to win now," you can tell them the truth: luck does not keep score.
tz: 你丟一枚硬幣五次，每次都是正面。接下來會怎樣？很多人覺得反面「該來了」——一定很快就會出現。但硬幣什麼都不記得。出現反面的機率仍然是二分之一。
這個錯誤叫做賭徒謬誤。謬誤是一種錯誤的思考方式。人們相信，如果某件事發生了很多次，接下來就比較可能發生相反的事。
最有名的例子發生在 1913 年蒙地卡羅的一家賭場。在一場輪盤遊戲中，球一次又一次落在黑色——連續 26 次！隨著黑色一直出現，玩家把越來越多的錢押在紅色上。他們確信紅色一定會來。結果他們輸掉了好幾百萬。
我們為什麼會這樣想？我們的大腦喜歡規律。我們期待一小串結果看起來是平均的，就像一長串結果那樣。但少少幾次丟硬幣，很容易看起來很奇怪。
記住：只有當每一次事件都是獨立的——也就是它不會影響下一次——賭徒謬誤才是錯誤。硬幣、擲骰子和輪盤都是這樣。
所以下次有人說「我已經輸了五次，現在一定會贏」時，你可以告訴他們實話：運氣是不會記分的。

b.title: The Gambler's Fallacy: Why Chance Has No Memory
text: In August 1913, something remarkable happened at the Monte Carlo Casino. At one roulette table, the ball fell on black 26 times in a row. As the streak grew, gamblers rushed to bet on red, convinced that the wheel was "due" to change. They lost a fortune. The story has become the classic illustration of the gambler's fallacy: the belief that if a random event has happened often recently, it is less likely to happen next.

The error comes from misunderstanding independence. A fair coin or roulette wheel has no memory, so each spin is unaffected by the last. After five heads, the chance of heads on the sixth flip is still exactly one half.

In 1971, the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman offered an explanation. They argued that people expect even small samples to look like the whole population — a belief they jokingly called "the law of small numbers". Because we know that a coin produces roughly equal heads and tails over many flips, we expect a short run to balance out as well, and a streak feels wrong.

The fallacy is not limited to casinos. Parents who have had several boys may feel a girl is "overdue", even though the chances barely change. Investors sometimes sell shares after a run of gains, expecting a fall simply because rises have continued.

Interestingly, people can make the opposite mistake as well. In the "hot hand" belief, a basketball player who has scored several shots is thought to be more likely to score again. Both errors come from the same habit: seeing meaning in random patterns.

It is important to note when the past does matter. If you draw cards from a deck without putting them back, earlier draws really do change the chances. The key question is always whether events are truly independent.
tz: 1913 年 8 月，蒙地卡羅賭場發生了一件不尋常的事。在一張輪盤桌上，球連續 26 次落在黑色。隨著連續的紀錄越拉越長，賭客們紛紛押紅色，深信輪盤「該」變了。結果他們輸掉了一大筆錢。這個故事成了賭徒謬誤的經典例證：誤以為一個隨機事件最近常常發生，接下來就比較不可能發生。
這個錯誤來自對「獨立性」的誤解。一枚公平的硬幣或一個輪盤沒有記憶，所以每一次轉動都不受上一次影響。連續五次正面之後，第六次丟出正面的機率仍然剛好是二分之一。
1971 年，心理學家阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼提出了一種解釋。他們主張，人們期待就算是很小的樣本，看起來也要像整體一樣——他們開玩笑地把這種信念稱為「小數法則」。因為我們知道丟很多次硬幣，正反面會大致相等，所以我們期待一小串結果也會平均下來，於是連續出現同一面就讓人覺得不對勁。
這個謬誤不只出現在賭場。已經生了好幾個男孩的父母，可能會覺得女孩「早該來了」，即使機率幾乎沒有改變。投資人有時會在股價連漲一段時間後賣出股票，只因為漲勢已經持續很久，就預期會下跌。
有趣的是，人們也可能犯相反的錯誤。在「手感發燙」的信念中，一個已經連進好幾球的籃球員，被認為更可能再投進。這兩種錯誤都來自同一個習慣：在隨機的模式中看見意義。
要注意的是，什麼時候過去真的有影響。如果你從一副牌裡抽牌而不放回去，先前抽出的牌確實會改變機率。關鍵的問題永遠是：這些事件是不是真的獨立？
