c.title: The Gambler's Fallacy and the Mind's Search for Balance
text: In August 1913, the ball at a roulette table in the Monte Carlo Casino landed on black 26 consecutive times. As the run lengthened, players staked ever larger sums on red, reasoning that the wheel was bound to correct itself. The casino reportedly made a fortune that night. The episode lends its name to the "Monte Carlo fallacy", better known as the gambler's fallacy: the mistaken belief that deviations in a random, independent process will soon be offset by opposite outcomes.

The logic seems persuasive because it borrows from a real principle. The law of large numbers states that, over many trials, the proportion of heads from a fair coin approaches one half. But the law operates by dilution, not compensation. An early surplus of heads is not cancelled out by a later surplus of tails; it simply becomes insignificant as the number of flips grows. The coin owes nobody anything.

In a 1971 paper, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman traced the error to what they called belief in the law of small numbers, the expectation that even brief sequences should mirror the properties of the process that generates them. Asked to invent random sequences, people typically alternate too often and avoid long runs, producing strings that look more "random" than genuine randomness does.

The fallacy appears to shape decisions far from the casino. A 2016 study by Daniel Chen, Tobias Moskowitz and Kelly Shue found that asylum judges, loan officers and baseball umpires were slightly less likely to make the same decision twice in a row, as if consecutive identical rulings felt statistically suspicious. Since each case should be judged on its own merits, the pattern implies that some outcomes were affected by the order in which cases happened to arrive.

Its mirror image, the "hot hand", has had a more complicated history. A famous 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Tversky concluded that streak shooting in basketball was a cognitive illusion. In 2018, however, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo identified a subtle statistical bias in the original analysis; correcting for it suggested that a modest hot hand may exist after all. The episode is a reminder that judging randomness is difficult even for experts.

Crucially, the gambler's reasoning becomes correct when events are dependent. In blackjack, cards that have been dealt are not returned to the deck, so the composition of what remains genuinely shifts. The discipline, then, lies in asking a single question before reading meaning into a streak: does the process actually remember?
tz: 1913 年 8 月，蒙地卡羅賭場一張輪盤桌上的球，連續 26 次落在黑色。隨著連續紀錄越拉越長，玩家押在紅色上的金額越來越大，他們的理由是輪盤一定會自我修正。據說那一晚賭場賺了一大筆錢。這個事件讓「蒙地卡羅謬誤」得名，它更廣為人知的名字是賭徒謬誤：誤以為在一個隨機且獨立的過程中，出現的偏差很快就會被相反的結果抵銷。
這個邏輯之所以有說服力，是因為它借用了一個真實的原理。大數法則指出，經過很多次試驗後，一枚公平硬幣出現正面的比例會趨近二分之一。但這個法則是靠「稀釋」運作，而不是靠「補償」。早期多出來的正面，並不會被後來多出來的反面抵銷；它只是隨著丟擲次數增加而變得微不足道。硬幣不欠任何人任何東西。
在 1971 年的一篇論文中，阿摩司・特沃斯基和丹尼爾・康納曼把這個錯誤追溯到他們所說的「相信小數法則」：期待即使是很短的序列，也應該反映出產生它的那個過程的特性。被要求自己編出隨機序列時，人們通常會太常交替、避開長串的連續，結果編出的序列看起來比真正的隨機還要「隨機」。
這個謬誤似乎也影響了賭場以外的決策。丹尼爾・陳、托比亞斯・莫斯科維茲和凱莉・舒在 2016 年的一項研究發現，庇護案件的法官、放款專員和棒球主審，連續兩次做出相同決定的可能性稍微低一些，彷彿連續相同的判決在統計上讓人覺得可疑。既然每個案件都應該依其本身的是非來判斷，這個模式意味著有些結果受到了案件碰巧到來的順序所影響。
它的鏡像——「手感發燙」——歷史就更複雜了。湯瑪斯・季洛維奇、羅伯特・瓦隆和特沃斯基在 1985 年一項著名的研究中斷定，籃球的連續命中只是一種認知錯覺。然而到了 2018 年，約書亞・米勒和亞當・桑胡爾霍在原始分析中找出一個細微的統計偏誤；修正之後的結果顯示，適度的手感發燙也許終究是存在的。這段經過提醒我們：即使是專家，要判斷隨機性也很困難。
關鍵在於，當事件彼此相依時，賭徒的推理就變得正確了。在二十一點中，已經發出的牌不會放回牌堆，所以剩下的牌的組成確實會改變。因此，真正需要的自律在於：在替一串連續結果賦予意義之前，先問一個問題——這個過程真的有記憶嗎？

a.title: When a Number Becomes the Goal
text: Your teacher wants students to read more, so she gives a prize to the student who reads the most pages. Soon, some students start choosing very short, easy books with big pictures. They read lots of pages, but do they really read more?
This problem has a name: Goodhart's law. It is named after Charles Goodhart, a British economist. A popular way to say his idea is: "When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure."

A measure is a number that tells us how something is going, like a test score or the number of pages read. At first, the number shows the truth well. But when people are rewarded only for the number, they find ways to make the number go up — even if the real goal does not improve.

Here is a famous story. In Hanoi, more than a hundred years ago, the government paid people for every rat tail they brought in. Soon, people were cutting off the tails and letting the rats go, so the rats could have more babies!
So, numbers are useful, but they are not the whole goal. Always remember what the number is really for.
tz: 你的老師希望學生多讀書，所以頒獎給讀最多頁的學生。很快地，有些學生開始挑很短、很簡單、圖很大的書。他們讀了很多頁，但他們真的讀得比較多嗎？
這個問題有個名字：古德哈特定律。它以英國經濟學家查爾斯・古德哈特命名。他的想法有一個流行的說法：「當一個衡量標準變成目標，它就不再是好的衡量標準。」
衡量標準是告訴我們事情進展如何的數字，例如考試分數或讀了幾頁。一開始，這個數字能很好地反映真實情況。但當人們只因為這個數字而得到獎勵，他們就會想辦法讓數字上升——即使真正的目標並沒有改善。
有一個著名的故事。一百多年前在河內，政府每收到一條老鼠尾巴就付錢給民眾。很快地，人們開始把老鼠尾巴剪下來，再把老鼠放走，讓牠們生更多小老鼠！
所以，數字很有用，但它們不是全部的目標。永遠記得這個數字真正的用途是什麼。

b.title: Goodhart's Law: When Measures Become Targets
text: Organisations love numbers. Schools track test scores, hospitals track waiting times, and companies track sales. Numbers make complex situations easier to understand and compare. But there is a catch, captured in a principle known as Goodhart's law: once people are rewarded for hitting a number, the number often stops telling the truth.

The idea is named after the British economist Charles Goodhart, who in 1975 observed that economic statistics tended to lose their reliability once governments tried to control them. The popular wording — "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" — came later, from the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern, who summarised his point in 1997.

Why does this happen? A measure is usually chosen because it is linked to something we care about, such as learning or health. When the measure itself becomes the goal, people find ways to raise it that do not improve the underlying thing. A hospital might reduce recorded waiting times by delaying when patients are officially registered. A school might focus narrowly on test techniques rather than deep understanding.

History offers vivid examples. In 1902, colonial officials in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail as proof of a kill. Residents soon began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, and some reportedly even farmed rats for profit.

Goodhart's law does not mean that measuring things is useless. It means that numbers should be used thoughtfully: combine several measures, check them against reality, change them when people learn to game them, and remember the purpose behind them.

A good question to ask about any target is simple: if this number went up, would the thing we actually care about really be better? If the answer is not clearly yes, it may be time to rethink the target.
tz: 組織都很愛數字。學校追蹤考試分數、醫院追蹤等候時間、公司追蹤銷售額。數字讓複雜的情況更容易理解和比較。但這裡有個陷阱，被一個稱為古德哈特定律的原則點了出來：一旦人們因為達到某個數字而得到獎勵，這個數字往往就不再說真話了。
這個概念以英國經濟學家查爾斯・古德哈特命名。他在 1975 年觀察到，一旦政府試圖控制經濟統計數字，這些數字就容易失去可靠性。流行的說法——「當一個衡量標準變成目標，它就不再是好的衡量標準」——則是後來人類學家瑪麗蓮・史翠珊在 1997 年總結他的觀點時提出的。
為什麼會這樣？一個衡量標準之所以被選上，通常是因為它和我們在乎的事情有關，例如學習或健康。當衡量標準本身變成目標，人們就會找到方法提高它，卻沒有改善真正的根本。醫院可能藉由延後病人正式掛號的時間，來減少紀錄上的等候時間。學校可能只狹隘地專注於考試技巧，而不是深入的理解。
歷史上有很生動的例子。1902 年，河內的殖民官員每收到一條老鼠尾巴當作捕殺的證明，就發一筆賞金。居民很快就開始剪下尾巴、放走老鼠讓牠們繁殖，據說有些人甚至為了賺錢而養老鼠。
古德哈特定律並不代表衡量事物沒有用。它的意思是，數字應該被審慎使用：結合好幾種衡量標準、用現實去檢驗它們、當人們學會鑽漏洞時就修改它們，並且記得它們背後的目的。
對任何目標都可以問一個簡單的問題：如果這個數字上升了，我們真正在乎的事情真的會變好嗎？如果答案不是很明確的「會」，也許就該重新思考這個目標了。

c.title: Gaming the Numbers: Goodhart's Law and Its Relatives
text: Modern institutions run on metrics. Governments set targets for emergency-room waiting times, universities compete in rankings, and online platforms optimise for clicks and minutes watched. Quantification promises accountability and clarity. Goodhart's law warns that the promise contains a trap: indicators that work well as passive observations often degrade once they are turned into goals that carry rewards or penalties.

Charles Goodhart, an economist advising the Bank of England, made the point in 1975 in the context of monetary policy, observing that statistical regularities tended to collapse once pressure was placed on them for control purposes. The pithier formulation now attached to his name — "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" — was coined by the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern in 1997. A closely related idea, Campbell's law, was proposed by the social psychologist Donald Campbell, who argued that the more a quantitative indicator is used for social decision-making, the more it will be subject to corruption and the more it will distort the processes it is meant to monitor.

The mechanisms vary. Sometimes people simply cheat, falsifying data outright. More often they respond rationally to incentives by shifting effort toward what is counted and away from what is not. Teachers may narrow instruction to tested content; hospitals may reclassify patients to meet deadlines; researchers may pursue publishable results rather than important ones. In each case, the indicator improves while the underlying goal stagnates or declines.

The colonial rat bounty in Hanoi in 1902, in which payments for severed tails reportedly encouraged residents to release injured rats and even to breed them, has become a classic illustration. Such episodes are sometimes grouped under the label "perverse incentives".

Recognising Goodhart's law does not mean abandoning measurement, which remains indispensable. Rather, it suggests design principles: use multiple indicators that are hard to manipulate simultaneously, rotate or refresh targets, combine numbers with qualitative judgement, and keep the underlying purpose in view. Some argue for using metrics primarily to learn and diagnose rather than to reward and punish.

The deeper lesson concerns the relationship between maps and territory. A number is a simplified map of something complex. When we steer by the map alone, we should not be surprised to find ourselves somewhere we never meant to go. Good measurement begins, and ends, with remembering what the map is for.
tz: 現代機構靠指標運作。政府為急診室等候時間設定目標，大學在排名中競爭，網路平台則針對點擊數和觀看分鐘數做最佳化。量化承諾帶來問責與清晰。古德哈特定律警告，這個承諾裡藏著陷阱：作為被動觀察時很好用的指標，一旦被變成附帶獎懲的目標，往往就會失真。

為英格蘭銀行提供建議的經濟學家查爾斯・古德哈特，在 1975 年以貨幣政策為背景提出這個觀點：一旦為了控制目的對統計規律施加壓力，這些規律就容易崩解。現在冠上他名字、更簡潔有力的說法——「當一個衡量標準變成目標，它就不再是好的衡量標準」——是人類學家瑪麗蓮・史翠珊在 1997 年提出的。一個密切相關的概念「坎貝爾定律」是社會心理學家唐納德・坎貝爾提出的，他主張：一個量化指標越常被用於社會決策，就越容易被腐化，也越會扭曲它原本要監測的過程。
機制各有不同。有時人們直接作弊，徹底竄改資料。更常見的是，他們理性地回應誘因，把力氣轉向被計算的部分，遠離不被計算的部分。老師可能把教學縮小到考試內容；醫院可能為了符合期限而重新分類病人；研究者可能追求容易發表、而非真正重要的成果。在每一個例子中，指標都改善了，根本的目標卻停滯甚至倒退。
1902 年河內殖民政府的老鼠賞金——據說以被剪下的尾巴計酬，反而促使居民放走受傷的老鼠，甚至繁殖老鼠——已經成為經典例子。這類事件有時被歸類為「反常誘因」。
認識古德哈特定律，並不代表要放棄衡量，衡量仍然不可或缺。相反地，它提示了一些設計原則：使用難以同時操弄的多項指標、輪替或更新目標、把數字和質性判斷結合起來，並且始終把根本目的放在眼前。有些人主張，指標主要應該用來學習和診斷，而不是用來獎勵和懲罰。
更深層的教訓和「地圖與實地」的關係有關。數字是一張描繪複雜事物的簡化地圖。當我們只看地圖駕駛時，就不該驚訝自己最後到了一個從來不想去的地方。好的衡量，始於、也終於記得這張地圖是用來做什麼的。

topic: Growth Mindset: The Power of "Not Yet"
zh: 成長型思維：「還沒」的力量
src: Mueller & Dweck (1998) · Sisk et al. (2018) · Yeager et al. (2019)
discuss: Think of something you couldn't do before but can do now. How did you learn it?

a.title: Not Yet!
text: Imagine two students who both fail a math test. The first one says, "I'm just bad at math." The second one says, "I haven't learned this yet. I'll try a new way." Which student do you think will improve more?
An American psychologist named Carol Dweck studied this for many years. She found that people often have one of two mindsets, or ways of thinking about their abilities.

People with a fixed mindset believe their talents cannot change. They often avoid hard tasks because they are afraid of looking stupid. People with a growth mindset believe they can get better with effort, good strategies, and help from others.

Dweck noticed something interesting about praise. When adults say, "You're so smart!" some children start to avoid challenges. When adults praise their hard work and their strategies, children are more willing to try difficult things.
One small word can help: "yet." Instead of saying "I can't do this," try saying, "I can't do this yet."
A growth mindset is not magic. Effort alone is not enough — you also need to try new strategies and ask for help. But believing you can grow is a good place to start.
tz: 想像兩個數學考試都不及格的學生。第一個說：「我就是數學很爛。」第二個說：「這個我還沒學會，我來試試新方法。」你覺得哪個學生會進步比較多？
一位名叫卡蘿・杜維克的美國心理學家研究這個問題很多年。她發現人們常常有兩種心態——也就是看待自己能力的兩種方式——的其中一種。
有固定型思維的人相信自己的天分無法改變。他們常常逃避困難的任務，因為怕自己看起來很笨。有成長型思維的人則相信，靠努力、好的策略和別人的幫助，自己可以變得更好。
杜維克注意到一件和稱讚有關的有趣事情。當大人說「你好聰明！」時，有些孩子會開始逃避挑戰。當大人稱讚孩子的努力和方法時，孩子比較願意嘗試困難的事。
一個小小的字就能幫上忙：「還（yet）」。與其說「我做不到」，試著說「我還做不到」。
成長型思維不是魔法。光靠努力是不夠的——你也需要嘗試新的策略、尋求協助。但相信自己能成長，是一個很好的起點。

b.title: Growth Mindset: The Power — and Limits — of Believing You Can Improve
text: Why do some students give up after a setback while others work harder? The Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck spent decades exploring this question. Her answer centres on what she calls mindsets: beliefs about whether abilities such as intelligence are fixed or can be developed.

People with a fixed mindset tend to see ability as something you either have or do not have. As a result, mistakes can feel like proof of failure, and challenges become threats to avoid. People with a growth mindset see ability as something that can be built through effort, good strategies and help from others, so setbacks become information rather than verdicts.

One influential study in 1998, led by Claudia Mueller and Dweck, praised children either for their intelligence or for their effort after a set of puzzles. When later offered a choice of tasks, many of those praised for being smart chose easier ones, and they performed worse after facing difficult problems. Those praised for effort were more willing to take on challenges.

Growth mindset ideas spread quickly into schools around the world. However, research has produced a more cautious picture. A large 2018 analysis found that, on average, mindset programmes had small effects on achievement, though they appeared more helpful for students from disadvantaged backgrounds or with lower grades. A 2019 national study in the United States found that a short online lesson modestly raised grades among lower-achieving students.

Dweck herself has warned against a "false growth mindset" — simply praising effort or telling students to try harder without teaching better strategies. Effort that keeps repeating the same unsuccessful method is unlikely to help, however hard a student tries.
The lesson, then, is a balanced one. Believing you can improve will not work miracles, but combined with good strategies and support, it can make learning from mistakes much easier.
tz: 為什麼有些學生遇到挫折就放棄，有些卻更加努力？史丹佛大學心理學家卡蘿・杜維克花了數十年探討這個問題。她的答案以她所說的「心態」為核心：也就是我們相信智力等能力是固定的，還是可以培養的。
有固定型思維的人傾向把能力看成「有就有、沒有就沒有」的東西。因此，錯誤可能讓人覺得是失敗的證明，挑戰則變成要躲開的威脅。有成長型思維的人則把能力看成可以透過努力、好的策略和他人協助建立起來的東西，所以挫折變成了資訊，而不是定論。
1998 年由克勞蒂亞・穆勒和杜維克主持的一項重要研究中，孩子們做完一組拼圖後，分別被稱讚聰明或被稱讚努力。之後讓他們選擇任務時，許多被稱讚聰明的孩子選了比較簡單的，而且在遇到困難的題目後表現變差。被稱讚努力的孩子則比較願意接受挑戰。
成長型思維的觀念很快就傳進世界各地的學校。然而，研究呈現出比較謹慎的圖像。2018 年一項大型分析發現，整體而言，心態課程對學業成就的效果很小，不過對弱勢背景或成績較低的學生似乎比較有幫助。2019 年美國一項全國性研究發現，一堂簡短的線上課程，讓成績較低的學生成績小幅提升。
杜維克本人也曾警告所謂的「假成長型思維」——只是稱讚努力，或叫學生更努力，卻沒有教他們更好的策略。一直重複同一個失敗方法的努力，不管學生多努力，都不太可能有幫助。
所以，這個教訓是一個平衡的教訓。相信自己能進步並不會創造奇蹟，但搭配好的策略和支持，它能讓從錯誤中學習變得容易得多。

c.title: Mindsets Under the Microscope
text: Few ideas from educational psychology have travelled as quickly from journal to classroom as Carol Dweck's theory of mindsets. Its core claim is elegantly simple: students who believe intelligence can be developed — a "growth mindset" — respond to difficulty differently from those who regard it as a fixed trait, and these beliefs shape learning over time.

The theory grew out of decades of research on how children interpret failure. In a frequently cited 1998 study, Claudia Mueller and Dweck found that fifth-graders praised for their intelligence after a successful task were subsequently more likely to choose easy problems, to enjoy difficult ones less and even to misrepresent their scores, whereas those praised for effort persisted more readily. The finding seemed to offer teachers a cheap and powerful lever: change the beliefs, and achievement would follow.

Enthusiasm outpaced evidence. Interventions were adopted widely, sometimes reduced to posters and slogans. When researchers began to test them at scale, results were sobering. A 2018 meta-analysis by Victoria Sisk and colleagues reported that the relationship between mindset and academic achievement was weak and that interventions produced, on average, very small effects. Some attempts to replicate earlier findings also failed. Critics also noted that some of the most enthusiastic claims came from small samples.

Defenders responded that the question is not whether mindset interventions transform everyone, but for whom and under what conditions they help. The National Study of Learning Mindsets, a randomised trial involving over 12,000 ninth-graders in the United States and published in 2019, found that a brief online intervention modestly improved grades among lower-achieving students, particularly in schools whose culture supported challenge-seeking. In this view, a small, cheap effect that reaches millions may still matter.

Dweck has also criticised what she calls a "false growth mindset": praising effort regardless of outcome, or equating the mindset with optimism. Productive struggle, she argues, requires new strategies and honest feedback, not merely persistence or cheerful encouragement.

The debate offers a useful lesson about educational ideas generally. Beliefs about ability do appear to matter, but they operate within classrooms, relationships and opportunities. Treating a mindset as a stand-alone cure overstates its power; dismissing it entirely ignores evidence that, for some students in some settings, it helps. Like the mindset itself, our view of the research should remain open to revision.
tz: 很少有教育心理學的概念，像卡蘿・杜維克的心態理論這樣，從期刊迅速走進教室。它的核心主張簡潔有力：相信智力可以培養的學生——「成長型思維」——面對困難時的反應，和把智力視為固定特質的學生不同，而這些信念會隨著時間影響學習。
這個理論源自數十年來對孩子如何詮釋失敗的研究。在 1998 年一項常被引用的研究中，克勞蒂亞・穆勒和杜維克發現，完成任務後被稱讚聰明的五年級學生，之後比較可能選擇簡單的題目、比較不喜歡困難的題目，甚至會謊報分數；被稱讚努力的學生則比較能堅持下去。這個發現似乎給了老師一個便宜又有力的槓桿：改變信念，成就就會隨之而來。
熱情跑在證據前面。各種介入課程被廣泛採用，有時被簡化成海報和口號。當研究者開始大規模檢驗它們時，結果令人清醒。2018 年由維多利亞・西斯克等人進行的統合分析指出，心態和學業成就之間的關係很弱，介入課程的平均效果非常小。有些重複早期發現的嘗試也失敗了。批評者也指出，一些最熱烈的主張來自很小的樣本。
支持者回應說，問題不在於心態介入能不能改變所有人，而在於它對誰、在什麼條件下有幫助。「全國學習心態研究」是一項涵蓋美國一萬兩千多名九年級學生的隨機試驗，於 2019 年發表，發現一個簡短的線上介入，讓成績較低的學生成績小幅進步，尤其是在校園文化支持挑戰的學校。從這個角度看，一個小而便宜、卻能觸及數百萬人的效果，仍然可能很重要。
杜維克也批評了她所說的「假成長型思維」：不管結果如何都稱讚努力，或把成長型思維等同於樂觀。她主張，有成效的掙扎需要新的策略和誠實的回饋，而不只是堅持或打氣。
這場辯論對教育觀念整體提供了一個有用的教訓。對能力的信念似乎確實重要，但它們是在教室、人際關係和機會之中發揮作用的。把心態當成單獨的萬靈丹，是高估了它的力量；完全否定它，則忽略了它對某些情境下的某些學生確實有幫助的證據。就像成長型思維本身一樣，我們對這些研究的看法也應該保持開放、隨時修正。

a.title: Why Good Looks Can Fool Us
text: Imagine a new student joins your class. She is good-looking and smiles a lot. Before she even speaks, many people may think she is also smart, kind, and hard-working. This is called the halo effect.
A halo is the circle of light that you see above angels' heads in old paintings. In the halo effect, one good thing about a person "shines" on everything else about them.

The idea comes from an American psychologist named Edward Thorndike. In 1920, he studied how army officers judged their soldiers. He found that if an officer liked one thing about a soldier, he usually gave that soldier high scores for everything else, too.
The halo effect also works the other way. If we notice one bad thing about someone, we may think everything about them is bad.
Companies know this well. They pay famous, attractive stars to show their products, because we often think the products must be good, too.
So next time you meet someone new, remember: one good or bad point does not tell the whole story. Get to know the person first.

光環就是在古老畫作中，天使頭上那圈光。在月暈效應裡，一個人身上的一個優點，會「照亮」他其他所有的地方。
這個概念來自一位名叫愛德華・桑代克的美國心理學家。1920 年，他研究軍官如何評價他們的士兵。他發現，如果軍官喜歡某個士兵的某一點，通常也會在其他所有項目給那個士兵高分。
月暈效應反過來也成立。如果我們注意到某人一個缺點，可能就會覺得他什麼都不好。
公司很清楚這一點。他們付錢請有名、有魅力的明星來展示產品，因為我們常常會覺得產品一定也很好。
所以下次認識新朋友時，記得：一個優點或缺點並不能說明一切。先好好認識這個人吧。

b.title: The Halo Effect: When One Trait Colours Everything
text: We like to believe that we judge people fairly, weighing each of their qualities separately. In reality, a single strong impression — good looks, a confident voice, a famous name — often spreads to everything else we think about a person. Psychologists call this the halo effect.

The term was introduced in 1920 by the American psychologist Edward Thorndike. Studying how military officers rated their soldiers on qualities such as intelligence, loyalty and leadership, he noticed that the ratings were suspiciously consistent. A soldier rated highly on one quality tended to be rated highly on all of them, as if the officers formed a general impression first and filled in the details afterwards.

Later studies found the same pattern in many settings. In a well-known 1977 experiment, students watched a video of a lecturer who behaved either warmly or coldly. Those who saw the warm version judged his appearance, mannerisms and even his accent as more appealing — and most did not realise their judgement had been influenced at all.

The effect has a negative twin, sometimes called the horn effect, in which one bad impression drags down our view of everything else. A spelling mistake on a job application, for example, can make an employer doubt the applicant's skills in unrelated areas.

These biases matter in classrooms, job interviews and courtrooms. Attractive people, for instance, are often assumed to be more competent, even when there is no evidence for it. To reduce the effect, some organisations score each quality separately, use the same questions for every candidate, or hide names and photos during early stages of selection.

We cannot switch off first impressions completely. But knowing about the halo effect can remind us to look for evidence before letting one shining detail decide the whole picture — or one flaw darken it.
tz: 我們喜歡相信自己評斷別人很公平，會分別衡量對方的每一項特質。但實際上，一個強烈的印象——好看的外表、自信的聲音、響亮的名字——常常會擴散到我們對這個人的所有看法上。心理學家稱之為月暈效應。
這個名詞是美國心理學家愛德華・桑代克在 1920 年提出的。他研究軍官如何在智力、忠誠和領導力等特質上替士兵評分，注意到這些評分一致得令人起疑：在某一項得到高分的士兵，往往每一項都得到高分，彷彿軍官們先形成一個整體印象，事後才把細節填上去。

這些偏誤在教室、工作面試和法庭上都很重要。例如，長得好看的人常被認為比較能幹，即使沒有任何證據。為了減少這個效應，有些機構會把每項特質分開評分、對每位應徵者問同樣的問題，或在篩選初期隱藏姓名和照片。
我們無法完全關掉第一印象。但認識月暈效應，可以提醒我們先找證據，而不是讓一個閃亮的細節決定整體印象——或讓一個缺點讓它黯淡無光。

c.title: Halo Effects: How Impressions Spill Over
text: Human judgement is rarely as modular as it feels. When we evaluate a person, a product or even an institution, we believe we are assessing separate attributes — competence, honesty, attractiveness — on their individual merits. In practice, a single salient trait frequently bleeds into all the others, producing what psychologists have called, for more than a century, the halo effect.

Edward Thorndike gave the phenomenon its name in a 1920 paper, "A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings". Examining officers' assessments of their men, he found correlations between supposedly independent qualities that were far too high to be plausible. Physique, intelligence, leadership and character moved together, suggesting that raters were responding to an overall impression rather than to the specific traits they had been asked to judge.

Perhaps the most striking demonstration came from Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson in 1977. Students watched one of two videotaped interviews with the same lecturer, who spoke with a European accent. In one he was warm and agreeable; in the other, cold and distrustful. Students who saw the warm version rated his appearance, mannerisms and accent as appealing, while the others found the very same features irritating. Crucially, participants insisted that their liking for the man had not affected their other ratings — some even claimed the causation ran the other way.

The consequences reach well beyond the laboratory. Research on hiring, grading and even legal decisions suggests that attractive or confident individuals are often credited with qualities they have not demonstrated, while a single negative cue can produce the opposite "horn" effect. Brands exploit the same mechanism when they pair products with admired celebrities, hoping that goodwill toward the person will transfer to the merchandise.

What makes the halo effect so stubborn is its invisibility. Because the global impression forms quickly and feels like perception rather than inference, we experience it as simply seeing the person as they are. Effective countermeasures therefore tend to be structural rather than personal: rating each criterion independently, using standardised questions, separating the people who judge different qualities, and removing irrelevant information such as names or photographs.

None of this means first impressions are worthless; they sometimes carry real information. The danger lies in allowing one vivid feature to answer questions it has nothing to do with. Good judgement begins with noticing which question we are actually answering.
tz: 人類的判斷很少像感覺上那樣各自獨立。當我們評估一個人、一項產品，甚至一個機構時，我們以為自己是在依各自的優劣，分別評估不同的特質——能力、誠實、吸引力。實際上，一個顯著的特質常常滲透到其他所有特質，造成心理學家一百多年來所說的月暈效應。
愛德華・桑代克在 1920 年的論文〈心理評分中的一種恆定誤差〉中為這個現象命名。他檢視軍官對部下的評估，發現本應彼此獨立的特質之間，相關程度高到不可信。體格、智力、領導力和品格一起升降，顯示評分者回應的是整體印象，而不是被要求評判的具體特質。
或許最驚人的例證來自理查・尼斯貝特和提摩西・威爾森 1977 年的研究。學生觀看同一位帶有歐洲口音的講師兩段訪談錄影中的一段：一段裡他溫暖隨和，另一段裡他冷淡多疑。看到溫暖版本的學生認為他的外表、舉止和口音很討喜，另一組則覺得同樣的特徵令人煩躁。關鍵是，受試者堅稱自己對這個人的好感並沒有影響其他評分——有些人甚至宣稱因果關係正好相反。
後果遠遠超出實驗室。關於招聘、評分甚至司法判決的研究顯示，外表好看或有自信的人，常被認定擁有他們並未展現的特質；而單一的負面線索，則可能產生相反的「尖角」效應。品牌把產品和受人喜愛的名人搭配時，利用的正是同一個機制，希望人們對名人的好感會轉移到商品上。
月暈效應之所以如此頑固，在於它看不見。因為整體印象形成得很快，而且感覺像是「看到的」而不是「推論出來的」，我們會覺得自己只是看見了這個人本來的樣子。因此，有效的對策往往是制度性的，而不是個人性的：每項標準分開評分、使用標準化的問題、讓不同的人評判不同的特質，以及移除姓名或照片等無關資訊。
這些都不代表第一印象毫無價值；它們有時確實帶有真實的資訊。危險在於讓一個鮮明的特徵，去回答和它毫不相干的問題。好的判斷，從察覺自己真正在回答哪個問題開始。

topic: The IKEA Effect: Why We Love What We Build
zh: IKEA 效應：為什麼自己動手做的東西特別可愛？
src: Norton, Mochon & Ariely (2012) · Mochon, Norton & Ariely (2012)
discuss: What have you made that you value more than other people might?
Why do you think the effect disappears when people don't finish?
How can a group avoid overvaluing its own ideas?

a.title: Why We Love What We Build
text: Have you ever made something with your own hands, like a paper boat, a cake or a simple shelf? Even if it was not perfect, you probably felt proud of it. You may have liked it more than a better one from a shop.
Scientists call this the IKEA effect. IKEA is a company that sells furniture in flat boxes, so people have to build it themselves at home.

In 2012, three researchers, Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely, tested this idea. Some people built a simple IKEA box. Others only looked at a box that was already built. Then everyone said how much they would pay for it. The builders were willing to pay more for their own boxes.

In another test, people folded paper animals. They valued their own simple work almost as much as beautiful paper animals made by experts. But other people did not agree. To them, the beginners' work was not worth much.
There was one important rule. The effect only worked when people finished the job. If they could not complete it, the love disappeared.
So hard work can make us love things. That is good, but be careful. Sometimes we like our own ideas just because they are ours, not because they are the best.
tz: 你有沒有親手做過東西，像是紙船、蛋糕或一個簡單的架子？就算它不完美，你大概還是覺得很驕傲。你甚至可能比店裡買的更好的那個還要喜歡它。
科學家把這叫做 IKEA 效應。IKEA 是一家把家具裝在扁平盒子裡賣的公司，所以大家得在家自己組裝。
2012 年，三位研究者——麥可・諾頓、丹尼爾・莫雄和丹・艾瑞利——測試了這個想法。有些人親手組裝了一個簡單的 IKEA 盒子，其他人只是看看已經組好的盒子。接著每個人都說出自己願意花多少錢買它。動手組裝的人願意為自己的盒子付更多錢。
在另一項測試中，人們摺紙動物。他們對自己簡單作品的評價，幾乎和專家摺的漂亮紙動物一樣高。但其他人並不這麼認為。在他們眼中，新手的作品不太值錢。
有一個重要的規則：只有在人們完成工作時，這個效應才會出現。如果他們沒辦法完成，那份喜愛就消失了。
所以努力付出會讓我們愛上一樣東西。這是好事，但要小心。有時候我們喜歡自己的想法，只是因為那是我們的，而不是因為它最好。

b.title: The IKEA Effect: When Effort Leads to Love
text: Flat-pack furniture is famous for confusing instructions and missing screws. Yet many people who struggle for an hour to build a bookshelf end up feeling surprisingly attached to it. Psychologists have a name for this: the IKEA effect, the tendency to place a higher value on things we have made ourselves.

The term comes from a 2012 paper by Michael Norton of Harvard Business School, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely. In one study, some participants assembled a plain IKEA storage box, while others received an identical box that was already put together. When asked how much they would pay, the builders offered noticeably more than the non-builders, even though their boxes were no better.

A second study used origami. Participants who folded paper cranes and frogs valued their amateur creations nearly as highly as models made by experts. Neutral observers, however, considered the beginners' work almost worthless. In other words, effort changed how the makers saw their work, not how good it actually was.

The researchers also found a key condition. When participants built something and then took it apart, or failed to finish it, the extra value disappeared. Labour seems to lead to love only when it ends in success.

Why might this happen? One explanation is that completing a task makes people feel competent, and they transfer that pride to the object. Another is that people want to believe their time was well spent.

The effect has practical uses. Companies let customers design their own trainers or add an ingredient to a recipe, hoping they will value the product more. But it has a downside too. Teams may overvalue ideas they invented themselves and ignore better solutions from outside. Knowing about the IKEA effect can help us ask an honest question: do I like this because it is good, or simply because it is mine?
tz: 組合式家具出了名地說明書難懂、螺絲又常常少一顆。然而，許多花了一個小時奮力組好書架的人，最後卻對它有種出乎意料的感情。心理學家為此取了個名字：IKEA 效應，也就是人們傾向於給自己做的東西更高的價值。
這個名詞來自 2012 年的一篇論文，作者是哈佛商學院的麥可・諾頓、丹尼爾・莫雄和丹・艾瑞利。在其中一項研究中，有些受試者組裝了一個樸素的 IKEA 收納盒，其他人則拿到一個已經組好、一模一樣的盒子。被問到願意付多少錢時，動手組裝的人出價明顯比沒有組裝的人高，即使他們的盒子並沒有比較好。

為什麼會這樣？一種解釋是，完成一項任務會讓人覺得自己有能力，於是把這份驕傲轉移到那樣東西上。另一種解釋是，人們想相信自己的時間花得值得。

c.title: Labour Leads to Love: The IKEA Effect
text: Few consumer experiences are as reliably frustrating as assembling flat-pack furniture. Yet the hour spent wrestling with an Allen key seems to buy something besides a bookshelf: affection. In 2012, Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely gave this phenomenon a memorable name, the IKEA effect, defined as the increase in valuation that people attach to products they have partly created themselves.

Their experiments were simple. Participants who assembled IKEA storage boxes were willing to pay significantly more for them than participants who merely inspected pre-assembled ones. In an origami study, novices valued their own clumsy cranes and frogs nearly as much as expert-made models, whereas observers who had not folded anything regarded the novices' efforts as close to worthless. The inflated valuation, in other words, was confined to the creators.

Crucially, the effect depended on completion. When participants built objects and then dismantled them, or were prevented from finishing, the premium vanished. The authors argued that effortful creation increases value chiefly when it signals competence: a finished product is visible proof that we are capable.

The idea resonates with a popular business story. In the 1950s, the tale goes, instant cake mixes sold poorly until manufacturers removed powdered egg and asked bakers to add a fresh one, restoring a sense of genuine contribution. Historians of marketing have questioned whether this account is accurate, and other factors, such as taste, may explain the change, but its endurance suggests how intuitive the IKEA effect feels.

The effect has obvious commercial applications, from build-your-own toys to customisable sneakers. It may also have psychological benefits, since investing effort can deepen people's commitment to a project. Yet it has a darker side. Organisations sometimes suffer from what is called the "not-invented-here" syndrome, rejecting external solutions in favour of inferior in-house ones. Inventors may overprice their products, and writers may resist editing paragraphs that cost them days of labour.
Follow-up work by Mochon and colleagues found that the effect grew stronger when people's sense of competence had been shaken, supporting the idea that making things partly serves to reassure us.

The practical lesson is not to avoid making things — the satisfaction is real and often valuable. It is to separate two judgments that effort tends to blur: how much a creation means to us, and how good it actually is to everyone else.
tz: 很少有哪種消費經驗，能像組裝組合式家具那樣穩定地讓人抓狂。然而，跟六角扳手奮戰的那一個小時，似乎除了書架之外還買到了別的東西：感情。2012 年，麥可・諾頓、丹尼爾・莫雄和丹・艾瑞利為這個現象取了一個好記的名字——IKEA 效應，定義是：人們對自己參與製作的產品，會給予更高的估價。
他們的實驗很簡單。親手組裝 IKEA 收納盒的受試者，願意付的錢明顯多於只檢查了現成盒子的受試者。在一項摺紙研究中，新手對自己笨拙的紙鶴和紙青蛙的評價，幾乎和專家的作品一樣高；而沒有摺任何東西的旁觀者，卻認為新手的作品近乎一文不值。換句話說，被灌水的估價只存在於創作者身上。
關鍵在於，這個效應取決於「完成」。當受試者做好東西之後又把它拆掉，或被阻止完成時，額外的價值就消失了。作者主張，費力的創作之所以會提高價值，主要是因為它代表了能力：完成的作品是我們有能力的看得見的證據。
這個想法呼應了一個流行的商業故事。據說在 1950 年代，即溶蛋糕粉一直賣不好，直到廠商拿掉了蛋粉，要烘焙的人自己加一顆新鮮的蛋，恢復了一種「真的有參與」的感覺。行銷史學者質疑過這個說法是否正確，而且口味等其他因素也可能解釋銷量的改變；但這個故事流傳至今，顯示了 IKEA 效應有多符合人們的直覺。
這個效應有明顯的商業用途，從自己組裝的玩具到可客製化的球鞋都是。它也可能有心理上的好處，因為投入心力能加深人們對一項計畫的投入感。但它也有陰暗的一面。組織有時會出現所謂的「非我發明」症候群，排斥外部的解決辦法，偏好較差的自家方案。發明者可能會把產品定價過高，作家也可能抗拒刪改那些花了他們好幾天心血的段落。
莫雄和同事的後續研究發現，當人們對自己能力的信心受到動搖時，這個效應會變得更強，這支持了一個想法：動手做東西，部分是為了讓我們安心。
實際的教訓並不是要避免動手做東西——那份滿足感是真實的，而且常常很有價值。而是要把努力容易混淆的兩種判斷分開：一件作品對我們有多重要，以及它在其他人眼中實際上有多好。

opts: With caution, noting it may not be accurate
As a proven fact supported by all historians
As a joke that has nothing to do with the effect
With anger at the dishonest manufacturers
q.why: 第 4 段：Historians … have questioned whether this account is accurate——作者有所保留。

q.q: What is the function of paragraph 5?
opts: To show both the benefits and the drawbacks of the effect
To explain how IKEA boxes were tested in the laboratory
To argue that writers should never edit their own work
To describe the history of build-your-own toys in detail
q.why: 第 5 段先講商業與心理上的好處，再以 Yet it has a darker side 轉到缺點。

q.q: A student refuses to change a project after classmates point out clear errors, saying, "I worked so hard on it, so it must be good." Based on the passage, how should you judge this?
opts: It is reasonable, since effort always improves the final result
It confuses the project's meaning to the maker with its quality
It is correct, because finished work is always proof of quality
It is wrong, because hard work never adds any personal value
q.why: 第 7 段：要分開「作品對我們有多重要」和「它實際上有多好」。

st.m: In 2012, Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely gave this phenomenon a memorable name, the IKEA effect, defined as the increase in valuation that people attach to products they have partly created themselves.
st.mz: 親手完成的東西會讓我們更珍惜，但要分清楚它對我們的意義和它實際的好壞。
t: Their experiments were simple.
Crucially, the effect depended on completion.
The idea resonates with a popular business story.
The effect has obvious commercial applications, from build-your-own toys to customisable sneakers.
Follow-up work by Mochon and colleagues found that the effect grew stronger when people's sense of competence had been shaken, supporting the idea that making things partly serves to reassure us.
st.c: It is to separate two judgments that effort tends to blur: how much a creation means to us, and how good it actually is to everyone else.

topic: King Midas and the Golden Touch
zh: 點石成金的邁達斯王

a.title: Be Careful What You Wish For
text: Long ago, in a Greek story, there was a king named Midas. He loved gold more than anything.
One day, Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus. To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish.
Midas said, 'I wish that everything I touch turns into gold!' His wish came true.
At first he was very happy. He touched a stone, a flower and a chair, and they all became gold.
But then he tried to eat. His bread and water turned into gold too! Midas was hungry and afraid.
He asked the god to take the gift back. Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: How the king's cooks made bread and wine
A king whose golden wish caused trouble
A friend of the god Dionysus who got lost
Why gold is such a beautiful metal
q.why: 全文講邁達斯的點金願望帶來麻煩。

q.q: According to the reading, which is TRUE?
opts: The god gave Midas three wishes to thank him.
Midas was hungry because his food turned into stone.
Midas got his wish after he helped the god's friend.
At first, Midas was afraid of his golden touch.
q.why: 第 2 段：Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus. To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish。只有一個願望；食物變成黃金；一開始他很開心。

q.q: Which is the right order? (a) His bread turned into gold. (b) He helped a friend of the god. (c) He asked the god to take the gift back.
q.why: 先幫了神的朋友（第 2 段）→ 想吃東西時麵包變成黃金（第 5 段）→ 請神收回禮物（第 6 段）。

q.q: In the text, “touch” means ___.
opts: look at something closely
eat something quickly
buy something at a shop
put your hand on something
q.why: touch = 碰觸。

q.q: What lesson did Midas learn?
opts: Gold is the most important thing of all
The gods never help ordinary people
Some things are worth more than gold
Wishes always make people happy
q.why: 最後一段：some things are worth more than gold。

q.q: A classmate says, “If I were rich, I would never have any problems.” What would Midas's story suggest?
opts: Money can't buy everything, like food and love
You are right — gold solves every problem
You should ask a god to give you money
You are right — being rich solves every problem
q.why: 故事寓意：金錢買不到所有真正重要的東西。

gt.en: He loved gold more than anything.
gt.zh: 他愛黃金勝過一切。

gt.en: To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish.
gt.zh: 為了感謝他，神給了邁達斯一個願望。

gt.en: His wish came true.
gt.zh: 他的願望實現了。

gt.en: Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.
gt.zh: 邁達斯學到，有些東西比黃金更有價值。

tz: 很久以前，在一個希臘故事裡，有一位名叫邁達斯的國王。他愛黃金勝過一切。
有一天，邁達斯幫助了酒神戴歐尼修斯的一位朋友。為了感謝他，酒神給了邁達斯一個願望。
邁達斯說：「我希望我碰到的每樣東西都變成黃金！」他的願望實現了。
一開始他非常開心。他摸了一顆石頭、一朵花和一張椅子，它們全都變成了黃金。
但接著他想吃東西。他的麵包和水也變成了黃金！邁達斯又餓又害怕。
他請求酒神把這份禮物收回去。邁達斯學到了：有些東西比黃金更有價值。

ph.ex: She loves her dog more than anything.
ph.exzh: 她愛她的狗勝過一切。

ph.ex: I hope your dream comes true.
ph.exzh: 希望你的夢想成真。

ph.ex: The caterpillar turned into a butterfly.
ph.exzh: 毛毛蟲變成了蝴蝶。

ph.ex: I'm sorry — I take back what I said.
ph.exzh: 對不起，我收回我說的話。

st.m: Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.
st.mz: 邁達斯國王學到：有些東西比黃金更珍貴。
t: One day, Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus.
Midas said, 'I wish that everything I touch turns into gold!' His wish came true.
At first he was very happy.
But then he tried to eat.
st.c: Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.

b.title: The Curse of the Golden Touch
text: In Greek mythology, Midas was a wealthy king of Phrygia who believed that more gold would bring him more happiness.

When Midas kindly looked after Silenus, the old teacher of the wine god Dionysus, the grateful god offered him any reward he desired. Without hesitating, Midas asked that everything he touched would turn to gold.

At first the gift seemed wonderful. Twigs, stones and apples glittered in his hands. But when he sat down to dinner, his bread hardened into metal and his wine became liquid gold. The richest man in the world was starving.
Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish. The god told him to wash in the River Pactolus, and according to the myth, that is why the river's sand sparkled with gold ever after.
In a famous later retelling by the American writer Nathaniel Hawthorne, Midas even turns his beloved daughter into a golden statue — a detail that makes the warning hit harder.
Today, the phrase 'the Midas touch' describes someone whose projects always make money, though the original story is really a warning about greed.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The American writer Hawthorne wrote the very first story about Midas.
The River Pactolus is still full of gold that people can find today.
Midas's golden wish showed how greed destroys what truly matters.
Dionysus was the Greek god in charge of gold and wealth.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：貪婪的願望毀掉真正重要的東西。

q.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
opts: The River Pactolus was golden before Midas washed in it.
In the original Greek myth, Midas turned his daughter to gold.
Today 'the Midas touch' is a warning used about greedy people.
Dionysus offered Midas a reward for helping Silenus.
q.why: 第 2 段：When Midas kindly looked after Silenus … the grateful god offered him any reward。河沙是在他洗過之後才閃著金光；女兒變金像是霍桑後來的改寫；今天這個說法是「稱讚」很會賺錢的人。

q.q: What is the purpose of paragraph 6?
opts: To explain how Midas finally lost his golden touch in the river
To contrast the phrase's modern meaning with the myth's warning
To praise people whose projects always make money
To retell Hawthorne's version of the story
q.why: 第 6 段：今天 the Midas touch 是稱讚很會賺錢的人，though the original story is really a warning about greed——在對比今昔的意思。

q.q: In paragraph 6, “greed” means ___.
opts: wanting much more than you need
great kindness to others
deep and lasting sadness
wanting to share what you have with others
q.why: greed = 貪婪。

q.q: Why does the writer say Hawthorne's daughter detail “makes the warning hit harder”?
opts: Golden statues are very expensive to make
Losing someone he loved shows greed's true cost
Hawthorne was an American, not a Greek
Golden statues show how beautiful the king's wish was
q.why: 第五段：把心愛的女兒變成金像，貪婪的代價更沉重。

q.q: A news article praises a businessman for having “the Midas touch.” Based on the text, what is surprising about this phrase?
opts: Today it's praise, but the story warns against greed
It means the businessman is very kind to others
Today it's a warning, but the story praises greed
It means the businessman is a kind of god
q.why: 最後一段：今天是讚美賺錢能力，原故事其實是對貪婪的警告。

tr.en: At first the gift seemed wonderful.
tr.zh: 一開始，這份禮物看起來好極了。

tr.en: The richest man in the world was starving.
tr.zh: 世界上最有錢的人卻在挨餓。

tr.en: Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish.
tr.zh: 走投無路的邁達斯懇求戴奧尼索斯收回這個願望。

tz: 在希臘神話中，邁達斯是弗里吉亞一位富有的國王，他相信更多的黃金會帶給他更多的快樂。
邁達斯好心照顧了酒神戴歐尼修斯的老師西勒諾斯，心懷感激的酒神願意給他任何他想要的報答。邁達斯毫不猶豫地要求：凡是他碰到的東西都要變成黃金。
一開始，這份禮物似乎好極了。樹枝、石頭和蘋果在他手中閃閃發亮。但當他坐下來吃晚餐時，麵包硬成了金屬，酒也變成了液態的黃金。世界上最富有的人，卻快要餓死了。
走投無路的邁達斯懇求戴歐尼修斯取消這個願望。酒神叫他到帕克托羅斯河裡洗澡；根據神話，這就是那條河的沙子從此閃著金光的原因。
在美國作家納撒尼爾・霍桑一個著名的改寫版本中，邁達斯甚至把他心愛的女兒變成了一座金像——這個細節讓故事的警告更加震撼。
今天，「點金術（the Midas touch）」這個說法用來形容做什麼都能賺錢的人，雖然原本的故事其實是一個關於貪婪的警告。

ph.ex: Can you look after my plants while I'm away?
ph.exzh: 我不在時，你可以幫我照顧植物嗎？

ph.ex: We sat down to dinner at seven.
ph.exzh: 我們七點坐下來吃晚餐。

ph.ex: He begged his mum to let him stay up late.
ph.exzh: 他懇求媽媽讓他晚點睡。

ph.ex: They lived happily ever after.
ph.exzh: 他們從此過著幸福快樂的日子。

ph.zh: 點石成金的本事（做什麼都賺錢）
ph.ex: She has the Midas touch — every shop she opens is a success.
ph.exzh: 她有點石成金的本事，開的每家店都很成功。

st.m: Today, the phrase 'the Midas touch' describes someone whose projects always make money, though the original story is really a warning about greed.
st.mz: 點石成金的故事其實是一個警告：貪心追求財富，反而會失去真正重要的東西。
t: When Midas kindly looked after Silenus, the old teacher of the wine god Dionysus, the grateful god offered him any reward he desired.
At first the gift seemed wonderful.
Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish.
In a famous later retelling by the American writer Nathaniel Hawthorne, Midas even turns his beloved daughter into a golden statue — a detail that makes the warning hit harder.
st.c: Today, the phrase 'the Midas touch' describes someone whose projects always make money, though the original story is really a warning about greed.

c.title: The Poverty of Gold
text: Few myths compress a moral so neatly as that of King Midas. Granted a wish by Dionysus in gratitude for sheltering the god's elderly companion Silenus, the Phrygian king asks that whatever he touches be turned to gold, and discovers at dinner that he has made himself unable to eat.

The story's force lies in its precise inversion. Gold is valuable precisely because it can be exchanged for other things; Midas, by converting everything into gold, abolishes the very things gold was meant to buy. His wealth becomes a form of poverty.

Ancient versions, preserved most famously by the Roman poet Ovid, end with Midas washing away his curse in the River Pactolus, an aetiological flourish explaining the gold-bearing sands of a real river.
Later tellers sharpened the tale. Nathaniel Hawthorne's nineteenth-century version adds a daughter who turns to metal at her father's embrace, shifting the moral from hunger to love.

Curiously, modern English has reversed the myth's meaning. To have 'the Midas touch' is now a compliment for commercial success, as though the cautionary half of the story had been quietly edited out — perhaps the most telling evidence of how persuasive the dream of endless wealth remains.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Midas was, above all, a successful king who knew how to make money.
Ovid invented the River Pactolus to explain where Midas's gold went.
The myth praises wealth, and our language has kept that meaning of praise.
The myth shows wealth becoming poverty, yet our language made it praise.
q.why: 主旨：財富變貧窮的寓言，現代英文卻把警告變成讚美。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “cautionary” means ___.
opts: very funny
about money
giving a warning
from ancient Rome
q.why: cautionary = 警示性的。

q.q: What does the writer mean by “His wealth becomes a form of poverty”?
opts: Turning all to gold destroys what gold should buy
Midas soon loses all of the gold that he has
Midas gives all of his gold to the poor people of his land
Midas gives all of his gold to the poor
q.why: 第二段：把一切變成黃金，反而消滅了黃金能買的東西。

q.q: How does the writer view the modern phrase 'the Midas touch'?
opts: As a correct summary of the myth's lesson
As an ironic reversal showing wealth's pull
As an insult to successful business people
As a phrase first used by Ovid himself
q.why: 最後一段：反轉神話原意——顯示無盡財富的夢多麼誘人。

q.q: What is the role of paragraph 4 (Hawthorne's version)?
opts: To prove that Ovid's version was wrong
To explain where the River Pactolus is
To show how retellings moved the moral to love
To show that Hawthorne kept Ovid's moral exactly the same
q.why: 第四段：shifting the moral from hunger to love。

q.q: An app promises: “Turn all your free time into money!” Based on the essay, what would be the strongest criticism?
opts: Turning everything into money can destroy rest and relationships
The app might not actually make you enough money in the end
Apps on phones are not really able to make money for anyone
The app might not actually turn enough of your free time into money
q.why: 第二段的邏輯：把一切換成金錢，反而失去金錢本來要換取的東西。

tz: 很少有神話能像邁達斯國王的故事一樣，把一個寓意濃縮得如此精準。弗里吉亞國王因為收留了酒神戴歐尼修斯年邁的同伴西勒諾斯，獲得酒神賜予一個願望；他要求凡是他碰到的東西都變成黃金，卻在晚餐時發現，自己讓自己再也吃不了東西。
這個故事的力量在於它精準的反轉。黃金之所以有價值，正是因為它能換到其他東西；而邁達斯把一切都變成黃金，等於消滅了黃金本來要用來購買的那些東西。他的財富變成了一種貧窮。
古代的版本——最有名的是由羅馬詩人奧維德保存下來的——結局是邁達斯在帕克托羅斯河裡洗去詛咒，用一段解釋來源的情節，說明了一條真實河流裡為什麼有含金的沙子。
後來的說書人讓故事更加尖銳。納撒尼爾・霍桑在十九世紀的版本加入了一個女兒，她在父親擁抱時變成了金屬，把寓意從飢餓轉向了愛。
奇妙的是，現代英文把這則神話的意思反了過來。擁有「點金術」如今是稱讚一個人生意成功，彷彿故事裡警告的那一半被悄悄刪掉了——這或許是最能說明「無盡財富」的夢想至今仍多麼誘人的證據。

ph.ex: She sent flowers in gratitude for their help.
ph.exzh: 她送花感謝他們的幫忙。

ph.ex: Points can be exchanged for small gifts.
ph.exzh: 點數可以兌換小禮物。

ph.ex: Dancing is a form of exercise.
ph.exzh: 跳舞是一種運動。

ph.ex: The teacher shifted our focus from grammar to speaking.
ph.exzh: 老師把我們的重點從文法轉到口說。
ph.m: shifting the moral from hunger to love

ph.ex: The funny part was edited out of the video.
ph.exzh: 好笑的那段被剪掉了。

ph.ex: He talks as though he knows everything.
ph.exzh: 他說話的樣子好像什麼都懂。

st.m: The story's force lies in its precise inversion.
st.mz: 邁達斯把一切都變成黃金，反而讓黃金失去價值，財富變成了貧窮；現代英文卻把這個警告當成讚美。
t: Ancient versions, preserved most famously by the Roman poet Ovid, end with Midas washing away his curse in the River Pactolus, an aetiological flourish explaining the gold-bearing sands of a real river.
Later tellers sharpened the tale.
st.c: To have 'the Midas touch' is now a compliment for commercial success, as though the cautionary half of the story had been quietly edited out — perhaps the most telling evidence of how persuasive the dream of endless wealth remains.

What are some things that are 'worth more than gold' to you?
Why do you think people today use 'the Midas touch' as praise?

topic: The Marshmallow Test: Is Waiting the Key to Success?
zh: 棉花糖實驗：能等待，就會成功嗎？
src: Mischel et al. (1972, 1988) · Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018) · Kidd et al. (2013)
discuss: Would you have waited for the second marshmallow? What trick would you use?
Why might trust affect how long someone is willing to wait?
Is self-control only about character, or also about circumstances? Explain.

a.title: One Marshmallow or Two?
text: Imagine you are four years old. A grown-up puts one marshmallow in front of you and says, "You can eat it now. But if you wait until I come back, you can have two." Then the grown-up leaves the room. What would you do?

This was a famous experiment by Walter Mischel, a psychologist at Stanford University in the United States. It started in the late 1960s. Some children ate the marshmallow right away. Others waited for up to 15 minutes.
The children who waited used clever tricks. Some covered their eyes. Some sang songs or turned around so they could not see the sweet.
Years later, Mischel found that children who had waited longer often did better at school. Many people thought the test showed that self-control is the key to success.

But in 2018, a bigger study found a weaker link. It showed that family money and home life also matter a lot. Another study found that children waited longer when the adult had kept promises before. If you can't trust the grown-up, eating the marshmallow now makes sense!
So waiting is a useful skill — and it is easier when we use good tricks and live in a world we can trust.
tz: 想像你四歲。一個大人把一顆棉花糖放在你面前，說：「你可以現在吃。但如果你等我回來，就可以拿到兩顆。」然後大人離開了房間。你會怎麼做？
這是美國史丹佛大學心理學家沃爾特・米歇爾做的一個著名實驗，始於 1960 年代末期。有些孩子馬上就把棉花糖吃掉了，有些則等了長達 15 分鐘。
等得住的孩子用了一些聰明的小技巧。有些人遮住眼睛，有些人唱歌，或轉過身去，讓自己看不到那顆糖。
多年後，米歇爾發現等比較久的孩子，在學校的表現往往比較好。很多人認為這個實驗證明了自制力是成功的關鍵。
但在 2018 年，一項規模更大的研究發現兩者的關聯比較弱。研究顯示，家庭經濟和家庭生活也有很大的影響。另一項研究則發現，如果大人之前遵守過承諾，孩子會等得比較久。如果你不能相信那個大人，現在就吃掉棉花糖其實很合理！
所以，等待是一項有用的技能——而當我們使用好的技巧、生活在一個值得信任的環境時，等待會比較容易。

ph.ex: There is a big tree in front of our school.
ph.exzh: 我們學校前面有一棵大樹。

ph.ex: Please answer my message right away.
ph.exzh: 請馬上回我的訊息。

ph.ex: She turned around and waved goodbye.
ph.exzh: 她轉過身揮手道別。

ph.ex: Your idea makes sense to me.
ph.exzh: 你的想法我覺得很合理。

q.q: What is the reading mainly about?
opts: How to make delicious marshmallows at home for young children
What a famous waiting test with sweets showed, and its limits
Why four-year-old children love to sing songs in class
How Stanford University became famous around the world

q.q: In paragraph 5, what does "It" in "It showed that family money and home life also matter" refer to?

the marshmallow
the grown-up's promise

q.q: In paragraph 4, "self-control" means ___.

q.q: Why might a child eat the marshmallow if the adult often breaks promises?
opts: The child may not believe a second one will come
The child does not really like marshmallows at all

b.title: The Marshmallow Test: What Waiting Really Tells Us
text: Few psychology experiments are as famous — or as charming — as the marshmallow test. Beginning in the late 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues at Stanford University offered young children a choice: eat one treat immediately, or wait alone for up to about fifteen minutes and receive two. Videos of children squirming, covering their eyes and singing to themselves have delighted audiences ever since.

The original aim was to understand the strategies children use to delay gratification. Mischel found that children who distracted themselves, or imagined the marshmallow as something else, such as a fluffy cloud, were able to wait much longer than those who stared at the treat.

Follow-up studies years later appeared to show something more dramatic. Children who had waited longer as preschoolers tended, as adolescents, to have higher test scores and were rated by parents as more competent. The test quickly became a symbol of the power of self-control.

However, the original sample was small and came mostly from families connected to Stanford. In 2018, a team of researchers repeated the study with nearly 1,000 children from more varied backgrounds. They found that the link between waiting and later achievement was about half as strong as earlier reported, and much smaller once family income and the home environment were taken into account.

Another study, published in 2013, added a twist. Before the test, some children met an adult who kept promises, while others met one who did not. Children with the reliable adult waited about four times longer. For children who have learned that promises are often broken, eating the treat immediately may be a sensible choice, not a sign of weak character.
The marshmallow test still teaches useful lessons about strategies for waiting, but it reminds us that self-control depends on circumstances as well as character.
tz: 很少有心理學實驗像棉花糖實驗這樣有名——又這麼可愛。從 1960 年代末期開始，心理學家沃爾特・米歇爾和他在史丹佛大學的同事給幼兒一個選擇：馬上吃掉一顆點心，或獨自等待最多大約十五分鐘，就能得到兩顆。孩子們扭來扭去、遮住眼睛、自己唱歌的影片，從那時起就一直讓觀眾看得津津有味。

多年後的追蹤研究似乎顯示了更戲劇性的結果。學齡前等得比較久的孩子，到了青少年時期往往考試分數比較高，父母也評價他們比較能幹。這個實驗很快就成了「自制力的力量」的象徵。
然而，最初的樣本很小，而且大多來自和史丹佛有關的家庭。2018 年，一組研究者用將近 1,000 名來自更多元背景的孩子重做了這項研究。他們發現，等待和日後成就之間的關聯，大約只有先前報告的一半強；而且把家庭收入和家庭環境考慮進去之後，關聯又小得多。

c.title: Rethinking the Marshmallow Test
text: For decades the marshmallow test has served as a parable about the virtue of patience. A child sits alone with a treat, having been told that waiting will double the reward; whether she resists, the story goes, foretells her future. It has appeared in countless talks, articles and parenting books. The reality uncovered by research is considerably more interesting, and more complicated, than the parable.

Walter Mischel's original experiments at Stanford's Bing Nursery School, conducted between the late 1960s and early 1970s, were designed to investigate the cognitive strategies underlying delay of gratification rather than to predict life outcomes. Mischel discovered that delay depended heavily on how children mentally represented the reward: those who focused on its "hot", tempting features, such as sweetness, gave in quickly, while those who reframed it in "cool", abstract terms, or distracted themselves, held out far longer.

The predictive claims came later. Follow-up studies published in 1988 and 1990 reported that preschoolers who had waited longer showed greater academic and social competence in adolescence, including higher SAT scores. These correlations, drawn from a small and relatively privileged sample, were widely popularised as evidence that self-control in early childhood forecasts success.

A 2018 conceptual replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan examined nearly 1,000 children from a national dataset with greater socioeconomic diversity. The association between delay at age four and achievement at fifteen was roughly half the size of earlier estimates, and it shrank by about two-thirds once controls for family background and early cognitive ability were introduced. The ability to wait, it appeared, was partly a reflection of the broader circumstances in which children were raised.

A 2013 study by Celeste Kidd and colleagues reframed the issue further. Children first experienced an adult who either kept or broke small promises. Those in the reliable condition subsequently waited roughly four times longer. Delay, in this light, can be a rational response to a trustworthy environment, and impatience a rational response to an unpredictable one.

None of this makes the original insights worthless. Strategies for managing temptation remain valuable and teachable. But the debate illustrates how a vivid experiment can be stretched into a moral fable, and how careful replication can restore the role of context that the fable left out. Self-control matters; so does the world that teaches children whether waiting is worthwhile.
tz: 數十年來，棉花糖實驗一直被當成一則關於耐心美德的寓言。一個孩子獨自和一顆點心坐在一起，被告知等待可以讓獎勵加倍；故事是這麼說的：她能不能忍住，就預示了她的未來。它出現在無數的演講、文章和教養書中。然而，研究揭露的真相，比這則寓言有趣得多，也複雜得多。
沃爾特・米歇爾在史丹佛大學必應幼兒園進行的原始實驗，時間是 1960 年代末到 1970 年代初，目的是研究延遲滿足背後的認知策略，而不是預測人生結果。米歇爾發現，能等多久很大程度取決於孩子在心裡如何表徵這個獎勵：專注於它「熱的」、誘人的特徵（例如甜味）的孩子很快就投降了；而把它重新想成「冷的」、抽象的樣子，或轉移自己注意力的孩子，則撐得久得多。
預測性的主張是後來才出現的。1988 年和 1990 年發表的追蹤研究指出，學齡前等得比較久的孩子，到了青少年時期在學業和社交上表現得更能幹，包括 SAT 分數比較高。這些相關性來自一個小而且相對優渥的樣本，卻被廣泛宣傳為「幼年自制力能預測成功」的證據。
2018 年，泰勒・瓦茨、葛瑞格・鄧肯和全浩南進行了一項概念性重複研究，檢視了來自一個社會經濟背景更多元的全國性資料庫、將近 1,000 名孩子。四歲時的等待能力和十五歲時成就之間的關聯，大約只有先前估計的一半；而在控制了家庭背景和早期認知能力之後，又縮小了大約三分之二。看來，等待的能力部分反映了孩子成長的整體環境。
2013 年席萊斯特・基德等人的研究，更進一步重新框架了這個問題。孩子們先遇到一位遵守或打破小承諾的大人。在「可靠」組的孩子，之後等待的時間大約是另一組的四倍。從這個角度看，等待可以是對值得信任的環境的理性回應，而不耐煩則可以是對無法預測的環境的理性回應。
這些都不會讓最初的洞見變得沒有價值。管理誘惑的策略仍然很有價值，而且可以教。但這場辯論說明了一個鮮明的實驗如何被延伸成一則道德寓言，以及謹慎的重複研究如何把寓言遺漏的「情境」找回來。自制力很重要；而教會孩子「等待是否值得」的那個世界，也同樣重要。

a.title: The Rich Get Richer
text: Two students start the school year. One already reads well, so she enjoys reading and reads many books. The other finds reading hard, so he avoids books. By the end of the year, the gap between them is even bigger.

This pattern is called the Matthew effect. The name comes from a line in the Bible's Gospel of Matthew. It says, in short, that those who have will be given more. People often describe it as "the rich get richer."

In 1968, an American sociologist named Robert Merton used the name for something he saw in science. Famous scientists often got more credit than unknown scientists for similar work. Their fame helped them get even more attention and money.
Later, a psychologist named Keith Stanovich found the same pattern in reading. Good readers read more, so they learn more words, and this makes reading even easier for them.
The Matthew effect is not fair, but it can be changed. Extra help early on can stop a small gap from becoming a big one.
If you find something hard, don't give up. A little extra practice now can start a good cycle instead of a bad one.
tz: 兩個學生開始新學年。一個已經很會讀書，所以她喜歡閱讀、讀了很多書。另一個覺得閱讀很難，所以他避開書本。到了學年結束，他們之間的差距變得更大了。
這種模式叫做馬太效應。這個名字來自聖經《馬太福音》裡的一句話。簡單來說，它的意思是：已經擁有的人，會得到更多。人們常把它形容為「富者越富」。
1968 年，一位名叫羅伯特・默頓的美國社會學家，用這個名字來描述他在科學界看到的現象。有名的科學家做了類似的研究，常常比沒沒無聞的科學家得到更多功勞。他們的名氣幫助他們得到更多的關注和經費。
後來，一位名叫基斯・史坦諾維奇的心理學家在閱讀上發現了同樣的模式。會讀書的人讀得更多，所以學到更多單字，這又讓閱讀對他們來說更容易。
馬太效應並不公平，但它是可以改變的。及早給予額外的幫助，就能阻止小差距變成大差距。
如果你覺得某件事很難，不要放棄。現在多一點練習，就能開啟一個好的循環，而不是壞的循環。

b.title: The Matthew Effect: How Advantage Builds on Advantage
text: In many areas of life, early advantages tend to grow. A student who reads well reads more, learns more words and finds reading easier still. A musician who wins an early competition receives more invitations to perform. This snowballing pattern is known as the Matthew effect, after a verse in the Gospel of Matthew that says, roughly, that to those who have, more will be given.

The term was introduced in 1968 by the American sociologist Robert K. Merton. Studying the world of science, Merton noticed that well-known researchers tended to receive disproportionate credit. When a famous scientist and an unknown one made similar discoveries, or worked together on a paper, the famous name usually attracted more attention. Recognition then brought further funding, students and opportunities, widening the gap. Merton also observed that the effect could help science, because famous names drew readers to important new work.

In 1986, the psychologist Keith Stanovich applied the idea to reading. Children who make a good start read more, which builds vocabulary and background knowledge, which in turn makes later reading easier and more enjoyable. Children who struggle early may avoid reading, falling further behind each year.

The Matthew effect has a related cousin, sometimes called the Matilda effect, named by the historian Margaret Rossiter in 1993. It describes how the contributions of women scientists have often been overlooked or credited to male colleagues. Their discoveries were sometimes remembered under other people's names for decades.

Understanding these patterns matters because they can make small, early differences look like natural talent. Researchers argue that early support, such as extra reading help or mentoring, can interrupt the cycle before gaps become large.
For individuals, the lesson is hopeful: small habits that build on each other — reading a little every day, practising steadily — can start a positive snowball of their own.
tz: 在生活的許多方面，早期的優勢往往會越來越大。一個會讀書的學生讀得更多、學到更多單字，閱讀也就變得更容易。一個早早贏得比賽的音樂家，會收到更多演出邀請。這種滾雪球般的模式被稱為馬太效應，名稱來自《馬太福音》中的一節經文，大意是：凡有的，還要加給他。
這個名詞是美國社會學家羅伯特・K・默頓在 1968 年提出的。默頓研究科學界時注意到，知名的研究者往往得到不成比例的功勞。當一位有名的科學家和一位沒沒無聞的科學家做出類似的發現，或一起合寫一篇論文時，通常是那個有名的名字吸引了更多關注。接著，被認可又帶來更多的經費、學生和機會，讓差距越來越大。默頓也觀察到，這個效應也可能對科學有幫助，因為有名的名字能把讀者吸引到重要的新研究上。
1986 年，心理學家基斯・史坦諾維奇把這個概念應用到閱讀上。起步好的孩子讀得更多，累積了字彙和背景知識，這又反過來讓之後的閱讀變得更容易、更有樂趣。一開始就吃力的孩子可能會逃避閱讀，一年比一年更落後。
馬太效應有一個相關的「表親」，有時被稱為瑪蒂達效應，是歷史學家瑪格麗特・羅西特在 1993 年命名的。它描述女性科學家的貢獻常常被忽視，或被歸功於男性同事。她們的發現有時好幾十年都被記在別人的名下。
了解這些模式很重要，因為它們可能讓早期的小差異看起來像是天生的才能。研究者主張，及早提供支持，例如額外的閱讀輔導或良師指導，就能在差距變大之前打斷這個循環。
對個人來說，這個教訓是充滿希望的：彼此累積的小習慣——每天讀一點書、穩定地練習——也能啟動屬於自己的正向雪球。

c.title: Cumulative Advantage: The Matthew Effect
text: "For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance." When the sociologist Robert K. Merton borrowed this line from the Gospel of Matthew in 1968, he was describing a pattern in the reward system of science. But the Matthew effect has since become a general name for cumulative advantage: the tendency for initial differences, sometimes small and sometimes arbitrary, to compound over time into large inequalities.

Merton's evidence came partly from interviews with Nobel laureates, who described how credit for joint work or simultaneous discoveries flowed disproportionately to the already eminent. A paper co-authored by a famous scientist and an unknown one would be remembered as the famous scientist's. Recognition, in turn, brought resources — laboratories, students, funding — that made further achievement more likely. Merton noted a functional side as well: eminent names help direct attention to significant work in an overwhelming literature.

The concept travelled widely. In education, Keith Stanovich's influential 1986 paper described "Matthew effects in reading", whereby early readers gain vocabulary and knowledge that make subsequent reading easier, while struggling readers fall progressively behind. Later research has found that such reading gaps are real but that their widening is not inevitable; in some datasets gaps remain stable rather than growing.

Network scientists have found analogous dynamics in citation patterns and the growth of the internet, where nodes that are already well connected attract new links at higher rates — a process called preferential attachment. A striking 2006 experiment by Matthew Salganik, Peter Dodds and Duncan Watts showed how this can work in cultural markets. When participants could see how many times songs had been downloaded by others, popularity became far more unequal and less predictable; small early leads, partly due to chance, snowballed.

The historian Margaret Rossiter later coined the "Matilda effect" to describe a related injustice: the systematic under-recognition of women scientists, whose work was often attributed to male colleagues. Both effects highlight that recognition reflects social processes, not merit alone.

Cumulative advantage is not destiny. Because it operates through mechanisms — attention, resources, opportunity — it can be counteracted by interventions aimed at those same mechanisms, such as early tutoring, blind review and deliberate efforts to spread opportunity more widely. Recognising the Matthew effect does not diminish genuine achievement; it reminds us that achievement grows in soil that not everyone is given.
tz: 「凡有的，還要加給他，叫他有餘。」當社會學家羅伯特・K・默頓在 1968 年借用《馬太福音》的這句話時，他描述的是科學界獎勵制度中的一種模式。但從那以後，馬太效應已經成為「累積優勢」的通稱：最初的差異——有時很小，有時是偶然的——隨著時間不斷累積，最後變成巨大的不平等。
默頓的證據部分來自對諾貝爾獎得主的訪談，他們描述合作研究或同時發現的功勞，如何不成比例地流向原本就已經很有名的人。一篇由知名科學家和無名科學家合寫的論文，會被記成是那位知名科學家的。被認可又反過來帶來資源——實驗室、學生、經費——讓進一步的成就更有可能。默頓也指出了它的正面功能：在多到看不完的文獻中，著名的名字有助於把注意力引導到重要的研究上。
這個概念傳播得很廣。在教育上，基斯・史坦諾維奇 1986 年那篇影響深遠的論文描述了「閱讀中的馬太效應」：早期會讀的孩子獲得字彙和知識，讓之後的閱讀更容易，而閱讀吃力的孩子則逐漸落後。後來的研究發現，這種閱讀差距確實存在，但它的擴大並不是必然的；在一些資料中，差距是維持穩定，而不是持續擴大。
網絡科學家在論文引用模式和網際網路的成長中也發現了類似的動態：已經有很多連結的節點，會以更高的速度吸引新連結——這個過程稱為「偏好依附」。馬修・薩甘尼克、彼得・多茲和鄧肯・瓦茨 2006 年一項引人注目的實驗，顯示了這在文化市場中如何運作。當受試者能看到歌曲被別人下載了幾次時，受歡迎程度變得極不平均，也更難預測；早期的小小領先——部分只是運氣——就像滾雪球一樣越滾越大。
歷史學家瑪格麗特・羅西特後來創造了「瑪蒂達效應」一詞，描述一種相關的不公：女性科學家系統性地得不到應有的認可，她們的研究常被歸功於男性同事。這兩種效應都凸顯出：認可反映的是社會過程，而不只是實力。
累積優勢並不是命中注定的。因為它是透過注意力、資源、機會等機制運作的，所以可以透過針對這些機制的介入來抵消，例如及早輔導、匿名審查，以及刻意讓機會分配得更廣。認識馬太效應並不會貶低真正的成就；它提醒我們，成就生長的那片土壤，並不是每個人都分得到。

topic: The Mere-Exposure Effect: Why Songs Grow on You
zh: 單純曝光效應：為什麼歌越聽越好聽？

a.title: Why Songs Grow on You
text: Have you ever heard a new song and thought, "This is boring"? Then, after hearing it ten times on the radio, you started to sing along and even like it. This happens to many people. It is called the mere-exposure effect.
"Mere" means "only" or "just." "Exposure" means seeing or hearing something. So the idea is simple: just seeing or hearing something many times can make us like it more.

An American psychologist named Robert Zajonc studied this in 1968. He showed people strange made-up words and Chinese-looking symbols. Some appeared many times, and some only once or twice. Later, people said the ones they had seen more often seemed nicer — even though they did not know what they meant.
Why? Things we know feel safe and easy for our brains. Things that are new can feel a little strange.
Companies use this idea. They show the same ads and logos again and again so that we feel friendly toward their products.
But there is a limit. If we hear the same song too many times, we can get tired of it. And if we really disliked something at first, seeing it more may not help.
tz: 你有沒有聽到一首新歌，心想「好無聊」？結果在廣播上聽了十次之後，你開始跟著唱，甚至喜歡上它。很多人都有這種經驗。這叫做單純曝光效應。
Mere 的意思是「只是、僅僅」。Exposure 的意思是看到或聽到某樣東西。所以這個概念很簡單：光是多次看到或聽到某樣東西，就能讓我們更喜歡它。
一位名叫羅伯特・扎瓊克的美國心理學家在 1968 年研究了這個現象。他讓受試者看一些奇怪的編造字和看起來像中文的符號。有些出現很多次，有些只出現一兩次。之後，受試者說比較常看到的那些看起來比較好——即使他們根本不知道那些是什麼意思。
為什麼？我們熟悉的東西，對大腦來說感覺安全又輕鬆。新的東西則可能讓人覺得有點奇怪。
公司會利用這個概念。他們一再播放同樣的廣告和商標，讓我們對他們的產品產生親切感。
但這是有限度的。如果同一首歌聽太多次，我們可能會聽膩。而且如果一開始就非常討厭某樣東西，多看幾次也不一定有用。

b.title: The Mere-Exposure Effect: Familiarity Breeds Liking
text: There is an old saying that familiarity breeds contempt — the more we know something, the less we respect it. Psychology suggests that, in many situations, the opposite is true. Simply being exposed to something repeatedly, without any reward or explanation, tends to make people like it more. This tendency is known as the mere-exposure effect.

The effect was studied systematically by the psychologist Robert Zajonc in 1968. He showed participants unfamiliar stimuli — nonsense words, Chinese-like characters and photographs of strangers' faces — different numbers of times. Afterwards, participants rated the items they had seen more frequently as more pleasant, even though nothing else about them had changed. The more often something appeared, the more it was liked.

Later research found that the effect can work even when people are not aware of the exposure. In some experiments, images flashed too quickly to be consciously recognised still became more liked. Another study in a university lecture hall found that women who attended a class more often were later rated as more attractive and likeable by students, although they had never spoken to anyone.

One explanation is processing fluency: familiar things are easier for the brain to recognise and understand, and that ease feels pleasant. We may mistake the comfort of familiarity for genuine liking.

The effect has limits. Too much repetition can lead to boredom, especially with simple stimuli, and exposure tends to intensify rather than reverse strong initial dislike. Even so, the mere-exposure effect helps explain why advertisers repeat slogans, why songs grow on us, and why we often prefer the familiar to the new.

Knowing this can make us more thoughtful consumers — and more patient with new people, foods and ideas that may simply need a second chance. Sometimes, the strangeness we feel at first is not a reason to reject something; it is just unfamiliarity.
tz: 有句老話說「熟悉生輕蔑」——越了解一樣東西，就越不尊重它。心理學卻指出，在許多情況下正好相反。光是反覆接觸某樣東西，沒有任何獎勵或解釋，就往往會讓人更喜歡它。這種傾向被稱為單純曝光效應。
心理學家羅伯特・扎瓊克在 1968 年系統性地研究了這個效應。他讓受試者看不熟悉的刺激物——無意義的字、類似中文的字元和陌生人的臉部照片——各看不同次數。之後，受試者認為比較常看到的東西比較討喜，即使它們其他方面完全沒變。某樣東西出現得越頻繁，就越受喜愛。
後來的研究發現，即使人們沒有意識到自己接觸過，這個效應仍然可能發生。在一些實驗中，閃過太快、無法被意識辨認的圖像，仍然變得更受喜愛。另一項在大學演講廳進行的研究發現，比較常來上課的女性，後來被學生評為更有魅力、更討人喜歡，儘管她們從沒和任何人說過話。
一種解釋是「處理流暢度」：熟悉的東西對大腦來說比較容易辨認和理解，而這種輕鬆感讓人覺得愉快。我們可能把熟悉帶來的舒適感，誤以為是真心的喜歡。
這個效應有其限度。過多的重複可能導致無聊，尤其是簡單的刺激物；而且接觸往往會加強、而不是扭轉一開始強烈的厭惡。即便如此，單純曝光效應有助於解釋為什麼廣告商一再重複口號、為什麼歌會越聽越喜歡，以及為什麼我們常常偏好熟悉的東西勝過新東西。
了解這一點，能讓我們成為更有思考力的消費者——也對新的人、食物和想法更有耐心，它們可能只是需要第二次機會。有時候，我們一開始感覺到的奇怪，並不是拒絕某樣東西的理由，而只是因為還不熟悉。

c.title: Familiarity and Fondness: The Mere-Exposure Effect
text: Among the most robust findings in social psychology is one that seems almost too simple to be true: repeated exposure to a stimulus, in the absence of any reward, tends to increase liking for it. Robert Zajonc, who named and systematically documented the phenomenon in a 1968 monograph, argued that this "mere exposure" was a sufficient condition for attitude enhancement — no persuasion, association or reasoning required.

Zajonc's demonstrations were deliberately austere. Participants viewed meaningless Turkish-sounding words, Chinese-like ideographs and yearbook photographs at varying frequencies, then rated how good each item seemed. Liking rose with exposure in a roughly logarithmic pattern, climbing steeply over the first few exposures and levelling off thereafter. A 1989 meta-analysis by Robert Bornstein, covering more than two hundred experiments, confirmed that the effect was reliable across a wide range of stimuli, while noting that it tended to be strongest when exposures were brief.

Perhaps most striking is that awareness is unnecessary. In studies using stimuli flashed too briefly for conscious recognition, participants who could not tell which shapes they had seen nonetheless preferred the previously exposed ones. This dissociation between recognition and preference suggested that affective reactions could form independently of explicit memory, a claim that fuelled lively theoretical debate. Later research has refined, but not overturned, this conclusion.

The dominant contemporary explanation emphasises perceptual fluency. Previously encountered stimuli are processed more easily, and people tend to misattribute this ease to positive qualities of the stimulus itself. An evolutionary interpretation complements this account: an organism that has repeatedly met something without harm has reason to treat it as safe.

The effect is not unlimited. Prolonged repetition breeds tedium, particularly for simple stimuli, and exposure appears to polarise rather than overturn existing attitudes, so that an initially disliked stimulus may become more disliked. Context matters as well; a slogan heard repeatedly in an irritating advertisement may acquire unpleasant associations of its own. Familiarity, in short, is a powerful influence but not an all-powerful one.

Nevertheless, the implications are wide-ranging, from marketing and political campaigning to the formation of friendships, since people who see each other often are more likely to become close. For the individual, the effect offers a quiet warning and a quiet encouragement: our preferences are less purely rational than they feel, and many unfamiliar things deserve more than one encounter before we judge them.
tz: 社會心理學最穩固的發現之一，簡單到幾乎令人難以置信：在沒有任何獎勵的情況下，反覆接觸一個刺激物，往往會增加對它的喜愛。羅伯特・扎瓊克在 1968 年的專論中為這個現象命名並系統性地記錄它，他主張這種「單純曝光」就足以提升態度——不需要說服、聯想或推理。
扎瓊克的示範刻意設計得非常簡單。受試者以不同頻率觀看聽起來像土耳其語的無意義字詞、類似中文的表意符號和畢業紀念冊照片，再評價每個項目看起來有多好。喜愛程度隨著曝光次數大致呈對數形態上升：前幾次曝光時急遽攀升，之後趨於平穩。羅伯特・伯恩斯坦 1989 年涵蓋兩百多個實驗的統合分析證實，這個效應在各種刺激物上都很可靠，同時也指出當曝光很短暫時效應往往最強。
最驚人的或許是：意識並不是必要的。在使用閃過太快、無法被意識辨認的刺激物的研究中，受試者雖然說不出自己看過哪些形狀，卻仍然偏好先前看過的那些。辨認和偏好之間的這種分離，顯示情感反應可以獨立於外顯記憶而形成，這個主張引發了熱烈的理論辯論。後來的研究修正了、但沒有推翻這個結論。
當代主流的解釋強調知覺流暢度。先前接觸過的刺激物處理起來比較容易，而人們傾向把這種輕鬆感錯誤歸因為刺激物本身的正面特質。演化的詮釋補充了這個說法：一個生物如果反覆遇到某樣東西都沒受傷，就有理由把它當成安全的。
這個效應並非沒有限度。長時間的重複會帶來乏味，尤其是對簡單的刺激物；而且曝光似乎會使既有態度兩極化，而不是推翻它，因此一開始被討厭的刺激物可能變得更被討厭。情境也很重要：在惹人厭的廣告裡反覆聽到的口號，可能會沾上它自己的負面聯想。簡而言之，熟悉感的影響力很大，但並非萬能。
儘管如此，它的影響範圍很廣，從行銷、政治競選到友誼的形成都有，因為常常見面的人更可能變得親近。對個人來說，這個效應同時給了一個安靜的警告和一個安靜的鼓勵：我們的偏好並不像感覺上那麼純粹理性，而許多陌生的事物，值得我們多接觸幾次再下判斷。

topic: Occam's Razor: Start With the Simplest Explanation

a.title: Keep It Simple
text: You hear a loud crash in the kitchen. You run in and see a broken cup on the floor and your cat sitting on the table. What happened? Maybe a ghost pushed the cup. Maybe a strong wind blew it down. Or maybe the cat knocked it over.

Most people would say the cat did it. This kind of thinking has a name: Occam's razor. It says that when there are several ways to explain something, we should usually start with the simplest one — the one that needs the fewest new guesses.
The idea is named after William of Ockham, an English thinker who lived about 700 years ago. A razor is a sharp tool for shaving. Occam's razor "shaves away" ideas that are not needed.
Doctors use this idea too. There is a saying: "When you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras." It means common problems are more likely than rare ones.
But Occam's razor is not a law. The simplest answer is not always the right one. Sometimes the truth really is complicated, so we must still check the facts.
Still, it is a great place to start when you try to solve a mystery!

大多數人會說是貓做的。這種思考方式有個名字：奧坎剃刀。它是說，當一件事有好幾種解釋方式時，我們通常應該先從最簡單的開始——也就是需要最少新猜測的那一個。
這個概念以奧坎的威廉命名，他是大約 700 年前的一位英國思想家。剃刀是用來刮鬍子的鋒利工具。奧坎剃刀會「剃掉」不需要的想法。
醫生也會用這個概念。有句話說：「聽到馬蹄聲，要想到馬，而不是斑馬。」意思是常見的問題比罕見的問題更有可能發生。
但奧坎剃刀不是定律。最簡單的答案不一定是對的。有時候真相確實很複雜，所以我們還是得查證事實。
不過，當你想解開一個謎團時，它是一個很棒的起點！

b.title: Occam's Razor: The Power of Simple Explanations
text: When your friend fails to reply to a message, you might imagine that she is angry with you, that her phone was stolen, or that she has simply not seen it yet. All three are possible, but the last requires the fewest extra assumptions. Choosing it as your starting point is an example of a principle known as Occam's razor.

The principle is named after William of Ockham, a fourteenth-century English friar and philosopher. He argued that we should not assume more things exist than are necessary to explain what we observe. The famous phrase "entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity" was written by later thinkers, but it captures his idea. The word "razor" suggests cutting away unnecessary parts of an explanation.

Occam's razor is widely used in science and medicine. Scientists often prefer the simplest theory that explains all the evidence, partly because simpler theories make clearer predictions and are easier to test. Medical students are taught a related rule: "When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras" — common illnesses are more likely than rare ones.

However, the razor is a guide, not a proof. It does not say that the simplest explanation is always true, only that it is a sensible place to begin. Sometimes reality is genuinely complex, and the simplest idea turns out to be wrong. Doctors, for instance, must remember that patients can have more than one illness at the same time.
The principle is also often misused. People may call an explanation "simple" because it is familiar or fits their opinions, even if it ignores important evidence.

Used carefully, though, Occam's razor helps us avoid needless guesswork and focus first on the most reasonable possibilities. It reminds us to keep our explanations as simple as possible — but not simpler than the evidence allows.
tz: 當朋友沒回你訊息時，你可能會想像她在生你的氣、她的手機被偷了，或者她只是還沒看到。三種都有可能，但最後一種需要的額外假設最少。把它當作思考的起點，就是一個叫做奧坎剃刀的原則的例子。
這個原則以奧坎的威廉命名，他是十四世紀的英國修士和哲學家。他主張，我們不應該假設存在的東西，多於解釋所觀察到的現象所必需的。那句有名的「如無必要，勿增實體」是後來的思想家寫的，但它抓住了他的想法。「剃刀」這個詞暗示著把解釋中不必要的部分削掉。
奧坎剃刀在科學和醫學上被廣泛使用。科學家通常偏好能解釋所有證據的最簡單理論，部分原因是比較簡單的理論能做出比較清楚的預測，也比較容易檢驗。醫學生會學到一條相關的規則：「聽到馬蹄聲，要想到馬，而不是斑馬」——常見的疾病比罕見的疾病更有可能。
然而，這把剃刀是一個指引，不是證明。它並不是說最簡單的解釋一定是真的，只是說它是一個合理的起點。有時候現實確實很複雜，最簡單的想法結果是錯的。例如，醫生必須記得，病人可能同時有不只一種疾病。
這個原則也常被誤用。人們可能因為某個解釋很熟悉，或符合自己的看法，就說它「簡單」，即使它忽略了重要的證據。
不過，只要謹慎使用，奧坎剃刀能幫助我們避免不必要的瞎猜，先專注在最合理的可能性上。它提醒我們，解釋要盡可能簡單——但不能比證據所允許的還簡單。

c.title: Cutting Away the Unnecessary: Occam's Razor
text: Among the tools of rational inquiry, few are invoked as often, or as loosely, as Occam's razor. In its common modern form, the principle advises that when competing hypotheses explain the same evidence equally well, we should prefer the one that makes the fewest assumptions. It is a heuristic for choosing among explanations, not a law of nature, and its value depends heavily on how it is applied.

The razor bears the name of William of Ockham, a fourteenth-century English Franciscan friar and logician, although versions of the idea appear earlier, in Aristotle and in medieval thinkers before him. The best-known Latin formulation, "entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem" — entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity — does not actually appear in Ockham's surviving writings; it was attributed to him centuries later. The image of a razor, shaving away superfluous assumptions, was likewise a later coinage.

Why should simplicity matter? Philosophers have offered several justifications. Simpler hypotheses are generally easier to test and to falsify. They are less prone to "overfitting" — accommodating every quirk of existing data at the cost of predicting new data poorly, a problem familiar from statistics and machine learning. And each additional assumption is an additional opportunity to be wrong, so, other things being equal, a leaner explanation carries fewer risks.

Yet history offers cautionary examples. Simplicity does not guarantee truth: the behaviour of light, for instance, turned out to require a description stranger and more complex than either of the elegant rival theories once proposed. In medicine, the clinical habit of seeking a single diagnosis is balanced by Hickam's dictum, which reminds doctors that patients can have several diseases at once.

The razor is also easily abused. "Simple" can be a matter of perspective: an explanation that seems straightforward because it is familiar, or because it confirms our expectations, may in fact require enormous hidden assumptions. Conspiracy theories, for example, often appear simple — a single hidden actor explains everything — while quietly assuming vast coordination and secrecy. Applied honestly, the razor would cut such theories rather than support them.

Properly understood, then, Occam's razor is a principle of intellectual economy rather than a shortcut to certainty. It tells us where to start and what to test first, while leaving the final verdict to the evidence. As a remark often attributed to Einstein puts it, explanations should be as simple as possible, but no simpler.
tz: 在理性探究的工具中，很少有像奧坎剃刀這樣被如此頻繁、又如此隨意地援引的。它常見的現代形式是：當互相競爭的假說同樣能解釋相同的證據時，我們應該偏好假設最少的那一個。它是一種在各種解釋中做選擇的經驗法則，而不是自然定律，它的價值很大程度取決於如何應用。
這把剃刀冠上了奧坎的威廉之名，他是十四世紀英國方濟會的修士和邏輯學家；不過這個想法的不同版本更早就出現過，例如亞里斯多德和他之前的中世紀思想家。最有名的拉丁文表述「如無必要，勿增實體」，其實並沒有出現在奧坎現存的著作中；那是幾個世紀後才被歸到他名下的。用剃刀刮除多餘假設的意象，同樣是後來才創造的說法。
為什麼簡單很重要？哲學家提出了幾個理由。比較簡單的假說通常比較容易檢驗和證偽。它們比較不容易「過度擬合」——為了遷就現有資料的每個小怪癖，而犧牲了預測新資料的能力，這是統計學和機器學習中常見的問題。而且每多一個假設，就多一個出錯的機會，所以在其他條件相同的情況下，比較精簡的解釋風險比較小。
然而歷史也提供了警惕的例子。簡單並不保證真實：例如，光的行為最後需要的描述，比過去提出的兩種優雅的對立理論都更奇特、更複雜。在醫學上，追求單一診斷的臨床習慣，會被「希坎姆格言」平衡——它提醒醫生，病人可能同時有好幾種疾病。
這把剃刀也很容易被濫用。「簡單」可能取決於觀點：一個看起來很直接的解釋，可能只是因為它很熟悉，或因為它符合我們的預期，實際上卻需要龐大的隱藏假設。例如，陰謀論常常看起來很簡單——一個隱藏的主使者就能解釋一切——卻悄悄假設了大規模的協調和保密。誠實地使用這把剃刀，應該會削掉這類理論，而不是支持它們。
所以，正確理解的話，奧坎剃刀是一種「思考經濟」的原則，而不是通往確定性的捷徑。它告訴我們從哪裡開始、先檢驗什麼，而把最後的判決留給證據。正如一句常被認為出自愛因斯坦的話：解釋應該盡可能簡單，但不能更簡單。

topic: The Pareto Principle: The 80/20 Rule
