a.title: The 80/20 Rule
text: Look at your closet. Do you wear all your clothes the same amount? Probably not. Many people wear a few favourite clothes most of the time and hardly touch the rest.
This is an example of the Pareto principle, also called the 80/20 rule. It says that, in many situations, a small part of the causes creates a large part of the results.
The idea started with an Italian economist named Vilfredo Pareto. Around 1900, he noticed that about 80 percent of the land in Italy belonged to about 20 percent of the people.
Later, a businessman named Joseph Juran saw similar patterns in factories. A few problems caused most of the mistakes. He gave the idea Pareto's name.

The numbers are not always exactly 80 and 20. Sometimes they are 90 and 10, or 70 and 30. The important idea is that results are often not shared equally. Still, the pattern appears surprisingly often.
You can use this idea when you study. Find the few topics that will help you the most, and spend more time on them. But don't forget the rest completely!
tz: 看看你的衣櫥。你每件衣服穿的次數都一樣多嗎？大概不是吧。很多人大部分時間都穿少數幾件最喜歡的衣服，其他的幾乎不碰。
這就是帕雷托法則的一個例子，它也被稱為 80/20 法則。它是說，在很多情況下，一小部分的原因造成了大部分的結果。
這個概念始於一位名叫維爾弗雷多・帕雷托的義大利經濟學家。大約 1900 年時，他注意到義大利大約 80% 的土地屬於大約 20% 的人。
後來，一位名叫約瑟夫・朱蘭的商人在工廠裡也看到類似的模式：少數幾個問題造成了大部分的錯誤。他用帕雷托的名字為這個概念命名。
數字不一定剛好是 80 和 20。有時候是 90 和 10，或 70 和 30。重要的概念是：結果往往不是平均分配的。不過，這種模式出現的頻率高得驚人。
讀書的時候你也可以用這個概念。找出對你幫助最大的少數幾個主題，花更多時間在上面。但也不要把其他部分完全忘了！

b.title: The Pareto Principle: Why a Few Things Matter Most
text: In many parts of life, effort and results are not evenly balanced. A few customers may bring a company most of its sales; a few bugs may cause most of a program's crashes; a few habits may shape most of your health. This uneven pattern is often summed up as the Pareto principle, or the 80/20 rule.

The principle is named after Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian economist and engineer. In the 1890s he studied how wealth was distributed and found that a large share of land and income in Italy, and in other countries he examined, was held by a relatively small share of the population.

The idea was popularised decades later by Joseph Juran, a pioneer of quality management. Working with manufacturers, Juran noticed that a "vital few" causes were usually responsible for most defects, while the "useful many" mattered far less individually. He named the pattern after Pareto, and it became a standard tool in business: focus first on the few problems that cause the most damage.

It is important to understand what the rule does not say. The numbers 80 and 20 are not a law of nature and do not have to add up to 100; real cases might be 90/10, 70/20 or something else entirely. The principle simply describes a common tendency toward imbalance. It is a useful guide, not a fixed rule.

It can also be misused. Ignoring the "less important" 80 percent can backfire — the small customers of today may become the large customers of tomorrow, and rare problems can still be serious. Good decisions require looking at the whole picture, not only the biggest slice.

Used wisely, though, the principle is a helpful tool for prioritising. For students, it might mean identifying the topics or mistakes that cost the most marks and tackling those first, before polishing the details.
tz: 在生活的許多方面，付出和結果並不是平均對應的。少數幾個客戶可能帶給公司大部分的營收；少數幾個程式錯誤可能造成大部分的當機；少數幾個習慣可能決定你大部分的健康。這種不平均的模式常被總結為帕雷托法則，也就是 80/20 法則。
這個法則以義大利經濟學家兼工程師維爾弗雷多・帕雷托命名。1890 年代，他研究財富如何分配，發現在義大利以及他研究的其他國家，很大一部分的土地和收入，掌握在人口中相對少數的人手裡。
數十年後，品質管理的先驅約瑟夫・朱蘭讓這個概念廣為流傳。朱蘭和製造商合作時注意到，通常是「關鍵的少數」原因造成了大部分的瑕疵，而「有用的多數」個別來說影響小得多。他用帕雷托的名字為這個模式命名，它也成了商業上的標準工具：先處理造成最大損害的少數問題。
了解這個法則「沒有」說什麼很重要。80 和 20 這兩個數字不是自然定律，加起來也不一定是 100；實際情況可能是 90/10、70/20，或完全不同的比例。這個法則只是描述一種常見的「不平均」傾向。它是一個有用的指引，而不是固定的規則。
它也可能被誤用。忽略那「比較不重要」的 80% 可能會適得其反——今天的小客戶可能成為明天的大客戶，罕見的問題也可能很嚴重。好的決定需要看全貌，而不只是最大的那一塊。
不過，只要用得聰明，這個法則是一個排定優先順序的好工具。對學生來說，這可能代表找出讓你失分最多的主題或錯誤，先處理它們，再去修飾細節。

c.title: The Vital Few: Uses and Abuses of the 80/20 Rule
text: Few rules of thumb are quoted as confidently as the claim that 80 percent of outcomes flow from 20 percent of causes. Managers apply it to customers, software engineers to bugs, and self-help authors to almost everything. The principle's popularity is understandable: it promises that effort, wisely concentrated, can yield disproportionate rewards. Yet its origins and limits are less widely understood than its slogan.

Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian engineer turned economist, observed in the 1890s that income and wealth in the countries he studied followed a strikingly consistent and highly unequal distribution. His mathematical description of that pattern — what statisticians now call a Pareto distribution — implied that a minority of the population held a majority of the wealth. The neat ratio of 80 to 20 was not, however, a figure Pareto proposed as a universal law. It was a description of one society's wealth, not a recipe for success.

The generalisation came from Joseph Juran, a quality-management pioneer who, in the 1940s, noticed that a handful of causes typically accounted for most manufacturing defects. Juran later acknowledged that attaching Pareto's name to this broader idea was somewhat misleading, but by then the label had stuck. His practical advice — separate the "vital few" from the "useful many" — proved enormously influential in industry.

Distributions of this kind do occur widely. A small fraction of scientific papers attract most citations; a few earthquakes release most seismic energy; a minority of websites receive the bulk of internet traffic. Such patterns often arise from processes in which success breeds further success, a dynamic sometimes called cumulative advantage.

The danger lies in treating a descriptive tendency as a prescriptive rule. The exact proportions vary, and they need not sum to 100. Applying the principle mechanically can encourage organisations to neglect segments that are small today but strategically important tomorrow, or to dismiss rare risks whose consequences are catastrophic. In public policy, moreover, an unequal distribution of outcomes is a fact to be explained, not automatically a pattern to be accepted.

Understood properly, the Pareto principle is less a law than a prompt. It invites us to ask where effort is producing the greatest return and whether our attention is allocated accordingly — while remembering that the remaining 80 percent is not necessarily unimportant. Used this way, it sharpens judgement rather than replacing it.
tz: 很少有經驗法則像「80% 的結果來自 20% 的原因」這個說法一樣被如此自信地引用。經理人把它用在客戶上，軟體工程師用在程式錯誤上，勵志作家則幾乎什麼都套用。這個法則受歡迎可以理解：它承諾只要把力氣集中在對的地方，就能得到不成比例的回報。然而，人們對它的起源和局限，遠不如對它的口號那麼了解。
維爾弗雷多・帕雷托是一位由工程師轉行的義大利經濟學家，他在 1890 年代觀察到，他所研究的國家中，收入和財富的分布呈現驚人一致、而且高度不平均的形態。他對這個模式的數學描述——統計學家現在稱為帕雷托分布——意味著少數人口掌握了多數財富。不過，80 比 20 這個工整的比例，並不是帕雷托提出的普遍定律。它描述的是一個社會的財富狀況，而不是成功的祕訣。
這個推廣來自品質管理先驅約瑟夫・朱蘭。他在 1940 年代注意到，通常是少數幾個原因造成了大部分的製造瑕疵。朱蘭後來承認，把帕雷托的名字套在這個更廣泛的概念上有點誤導，但那時這個標籤已經定型了。他的實用建議——區分「關鍵的少數」和「有用的多數」——在產業界影響極大。
這類分布確實很常見。少數科學論文獲得了大部分的引用；少數幾次地震釋放了大部分的地震能量；少數網站獲得了大部分的網路流量。這些模式常常來自「成功帶來更多成功」的過程，這種動態有時被稱為累積優勢。
危險在於把一種描述性的傾向，當成規範性的規則。確切的比例會變動，加起來也不必是 100。機械式地套用這個法則，可能讓組織忽略那些今天很小、但明天具有戰略重要性的部分，或忽視後果是災難性的罕見風險。此外，在公共政策上，結果分配不均是一個需要被解釋的事實，而不是理所當然要被接受的模式。
正確理解的話，帕雷托法則與其說是定律，不如說是一個提示。它邀請我們去問：力氣在哪裡產生最大的回報？我們的注意力是否據此分配？——同時記得，剩下的 80% 不一定就不重要。這樣使用時，它能讓判斷更敏銳，而不是取代判斷。

a.title: Why Work Takes All the Time You Have
text: Your teacher gives you two weeks to write a short report. What do you do? Many students wait until the last few days. Then they work very hard and finish just in time. Strangely, if the teacher had given them only one week, they might have finished just in time, too.
This idea is called Parkinson's law: "Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." In simple words, a job grows to fill all the time you give it.

The law comes from a British writer named C. Northcote Parkinson. In 1955, he wrote a funny article in a magazine called The Economist. He told the story of an old woman who spent a whole day sending one postcard. She looked for the card, then her glasses, then the address, and so on. A busy person could do it in three minutes.
Parkinson was joking about offices, where the number of workers often grows even when there is not more work to do. But his idea is also true for many of us.

How can we beat it? Give yourself shorter deadlines. Break a big job into small steps, and give each step its own deadline. But do not make deadlines too short, or you may feel stressed and make mistakes.
tz: 老師給你兩個星期寫一份短報告。你會怎麼做？很多學生會等到最後幾天，然後拚命趕工，剛好及時完成。奇怪的是，如果老師只給他們一個星期，他們可能也會剛好及時完成。
這個想法叫做帕金森定律：「工作會擴張，直到填滿完成它所能用的時間。」簡單來說，一件工作會膨脹到填滿你給它的所有時間。
這條定律來自一位名叫西里爾・諾斯古德・帕金森的英國作家。1955 年，他在一本叫《經濟學人》的雜誌上寫了一篇好笑的文章。他講了一個老太太花一整天寄一張明信片的故事。她先找明信片，再找眼鏡，再找地址，諸如此類。一個忙碌的人三分鐘就能做完。
帕金森是在拿辦公室開玩笑：在那裡，即使沒有更多工作要做，員工人數也常常越來越多。但他的想法對我們很多人來說也是真的。
我們要怎麼打敗它？給自己更短的截止期限。把一件大工作拆成小步驟，並給每個步驟訂自己的截止期限。不過不要把期限訂得太短，否則你可能會覺得壓力很大，還會犯錯。

b.title: Parkinson's Law: How Deadlines Shape Our Work
text: "Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." This line opened a humorous essay published in The Economist in 1955 by the British historian C. Northcote Parkinson. It has since become one of the most quoted rules about time and productivity, known simply as Parkinson's law.

Parkinson's original target was government. He pointed out that the number of officials in Britain's navy administration kept rising even as the number of ships fell. Officials, he joked, want to multiply subordinates, not rivals, and they create work for each other. The essay was satire, but readers recognised something true about how organisations grow.

Today, the law is usually applied to individuals. A task with a generous deadline tends to fill it, often because people delay starting, add unnecessary details or simply work more slowly. Project managers sometimes call the habit of starting only when a deadline is close "student syndrome". A meeting booked for two hours, likewise, rarely ends early.

Research on deadlines supports part of this picture. In a 2002 study, Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch asked people to complete three proofreading tasks over three weeks. Those given evenly spaced deadlines found the most errors and were late least often. Those who chose their own deadlines did better than those with a single final deadline, but not as well as the first group. People seem to know they procrastinate, yet they do not always choose the best deadlines for themselves.

Parkinson's law also has limits. Very tight deadlines can raise stress and lower quality, and people often underestimate how long tasks take — a tendency psychologists call the planning fallacy. The practical lesson is to set deadlines that are challenging but realistic, and to split large projects into smaller, scheduled steps. Used this way, a deadline becomes a tool rather than a source of panic.
tz: 「工作會擴張，直到填滿完成它所能用的時間。」這句話是英國歷史學家西里爾・諾斯古德・帕金森 1955 年刊登在《經濟學人》上一篇幽默文章的開頭。從那以後，它成了關於時間與生產力最常被引用的規則之一，簡稱帕金森定律。
帕金森最初的目標是政府。他指出，英國海軍行政部門的官員人數不斷增加，即使船艦的數量在減少。他開玩笑說，官員想增加的是下屬而不是對手，而且他們會替彼此製造工作。這篇文章是諷刺作品，但讀者們看出了組織成長方式中某些真實的東西。
如今，這條定律通常被用在個人身上。一件截止期限很寬鬆的任務往往會把時間填滿，常常是因為人們拖延開始、加上不必要的細節，或乾脆做得比較慢。專案經理有時把「期限快到了才開始」的習慣稱為「學生症候群」。同樣地，排了兩個小時的會議也很少提早結束。
關於截止期限的研究支持了這幅圖像的一部分。在 2002 年的一項研究中，丹・艾瑞利和克勞斯・韋坦布洛赫請人們在三週內完成三項校對工作。拿到平均分布期限的人找出最多錯誤，遲交的次數也最少。自己選擇期限的人，表現比只有一個最終期限的人好，但不如第一組。人們似乎知道自己會拖延，卻不一定會替自己選擇最好的期限。
帕金森定律也有它的限制。太緊的期限會增加壓力、降低品質，而且人們常常低估一件事要花多久——心理學家稱這種傾向為「規劃謬誤」。實際的教訓是：設定有挑戰性但實際可行的期限，並把大型計畫拆成較小、排好時程的步驟。這樣使用時，期限就成了工具，而不是恐慌的來源。

c.title: Parkinson's Law: Satire, Bureaucracy and the Elastic Hour
text: Few jokes have enjoyed as long a career as the one C. Northcote Parkinson published in The Economist in 1955. "Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion," it began, before describing an elderly lady who devotes an entire day to sending a single postcard — an hour to find the card, another to hunt for her spectacles — while a busy person would need three minutes. The essay became the basis of a bestselling book, and its opening sentence acquired the status of a law.

Parkinson, a naval historian, was chiefly mocking bureaucracy. He observed that between 1914 and 1928 the number of major warships in the Royal Navy fell sharply while the staff of the Admiralty grew substantially. He proposed two mechanisms: officials prefer to multiply subordinates rather than rivals, and officials make work for one another. In the same book he added a law of triviality, illustrated by a committee that approves a costly reactor in minutes but debates a bicycle shed at length, because everyone feels qualified to discuss the shed.

Detached from its satirical origins, the law is now applied mainly to individual behaviour, and there is psychological evidence consistent with it. Experiments in which participants were given excess time for a simple task have found that they tended to use more of it, and to work more slowly on later tasks as well. The planning fallacy, named by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979, compounds the problem: people routinely underestimate how long their own projects will take, even when similar projects have run late before.

Deadlines are the obvious countermeasure, and research by Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch in 2002 clarified how they work. People who knew they were prone to delay willingly imposed deadlines on themselves, which improved their performance relative to having one final deadline. Yet self-chosen deadlines were less effective than evenly spaced external ones, suggesting that people recognise their weakness but do not fully correct for it.

The law should not be read as a licence for ever-shorter time limits. Excessive time pressure is associated with stress, errors and shallow thinking, and some tasks — creative ones in particular — benefit from periods of apparent idleness. Moreover, Parkinson's law describes a tendency, not an inevitability; motivated people with clear goals often finish early.

The most useful reading of Parkinson's insight may be this: time is elastic in our hands, and without structure it stretches. The remedy is not panic but design — breaking work into concrete steps, attaching realistic checkpoints, and deciding in advance what "finished" means.
tz: 很少有哪個笑話能像西里爾・諾斯古德・帕金森 1955 年刊登在《經濟學人》上的那一個，流傳得這麼久。文章一開頭寫道：「工作會擴張，直到填滿完成它所能用的時間。」接著描述一位老太太花了一整天寄一張明信片——一個小時找明信片，另一個小時找眼鏡——而一個忙碌的人只需要三分鐘。這篇文章後來成了一本暢銷書的基礎，開頭那句話也取得了「定律」的地位。
帕金森是一位海軍歷史學家，他主要是在嘲諷官僚體系。他觀察到，在 1914 到 1928 年間，英國皇家海軍的主力戰艦數量大幅減少，海軍部的職員卻大量增加。他提出兩個機制：官員寧可增加下屬而不是對手，而且官員們會替彼此製造工作。在同一本書裡，他又加了一條「瑣事定律」，用一個委員會來說明：這個委員會幾分鐘就通過了昂貴的反應爐，卻花了很長時間爭論一座腳踏車棚，因為每個人都覺得自己有資格討論車棚。
脫離了諷刺的起源之後，這條定律如今主要被用在個人行為上，而且有和它一致的心理學證據。在一些實驗中，受試者做一件簡單任務時被給予多餘的時間，結果他們往往會用掉更多時間，而且在之後的任務中也做得比較慢。丹尼爾・康納曼和阿摩司・特沃斯基在 1979 年命名的「規劃謬誤」讓問題更嚴重：人們經常低估自己的計畫要花多久，即使類似的計畫以前就延誤過。
截止期限是顯而易見的對策，而丹・艾瑞利和克勞斯・韋坦布洛赫 2002 年的研究釐清了它的運作方式。知道自己容易拖延的人，會自願替自己訂期限，這讓他們的表現比只有一個最終期限時更好。然而，自己選的期限不如平均分布的外部期限有效，這顯示人們雖然認得自己的弱點，卻沒有完全修正它。
這條定律不該被解讀成可以無止盡縮短時限的許可。過度的時間壓力和壓力、錯誤以及淺薄的思考有關，而且有些任務——尤其是創意性的任務——會從看似無所事事的時段中受益。此外，帕金森定律描述的是一種傾向，而不是必然；有動機、目標明確的人常常會提早完成。
對帕金森洞見最有用的解讀也許是：時間在我們手中是有彈性的，沒有結構，它就會被拉長。解方不是恐慌，而是設計——把工作拆成具體的步驟、附上實際可行的檢查點，並事先決定「完成」是什麼意思。

topic: The Pygmalion Effect: Can Belief Help You Grow?

a.title: When Teachers Believe in You
text: Can a teacher's belief make a student smarter? Some scientists think it can. This idea is called the Pygmalion effect.
The name comes from an old Greek story. A man named Pygmalion made a statue of a beautiful woman. He loved it so much that, in the story, it came to life.

In the 1960s, an American psychologist named Robert Rosenthal and a school principal named Lenore Jacobson did an experiment at a primary school in California. First, all the students took a test. Then the researchers told the teachers that some students were "ready to bloom" — they would improve a lot that year.
But there was a secret. These students were chosen randomly! They were not really different from their classmates.

At the end of the year, the "bloomers" — especially the youngest ones — did better on the test than the other students. Maybe their teachers gave them more attention, more praise, and harder questions.

Later scientists found that the effect is real but often smaller than people first thought. Still, the lesson is important: what others expect from us — and what we expect from ourselves — can change how we grow.
tz: 老師的信念能讓學生變聰明嗎？有些科學家認為可以。這個想法叫做比馬龍效應。
這個名字來自一個古希臘故事。一個名叫比馬龍的男子雕了一座美麗女子的雕像。他愛它愛到——在故事裡——雕像活了過來。
1960 年代，一位名叫羅伯特・羅森塔爾的美國心理學家和一位名叫勒諾・雅各布森的校長，在加州一所小學做了一個實驗。首先，所有學生都做了一份測驗。接著研究者告訴老師，有些學生「即將開花」——他們那一年會進步很多。
但這裡面有個祕密：這些學生是隨機挑選的！他們其實和同學沒有什麼不同。
到了學年結束，這些「開花的學生」——尤其是年紀最小的——測驗成績比其他學生好。也許是他們的老師給了他們更多關注、更多稱讚，以及更有挑戰性的問題。
後來的科學家發現，這個效應是真的，但常常比大家一開始以為的還小。不過，這個教訓很重要：別人對我們的期待——以及我們對自己的期待——能改變我們成長的樣子。

b.title: The Pygmalion Effect: Can Expectations Shape Ability?
text: In Greek myth, the sculptor Pygmalion fell in love with a statue he had carved, and his devotion brought it to life. Psychologists borrowed his name for a modern question: can the expectations of teachers, parents or managers actually change how well people perform?

The best-known study was carried out in the 1960s by the psychologist Robert Rosenthal and the school principal Lenore Jacobson at an elementary school in California. All pupils took what teachers were told was a test that could identify "late bloomers" — children about to make unusual intellectual gains. In fact, it was an ordinary test, and about one in five pupils were labelled bloomers purely at random.

When the children were tested again months later, the so-called bloomers in the youngest classes showed noticeably larger gains in IQ scores than their classmates. Rosenthal and Jacobson published their results in 1968 in a book titled Pygmalion in the Classroom, arguing that teachers' raised expectations had become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

How could a belief turn into reality? Later research pointed to subtle changes in behaviour. Teachers tend to give students they expect more from warmer attention, more challenging material, more time to answer and more detailed feedback. Over time, those differences can add up.

The study also attracted strong criticism. Some researchers questioned its methods and found that the results were driven by a small number of children. Others were unable to repeat the original findings. Later reviews concluded that expectation effects are real but usually modest, and strongest when teachers know little about students at the start.

The lesson is therefore not that belief alone works miracles. It is that expectations quietly shape opportunities — and that treating every learner as capable of growth is one of the simplest things a teacher, or a classmate, can do.
tz: 在希臘神話中，雕刻家比馬龍愛上了自己雕刻的雕像，他的深情讓雕像活了過來。心理學家借用他的名字來探討一個現代的問題：老師、父母或主管的期望，真的能改變一個人的表現嗎？
最有名的研究是 1960 年代由心理學家羅伯特・羅森塔爾和校長勒諾・雅各布森在加州一所小學進行的。所有學生都做了一份測驗——老師被告知這份測驗能找出「大器晚成者」，也就是即將在智力上有不尋常進步的孩子。事實上，那只是一份普通的測驗，大約五分之一的學生是完全隨機被標記為「晚開花的人」。
幾個月後再次測驗時，最低年級中這些所謂的「晚開花者」，IQ 分數的進步明顯比同學大。羅森塔爾和雅各布森在 1968 年把結果寫成《教室裡的比馬龍》一書出版，主張老師提高的期望變成了自我實現的預言。
信念怎麼會變成現實？後來的研究指出了行為上的細微改變。老師往往會給自己期望較高的學生更溫暖的關注、更有挑戰性的教材、更多回答時間，以及更詳細的回饋。時間一久，這些差異就會累積起來。
這項研究也招來強烈的批評。有些研究者質疑它的方法，並發現結果是由少數幾個孩子造成的。也有人無法重現原本的發現。後來的回顧研究認為，期望效應是真的，但通常不大，而且在老師一開始對學生了解不多時最明顯。
因此，這個教訓並不是「光靠信念就能創造奇蹟」，而是：期望會悄悄影響每個人得到的機會——而把每位學習者都當成能夠成長的人，是老師或同學能做到的最簡單的事情之一。

c.title: Expectation, Self-Fulfilment and the Pygmalion Debate
text: The notion that people tend to rise — or sink — to the level expected of them is an old one, captured in myth and in George Bernard Shaw's play Pygmalion, in which a phonetics professor transforms a flower seller's speech. In psychology, the idea became an empirical claim in the 1960s, and it has remained both influential and contested ever since.

Robert Rosenthal had already shown that experimenters' expectations could subtly influence their results, even in studies of laboratory rats. Teaming up with Lenore Jacobson, principal of an elementary school in South San Francisco, he extended the idea to classrooms. Teachers were told that a test had identified certain children as poised for an academic "spurt"; the names had in fact been drawn at random. Eight months later, the designated children in the first and second grades showed markedly greater gains on an IQ measure than their peers.

Pygmalion in the Classroom (1968) became a sensation, cited in debates about educational inequality and in courtrooms. Critics, however, were quick to point out problems: the IQ test was poorly suited to the youngest pupils, some individual scores were implausible, and several attempts at replication failed. The psychologist Robert Thorndike's review was famously scathing.

Subsequent research produced a more nuanced picture. Meta-analyses suggest that teacher expectation effects are genuine but typically small, and that they are largest when expectations are formed early, before teachers have much real information about students. Importantly, most teacher expectations turn out to be fairly accurate predictions rather than powerful causes; the self-fulfilling portion is a modest addition. Effects may be larger, however, for students from stigmatised groups, for whom low expectations can accumulate over years.

The mechanisms, where they operate, are mundane rather than mysterious: differences in warmth, in the difficulty of questions posed, in waiting time and in the quality of feedback. The mirror image, sometimes called the Golem effect, describes how low expectations can depress performance through the same channels.

The practical lesson survives the scholarly debate. Even if expectations do not transform intelligence, they shape the everyday opportunities students receive — and those opportunities, distributed fairly, cost almost nothing. A teacher who asks every student challenging questions and waits patiently for answers is, in effect, refusing to let a label decide who gets the chance to grow.
tz: 「人往往會提升——或下沉——到別人期望的程度」這個觀念由來已久，神話中有，蕭伯納的劇作《賣花女》（原名 Pygmalion）中也有：一位語音學教授改造了賣花女的說話方式。在心理學中，這個想法在 1960 年代成為一個實證主張，此後一直既有影響力、又充滿爭議。
羅伯特・羅森塔爾先前就已證明，實驗者的期望會微妙地影響實驗結果，連實驗室老鼠的研究也不例外。他與南舊金山一所小學的校長勒諾・雅各布森合作，把這個想法延伸到教室。老師們被告知，一份測驗找出了某些即將在學業上「突飛猛進」的孩子；但這些名字其實是隨機抽出的。八個月後，一、二年級中被指定的孩子，在一項 IQ 測量上的進步明顯大於同儕。
《教室裡的比馬龍》（1968）轟動一時，在教育不平等的辯論中、甚至在法庭上都被引用。然而批評者很快就指出問題：這份 IQ 測驗不太適合最年幼的學生、有些個別分數令人難以置信，而且好幾次重複實驗都失敗了。心理學家羅伯特・桑代克的書評更是出了名的嚴厲。
後續研究描繪出更細膩的圖像。統合分析顯示，教師期望效應是真實的，但通常很小；而且在期望形成得早、老師對學生還沒有太多真實資訊時最大。重要的是，大多數教師期望其實是相當準確的「預測」，而不是強大的「原因」；自我實現的部分只是不大的附加效果。不過，對來自被污名化群體的學生來說，效應可能較大，因為低期望會年復一年地累積。

這個實用的教訓經得起學術辯論的考驗。即使期望不能改變智力，它們也會影響學生每天得到的機會——而這些機會只要公平分配，幾乎不需要任何成本。一位對每個學生都提出有挑戰性的問題、並耐心等待回答的老師，實際上就是拒絕讓一個標籤決定誰能得到成長的機會。

a.title: Everyone Is Looking at Me… Or Not?
text: Have you ever spilled juice on your shirt and felt like the whole school was staring at you? You may have wanted to hide all day. But here is some good news: most people probably did not even notice.
Psychologists call this the spotlight effect. We feel as if a bright spotlight is following us, like an actor on a stage. In fact, other people pay much less attention to us than we think.

In 2000, researchers at Cornell University in the United States tested this idea. They asked students to wear a T-shirt with a big picture of an old pop singer on it. Most students thought it was very embarrassing.
The students walked into a room full of other students. Later, they guessed that about half of the people had noticed the shirt. But really, only about a quarter of them had.
Why does this happen? We see the world from inside our own heads, so our own problems seem huge. But everyone else is busy thinking about themselves!
So the next time you make a small mistake, take a deep breath. The spotlight is much smaller than you think.

心理學家稱之為聚光燈效應。我們覺得好像有一盞亮亮的聚光燈跟著自己，就像舞台上的演員。事實上，別人對我們的注意力比我們以為的少得多。
2000 年，美國康乃爾大學的研究者測試了這個想法。他們請學生穿上一件印著一位老牌流行歌手大頭照的 T 恤。大多數學生都覺得很尷尬。
這些學生走進一間坐滿其他學生的房間。之後，他們猜大約一半的人注意到了那件衣服。但實際上，只有大約四分之一的人注意到。
為什麼會這樣？我們從自己的腦袋裡看世界，所以自己的問題顯得很巨大。但其他每個人都忙著想自己的事呢！
所以下次你犯了小錯時，深呼吸一下。那盞聚光燈比你想的小多了。

b.title: The Spotlight Effect: Why We Overestimate How Much Others Notice
text: You arrive at school with a terrible haircut, or you trip on the stairs, or you answer a question wrongly in class. In that moment it can feel as if every eye is on you. Psychologists have a name for this feeling: the spotlight effect, our tendency to overestimate how much other people notice our appearance and behaviour.

The effect was demonstrated in a well-known 2000 study by Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues at Cornell University. Students were asked to put on a T-shirt showing the singer Barry Manilow — a choice most of them found deeply embarrassing — and then briefly enter a room where other students were filling out questionnaires. Afterwards, the T-shirt wearers estimated that about half of the people in the room would be able to name the singer on their shirt. In reality, fewer than a quarter could.

Why do we make this error? One reason is that we are the centre of our own experience. We know exactly how we look and feel, and we find it hard to adjust for the fact that others are far less focused on us. Meanwhile, most people are busy worrying about their own appearance and performance.

The spotlight effect applies to positive moments too. A clever comment or a new pair of shoes is also noticed less than we expect. Students who hope a new hairstyle will impress the whole class may be disappointed when few people mention it.
Understanding the effect can be freeing. If others pay less attention to our small mistakes than we fear, we may feel braver about speaking up in class, trying a new sport or asking a question.
The spotlight, in other words, is mostly in our heads — and so is much of the embarrassment that comes with it. Once we see this, it becomes easier to take small risks.
tz: 你頂著一頭很糟的髮型到學校，或在樓梯上絆了一下，或在課堂上答錯了問題。那一刻，你可能覺得每雙眼睛都在看你。心理學家為這種感覺取了名字：聚光燈效應，也就是我們傾向高估別人注意自己外表和行為的程度。
湯瑪斯・季洛維奇和康乃爾大學的同事在 2000 年一項知名研究中證明了這個效應。研究者請學生穿上一件印著歌手巴瑞・曼尼洛的 T 恤——大多數學生覺得這非常丟臉——然後短暫走進一間其他學生正在填問卷的房間。之後，穿 T 恤的學生估計房間裡大約一半的人能說出衣服上的歌手是誰。實際上，能說出來的不到四分之一。

聚光燈效應也適用於正面的時刻。一句聰明的話或一雙新鞋，被注意到的程度也比我們預期的少。希望新髮型讓全班驚豔的學生，可能會失望地發現幾乎沒人提起。

c.title: Centre Stage in Our Own Minds
text: Social life involves constant, mostly unconscious, attempts to imagine how we appear to others. Because we cannot directly observe other minds, we estimate their attention using the most vivid information available — our own. The result is a systematic error that psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky termed the spotlight effect: the belief that our appearance and actions are noticed and remembered more than they actually are. It is an error almost everyone makes, often without realising it.

Their best-known study, published in 2000, used deliberately awkward clothing. Cornell undergraduates donned a T-shirt bearing the face of Barry Manilow, a singer few students considered fashionable, and entered a room of peers. Wearers predicted that roughly half of the observers would notice the shirt; only about a quarter did. In a follow-up, when participants wore shirts featuring figures they themselves admired, the overestimation persisted. Other people, it seems, were simply too occupied with their own concerns to pay much attention.

The researchers attributed the bias partly to anchoring and insufficient adjustment. People begin with their own intense awareness of a detail and adjust downward to estimate others' awareness, but they fail to adjust enough. Related research found that participants also overestimated how much their contribution to a group discussion — good or bad — stood out to other members.

The spotlight effect has a close cousin, the illusion of transparency: the belief that our internal states, such as nervousness during a speech, are more visible to others than they really are. Studies found that speakers who were told about this illusion felt more relaxed and were rated by observers as delivering better speeches.

These findings carry practical implications for adolescents, for whom concern about peer evaluation is especially intense. Psychologists have long described an "imaginary audience" in teenage thinking, a sense of being constantly watched and judged. Recognising that such scrutiny is largely imagined does not eliminate self-consciousness, but it can reduce the paralysing fear of small embarrassments that keeps people from participating, experimenting and learning.

The irony is that everyone is simultaneously the star of their own drama and a distracted member of everyone else's audience. Remembering both roles may be one of the simplest ways to loosen the grip of self-consciousness. It also frees attention for what actually matters: the task in front of us.
tz: 社交生活充滿了持續、而且大多是無意識的嘗試：想像自己在別人眼中的樣子。由於我們無法直接觀察別人的心思，只好用手邊最鮮明的資訊——我們自己的感受——來估計別人的注意力。結果就是一種系統性的錯誤，心理學家湯瑪斯・季洛維奇、維多利亞・梅德維克和肯尼斯・薩維茨基稱之為聚光燈效應：相信自己的外表和行為被注意、被記住的程度，比實際上更高。這是幾乎每個人都會犯的錯誤，而且常常沒有察覺。
他們最有名的研究在 2000 年發表，刻意使用令人尷尬的衣服。康乃爾大學的大學生穿上印著巴瑞・曼尼洛臉孔的 T 恤——很少學生覺得這位歌手時髦——走進一間坐滿同儕的房間。穿著者預測大約一半的觀察者會注意到這件衣服；實際上只有約四分之一。在後續研究中，當受試者穿上印有他們自己欣賞的人物的衣服時，高估的情況依然存在。看來，其他人只是太忙於自己的事，沒有餘力多加注意。
研究者把這種偏誤部分歸因於錨定和調整不足。人們從自己對某個細節的強烈意識出發，再往下調整來估計別人的注意程度，卻調整得不夠。相關研究也發現，受試者會高估自己在小組討論中的發言——不論好壞——在其他成員眼中有多突出。
聚光燈效應有一個近親：透明度錯覺，也就是相信自己的內在狀態（例如演講時的緊張）比實際上更容易被別人看出來。研究發現，被告知這種錯覺的演講者感覺比較放鬆，觀察者也評價他們的演講表現比較好。
這些發現對青少年特別有實際意義，因為他們對同儕評價的在意格外強烈。心理學家很早就描述過青少年思考中的「想像觀眾」——一種一直被觀看、被評判的感覺。認清這種注視大多是想像出來的，並不會消除自我意識，但能減少對小小尷尬的那種讓人動彈不得的恐懼——正是這種恐懼讓人不敢參與、嘗試和學習。
諷刺的是，每個人同時都是自己戲裡的主角，也是別人戲裡心不在焉的觀眾。記住這兩種角色，可能是放鬆自我意識束縛最簡單的方法之一。它也能把注意力釋放出來，留給真正重要的事：眼前的任務。

topic: The Streisand Effect: When Hiding Something Makes It Famous
zh: 史翠珊效應：越想藏，越多人看到？
src: Masnick (2005) · Brehm (1966) · California Coastal Records Project
discuss: Can you think of something that became more popular after someone tried to hide it?
Why do you think people want what they are told they cannot have?
If you saw false information about yourself online, how would you respond?

a.title: When Hiding Something Makes It Famous
text: Imagine you post a silly photo, and then you ask everyone to stop sharing it. What happens? Often, more people want to see it! Trying to hide something can make it more popular. This is called the Streisand effect.

The name comes from Barbra Streisand, a famous American singer. In 2003, a photographer took thousands of photos of the California coast from the air to show how the land was changing. One photo showed Streisand's large house by the sea.

Streisand did not want people to see the photo, so she took the photographer to court. Before that, the photo had been downloaded only six times, and two of those were by her own lawyers. But after news about the case spread, more than 400,000 people visited the website in just one month.
She lost the case, and the photo became famous around the world. In 2005, a writer named Mike Masnick gave the effect its name.
Why does this happen? When something is hidden, people become curious. They also do not like being told what they cannot see. And news about the fight makes even more people hear about it.
So before you try to hide something online, think twice. Sometimes the best thing to do is to let it go.
tz: 想像你貼了一張好笑的照片，然後拜託大家不要再分享。結果會怎樣？常常是更多人想看！想把某樣東西藏起來，反而可能讓它更受矚目。這就叫做史翠珊效應。
這個名稱來自美國知名歌手芭芭拉・史翠珊。2003 年，一位攝影師從空中拍了好幾千張加州海岸的照片，用來記錄土地的變化。其中一張照片拍到了史翠珊在海邊的大房子。
史翠珊不想讓人看到這張照片，於是把攝影師告上法院。在那之前，這張照片只被下載過六次，其中兩次還是她自己的律師。但在這起官司的新聞傳開之後，光是一個月就有超過四十萬人造訪了那個網站。
她輸了官司，這張照片也紅遍全世界。2005 年，一位名叫麥克・馬斯尼克的作家替這個效應取了名字。
為什麼會這樣？當某樣東西被藏起來時，人們就會好奇。人們也不喜歡被告知什麼東西不能看。而且關於這場紛爭的新聞，會讓更多人聽說這件事。
所以在你試著把網路上的東西藏起來之前，要三思。有時候最好的做法就是放手。

b.title: The Streisand Effect: How Censorship Can Backfire
text: In 2003, the photographer Kenneth Adelman was documenting coastal erosion in California. As part of a public project, he photographed about 12,000 sections of the coastline from a helicopter and posted the images online. One of them happened to include the clifftop home of the singer and actress Barbra Streisand.

Streisand sued Adelman and the website, asking for the photo to be removed and for millions of dollars in damages. Before the lawsuit, the image had been downloaded just six times — twice by her own lawyers. Once the media reported on the case, however, more than 420,000 people visited the site within a month. A court later dismissed the lawsuit, and the photo soon became famous worldwide.

Two years later, the technology writer Mike Masnick coined the term "Streisand effect" to describe what happens when an attempt to hide, remove or censor information draws far more attention to it. Since then, the pattern has been seen many times, from companies trying to delete critical reviews to governments banning books that then become bestsellers.

Psychologists offer several explanations. One is curiosity: forbidden information seems valuable precisely because someone wants it hidden. Another is reactance, a concept developed by Jack Brehm in 1966. When people feel their freedom is threatened, they are motivated to restore it, for example by seeking out the very thing they were told to avoid. Finally, the conflict itself becomes news, spreading the story to audiences who would never have noticed it.

The effect is not guaranteed. Many attempts at removing information succeed quietly, and we never hear about them precisely because they worked. But the risk is real, especially online, where copies spread quickly and are hard to delete. Before trying to make something disappear, it is worth asking whether the attempt might make it famous instead.
tz: 2003 年，攝影師肯尼斯・阿德爾曼正在記錄加州的海岸侵蝕。作為一項公共計畫的一部分，他從直升機上拍攝了大約一萬兩千段海岸線，並把照片放上網路。其中一張碰巧拍到了歌手兼演員芭芭拉・史翠珊位於懸崖頂上的住宅。
史翠珊控告阿德爾曼和那個網站，要求移除照片，並求償數百萬美元。在提告之前，這張照片只被下載過六次——其中兩次是她自己的律師。然而，一旦媒體報導了這起官司，一個月內就有超過四十二萬人造訪那個網站。法院後來駁回了這起訴訟，這張照片也很快紅遍全世界。
兩年後，科技作家麥克・馬斯尼克創造了「史翠珊效應」這個詞，用來描述當有人試圖隱藏、移除或審查資訊時，反而讓它引來更多關注的現象。從那以後，這種模式出現過很多次，從公司試圖刪除負評，到政府禁書，結果那些書反而成了暢銷書。
心理學家提出了幾種解釋。一是好奇心：被禁止的資訊之所以顯得有價值，正是因為有人想把它藏起來。二是「心理抗拒」，這是傑克・布雷姆在 1966 年提出的概念。當人們覺得自己的自由受到威脅時，就會有動機去恢復它，例如偏偏去找自己被告知要避開的東西。最後，衝突本身就成了新聞，把這件事傳播給原本根本不會注意到的人。
這個效應並不是必然的。許多移除資訊的嘗試都悄悄成功了，而我們從來沒聽說過它們，正是因為它們成功了。但風險是真實的，在網路上尤其如此，因為複本傳得很快，又很難刪除。在試圖讓某樣東西消失之前，值得先問問自己：這樣做會不會反而讓它出名？

c.title: The Streisand Effect: When Suppression Amplifies
text: In 2003, Barbra Streisand filed a lawsuit seeking 50 million dollars from the photographer Kenneth Adelman, whose California Coastal Records Project had published an aerial image of her Malibu estate among roughly 12,000 photographs documenting erosion. Before the suit, the image had been downloaded six times, two of them by her attorneys. In the month after the case became news, the site received more than 420,000 visits. The suit was dismissed, and Streisand was ordered to pay Adelman's legal fees.

In 2005, the blogger Mike Masnick gave the phenomenon its name: the Streisand effect, in which an attempt to suppress information has the unintended consequence of publicising it more widely. The label caught on because the pattern recurs with striking regularity, from corporations issuing legal threats against critics to governments blocking websites, only to see the targeted content copied, mirrored and discussed across the internet.

Several mechanisms appear to be at work. The first is informational: an act of suppression signals that the material is important, sensitive or embarrassing, inviting the inference that it must be worth seeing. The second is psychological reactance, described by Jack Brehm in 1966. When people perceive a threat to their freedom, including their freedom to access information, they tend to value the restricted option more and act to reclaim it. The third is social: conflicts make compelling stories, and media coverage of the attempted suppression reaches audiences who would never have encountered the original material.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that censorship generally backfires. The Streisand effect is subject to an obvious selection bias: failed suppressions become famous by definition, whereas successful ones remain invisible. Research on state censorship suggests that even modest barriers, such as slowing access to a website rather than blocking it outright, can sharply reduce how many people seek out information, because most users are unwilling to make extra effort. Backfire seems most likely when an attempt is clumsy and highly visible, and when an engaged audience has both the motive and the means to spread copies.

For organisations and individuals alike, the lesson is less "never act" than "anticipate the reaction". A quiet request, a correction or simply a reply may achieve more than a lawsuit. Once information is public online, the costs of trying to erase it have to be weighed against the attention the effort itself may generate.
tz: 2003 年，芭芭拉・史翠珊提起訴訟，向攝影師肯尼斯・阿德爾曼求償五千萬美元。阿德爾曼的「加州海岸紀錄計畫」為了記錄侵蝕，公開了大約一萬兩千張照片，其中一張是她在馬里布豪宅的空拍照。在提告之前，這張照片只被下載過六次，其中兩次是她的律師。官司成為新聞後的那個月，網站的造訪次數超過四十二萬次。這起訴訟被駁回，史翠珊還被判須支付阿德爾曼的律師費。
2005 年，部落客麥克・馬斯尼克替這個現象取了名字：史翠珊效應，指試圖壓下資訊，卻意外讓它更廣為人知的結果。這個名稱之所以流行起來，是因為這種模式以驚人的規律反覆出現：從企業對批評者發出法律威脅，到政府封鎖網站，最後卻眼睜睜看著目標內容在網路上被複製、建立鏡像並廣泛討論。
有幾種機制似乎在發揮作用。第一種和資訊有關：壓制的舉動本身就透露出這份資料很重要、敏感或令人難堪，讓人推論它一定值得一看。第二種是傑克・布雷姆在 1966 年描述的「心理抗拒」。當人們察覺自己的自由——包括取得資訊的自由——受到威脅時，往往會更重視被限制的選項，並採取行動把它拿回來。第三種是社會性的：衝突是引人入勝的故事，而媒體對這場壓制行動的報導，會觸及原本根本不會接觸到原始資料的閱聽人。
然而，如果因此斷定審查通常都會適得其反，那就錯了。史翠珊效應明顯受到選擇偏誤的影響：失敗的壓制行動照定義就會出名，成功的則始終看不見。關於國家審查的研究顯示，即使是不大的障礙，例如讓網站連線變慢而不是直接封鎖，也能大幅減少去找資訊的人數，因為大多數使用者不願意多花力氣。當壓制的手法笨拙又高調，而且有一群投入的閱聽人既有動機又有辦法散布複本時，最可能出現反效果。
對組織和個人來說，教訓與其說是「永遠不要行動」，不如說是「預料對方的反應」。一個低調的請求、一則更正，或只是一則回應，可能比一場訴訟更有效。一旦資訊在網路上公開了，試圖抹去它的代價，就必須和這個舉動本身可能引來的關注一起權衡。

a.title: The Planes That Came Back
text: During World War II, many planes flew over enemy land. Some came back with lots of bullet holes in their wings and bodies. Others never came back at all.
The army wanted to make the planes safer. One idea was to add strong metal to the places with the most holes. That sounds smart, right?

But a mathematician named Abraham Wald saw a problem. The army was only looking at the planes that came back. The planes hit in other places — like the engines — were missing because they had crashed. So Wald said: protect the places with no holes!
This mistake is called survivorship bias. It happens when we only look at the "survivors" — the people or things that made it — and forget about the ones we cannot see.
For example, you may hear about a famous person who left school and became rich. But you don't hear about the many people who did the same thing and did not succeed.
So, when you hear a success story, ask: "Who is missing from this story?" The answer may change what you learn from it.

軍方想讓飛機更安全。有一個想法是在彈孔最多的地方加上堅固的金屬。聽起來很聰明，對吧？
但一位名叫亞伯拉罕・沃德的數學家看出了問題。軍方只看了「有回來」的飛機。被打中其他地方——例如引擎——的飛機根本不在那裡，因為它們已經墜毀了。所以沃德說：要保護的是「沒有彈孔」的地方！
這種錯誤叫做倖存者偏差。當我們只看「倖存者」——成功撐過來的人或東西——卻忘了那些我們看不見的，就會發生這種錯誤。
例如，你可能聽過某個名人輟學後變得很有錢。但你不會聽到許多做了同樣的事、卻沒有成功的人。
所以，當你聽到一個成功故事時，問問自己：「這個故事少了誰？」這個答案可能會改變你從中學到的東西。

b.title: Survivorship Bias: Learning From What Is Missing
text: We learn a great deal from success stories — the entrepreneur who dropped out of university and built a global company, the band that was rejected forty times before becoming famous. Yet these stories can mislead us, because they show only the winners. The people who followed the same path and failed are rarely interviewed. This blind spot is known as survivorship bias.

Its most famous illustration comes from the Second World War. The American military studied bombers returning from missions and mapped where they had been hit. Holes clustered on the wings and the body, while the engines were relatively untouched. The obvious conclusion was to add armour where the damage was greatest.

The statistician Abraham Wald, working with a research group at Columbia University, pointed out the flaw. The sample included only aircraft that had survived. Planes hit in the engines were missing precisely because those hits had brought them down. The armour, he argued, belonged where the returning planes showed the fewest holes.

The same error appears in many places. Investors may look at the average performance of existing funds without noticing that the worst-performing ones have already closed. People say "they don't build them like they used to" about old buildings, forgetting that the poorly built ones collapsed or were torn down long ago.

Survivorship bias is especially dangerous because the missing evidence is, by definition, invisible. Correcting for it requires actively asking what data might have been filtered out — who dropped out, what failed, which cases never reached us. Good researchers deliberately seek out the failures as well as the successes.

This does not mean success stories are worthless or that we should ignore them. It means we should read them alongside the failures, and remember that the most important evidence is sometimes the evidence we never see.
tz: 我們從成功故事中學到很多——大學輟學後建立全球企業的創業家、被拒絕四十次才成名的樂團。然而，這些故事可能誤導我們，因為它們只呈現贏家。走同一條路卻失敗的人，很少有人去採訪。這個盲點被稱為倖存者偏差。
它最有名的例子來自第二次世界大戰。美國軍方研究執行任務後返航的轟炸機，標出它們被擊中的位置。彈孔集中在機翼和機身，引擎則相對完好。顯而易見的結論是：在損傷最嚴重的地方加裝裝甲。
在哥倫比亞大學一個研究小組工作的統計學家亞伯拉罕・沃德指出了其中的瑕疵：樣本只包含存活下來的飛機。引擎被擊中的飛機之所以不見，正是因為那些攻擊把它們打下來了。他主張，裝甲應該加在返航飛機彈孔「最少」的地方。

倖存者偏差之所以特別危險，是因為缺少的證據本來就看不見。要修正它，就必須主動去問：哪些資料可能被過濾掉了——誰退出了、什麼失敗了、哪些案例從來沒有傳到我們這裡。好的研究者會刻意去找失敗的案例，而不只是成功的。

c.title: The Silent Evidence of Survivorship Bias
text: Every dataset is shaped by the process that produced it. When that process quietly removes certain cases — the failures, the dropouts, the dead — the remaining evidence can tell a confident story that is systematically wrong. This distortion, known as survivorship bias, is less a single mistake than a family of errors that share one feature: the decisive information has been filtered out before anyone looks.

The canonical example concerns Allied aircraft in the Second World War. Analysts examining bombers that returned from missions over Europe noted heavy damage to the fuselage and wings and comparatively little to the engines, and proposed reinforcing the most damaged areas. Abraham Wald, a mathematician with the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, recognised that the sample was conditioned on survival. Engine hits were underrepresented not because they were rare but because they were fatal. The popular retelling simplifies Wald's work, which consisted of technical memoranda on estimating vulnerability, but its central insight is accurate.

Finance offers a quieter version. Studies of mutual fund performance that consider only funds still in existence overstate average returns, because poorly performing funds are frequently closed or merged and disappear from the record. Researchers who correct for this effect find that the industry's typical performance is noticeably weaker than the surviving sample suggests.

The bias also distorts our sense of history and success. The ancient buildings that remain standing are, by selection, the sturdiest ones, which can create the impression that earlier builders were universally superior. Business books that extract lessons from thriving companies seldom examine firms that adopted identical strategies and collapsed. Without the failures, it is impossible to know whether the celebrated practices caused success or merely coincided with it.

Guarding against survivorship bias requires a habit of counterfactual thinking: asking what the complete population looked like before the filter operated. In scientific practice this means tracking every participant who enters a study, including those who drop out, and publishing negative results as well as positive ones.

A story told by the Roman writer Cicero captures the principle neatly. Shown painted tablets left by sailors who had prayed during a storm and survived, a sceptic asked where the tablets were from those who had prayed and drowned. Evidence is persuasive only when we know what was excluded from it. Asking that question is often the first step toward a truer picture.
tz: 每一組資料都被產生它的過程所塑造。當這個過程悄悄移除了某些案例——失敗的、退出的、死去的——剩下的證據就可能講出一個充滿自信、卻系統性錯誤的故事。這種扭曲被稱為倖存者偏差，它與其說是單一錯誤，不如說是一整個錯誤家族，它們有一個共同特徵：關鍵資訊在任何人去看之前就已經被過濾掉了。
最經典的例子和二戰盟軍的飛機有關。分析人員檢查從歐洲上空任務返航的轟炸機，注意到機身和機翼損傷嚴重，引擎相對較少，於是提議強化損傷最多的部位。哥倫比亞大學統計研究小組的數學家亞伯拉罕・沃德意識到，這個樣本是以「存活」為前提的。引擎中彈的比例偏低，不是因為很少發生，而是因為一旦發生就是致命的。流行的說法簡化了沃德的研究——他的工作其實是一系列估算飛機脆弱度的技術備忘錄——但核心洞見是正確的。
金融領域有一個比較不起眼的版本。只考慮現存基金的共同基金績效研究，會高估平均報酬，因為表現差的基金經常被關閉或合併，從紀錄中消失。修正這個效應的研究者發現，整個產業的典型表現明顯比存活樣本所顯示的還弱。
這種偏差也扭曲了我們對歷史和成功的認知。仍然屹立的古建築，因為經過篩選，正是最堅固的那些，這可能讓人以為古代建築師全都比較優秀。從興盛企業中萃取教訓的商業書籍，很少檢視採取相同策略卻倒閉的公司。沒有失敗案例，就不可能知道那些受讚揚的做法是造成了成功，還是只是剛好同時出現。
要防範倖存者偏差，需要養成反事實思考的習慣：去問在過濾發生之前，完整的群體是什麼樣子。在科學實務上，這代表要追蹤每一位進入研究的受試者，包括中途退出的人，並且負面結果和正面結果都要發表。
羅馬作家西塞羅講過的一個故事，把這個原則說得很清楚。有人給一位懷疑論者看水手們留下的彩繪石板——那些水手在暴風雨中祈禱後倖存了下來——他反問：那些祈禱了卻淹死的人，他們的石板在哪裡？只有當我們知道哪些東西被排除在外時，證據才有說服力。問出這個問題，往往是看見更真實全貌的第一步。

topic: The 10,000-Hour Rule: Is Practice Everything?
zh: 一萬小時法則：練習一萬小時就能成為專家嗎？

a.title: Is 10,000 Hours the Secret to Success?
text: Maybe you have heard this rule: if you practise something for 10,000 hours, you will become an expert. That is about three hours a day for ten years! But is it true?

The rule became famous in 2008, when the writer Malcolm Gladwell wrote about it in his book Outliers. He used the example of the Beatles, who played music for many hours in Germany before they became famous.

Gladwell's idea came from a study by a psychologist named Anders Ericsson. In 1993, Ericsson studied young violin players at a music school in Berlin. The best players had practised about 10,000 hours by the age of twenty, more than the other players.

But Ericsson later said the rule was too simple. First, 10,000 was only an average. Some top players practised much less. Second, the kind of practice matters a lot. Just playing the same easy songs again and again does not help much. Good practice is hard. You work on your weak points, you get feedback from a teacher, and you try things that are a little too difficult.
Other studies show that practice is important, but it is not the only thing. Age, the way we learn and even luck can matter, too.
So forget the magic number. Practise smart, not just long.
tz: 也許你聽過這個規則：如果你練習某件事一萬個小時，你就會成為專家。那大約是每天三小時、持續十年！但這是真的嗎？
這個規則在 2008 年變得很有名，當時作家麥爾坎・葛拉威爾在他的書《異數》中寫到它。他舉了披頭四的例子：他們在成名之前，曾在德國演奏了好多好多個小時。
葛拉威爾的想法來自心理學家安德斯・艾瑞克森的一項研究。1993 年，艾瑞克森研究了柏林一所音樂學校裡的年輕小提琴手。最優秀的演奏者到了二十歲時大約已經練習了一萬小時，比其他演奏者多。
但艾瑞克森後來說這個規則太簡化了。第一，一萬只是個平均數，有些頂尖的演奏者練得少很多。第二，練習的種類非常重要。只是一再演奏同樣簡單的曲子，幫助並不大。好的練習是辛苦的：你要加強自己的弱點、從老師那裡得到回饋，並嘗試稍微有點太難的東西。
其他研究顯示，練習很重要，但它不是唯一的因素。年齡、我們學習的方式，甚至運氣，也都可能有影響。
所以忘掉那個神奇的數字吧。要聰明地練習，而不只是練得久。

b.title: The 10,000-Hour Rule: Practice, Talent and Myth
text: Few ideas about success are as popular as the "10,000-hour rule": practise anything for 10,000 hours and you will reach world-class level. The rule spread widely after Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 bestseller Outliers, which used examples such as the Beatles' long nights performing in Hamburg and Bill Gates's early access to a computer.

The number came from a 1993 study led by the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson. His team asked violin students at a top music academy in Berlin to estimate how much they had practised over their lives. By age twenty, the best students had averaged around 10,000 hours of practice alone, clearly more than students judged to be less accomplished.

Ericsson, however, was unhappy with how his work was summarised. He stressed that 10,000 was an average, not a magic threshold; many of the best violinists had practised far less. More importantly, he argued that what matters is not simply time but deliberate practice: focused effort on specific weaknesses, guided by a teacher, with immediate feedback and tasks just beyond one's current ability. Hours of comfortable repetition, by contrast, produce little improvement.

Later research questioned how much practice can explain. A 2014 review of many studies by Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald found that deliberate practice accounted for about a quarter of the differences in performance in games such as chess and around a fifth in music. In sports the figure was lower, and in education and professions it was very small. Other factors, such as the age people start, working memory and personality, also seem to play a role.

None of this means that practice is unimportant or a waste of time. Nobody becomes an expert without it. But the useful lesson is about quality rather than quantity: practising the right way may matter more than reaching any particular number.
tz: 很少有關於成功的想法像「一萬小時法則」這麼受歡迎：任何事練習一萬小時，你就能達到世界級的水準。這個規則在麥爾坎・葛拉威爾 2008 年的暢銷書《異數》出版後廣為流傳，書中舉了披頭四在漢堡長夜演出、比爾・蓋茲很早就能使用電腦等例子。
這個數字來自心理學家 K・安德斯・艾瑞克森在 1993 年主持的一項研究。他的團隊請柏林一所頂尖音樂學院的小提琴學生，估計自己這輩子練習了多少時間。到二十歲時，最優秀的學生平均獨自練習了大約一萬小時，明顯比被評為較不出色的學生多。
然而，艾瑞克森對別人總結他研究的方式並不滿意。他強調一萬是平均數，不是神奇的門檻；許多最優秀的小提琴手練得少很多。更重要的是，他主張重要的不只是時間，而是「刻意練習」：在老師的指導下，專注地針對特定弱點下功夫，得到即時回饋，並挑戰剛好超出自己目前能力的任務。相反地，好幾個小時舒舒服服的重複，幾乎不會帶來進步。
後來的研究質疑練習到底能解釋多少。布魯克・麥克納馬拉、大衛・漢布里克和弗雷德里克・奧斯瓦爾德在 2014 年綜合許多研究後發現，在西洋棋之類的遊戲中，刻意練習大約能解釋四分之一的表現差異，在音樂中約五分之一。在運動方面這個數字更低，而在教育和職業上則非常小。其他因素，例如開始的年齡、工作記憶和個性，似乎也有影響。
這些都不代表練習不重要，或是在浪費時間。沒有人能不練習就成為專家。但有用的教訓在於質而不是量：用對的方式練習，可能比達到任何特定的數字更重要。

c.title: Beyond 10,000 Hours: What Expertise Really Requires
text: In popular culture, expertise has acquired a price: 10,000 hours. The figure entered public conversation through Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers (2008), which presented it as a near-universal requirement for mastery, illustrated by the Beatles' marathon performances in Hamburg. The rule's appeal is obvious. It is democratic, implying that greatness is available to anyone willing to put in the time, and it is precise enough to sound scientific.

Its scientific source was a 1993 paper by K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer. Studying violinists at a Berlin music academy, they found that the students rated most accomplished had accumulated an average of roughly 10,000 hours of solitary practice by age twenty, substantially more than less accomplished peers. From such findings, Ericsson developed a broader theory in which deliberate practice, rather than innate talent, was the principal driver of expert performance.

Ericsson himself later objected that the popular rule distorted his work. Ten thousand was an average, not a threshold, and it varied widely across individuals and domains. More fundamentally, he insisted on the distinction between deliberate practice — effortful, goal-directed activity designed by a teacher to target specific weaknesses, with rapid feedback — and mere experience. Years of routine performance can leave skills stagnant; drivers with decades behind the wheel are rarely better than they were in their first few years.

The stronger claim, that practice alone explains expertise, has fared less well. A 2014 meta-analysis by Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald estimated that deliberate practice accounted for about 26 percent of the variance in performance in games, 21 percent in music and 18 percent in sports, but only around 4 percent in education and less than 1 percent in professions. Critics of the meta-analysis argued that it used too broad a definition of deliberate practice, and the debate over methodology continues.

Researchers increasingly favour a multifactorial view, in which practice interacts with factors such as starting age, working memory capacity, personality, the quality of coaching and access to opportunities. Such a view need not be fatalistic: environments and teaching can be improved, and practice remains necessary even where it is not sufficient.

Perhaps the most valuable legacy of the 10,000-hour debate is a shift in emphasis from the clock to the method. The question worth asking is not "How many hours have I done?" but "Is this practice pushing me beyond what I can already do?"
tz: 在流行文化中，專業能力有了一個價碼：一萬小時。這個數字透過麥爾坎・葛拉威爾的《異數》（2008）進入大眾的討論，書中把它描述成精通一門技藝近乎普遍的條件，並以披頭四在漢堡馬拉松式的演出為例。這個規則的吸引力顯而易見。它很「平等」，暗示只要願意投入時間，任何人都能變得偉大；而且它精確到聽起來很科學。
它的科學來源是 K・安德斯・艾瑞克森、拉爾夫・克蘭普和克萊門斯・特希-羅默在 1993 年發表的論文。他們研究柏林一所音樂學院的小提琴手，發現被評為最出色的學生，到二十歲時平均累積了大約一萬小時的獨自練習，遠多於較不出色的同儕。艾瑞克森根據這類發現發展出更廣的理論：刻意練習，而不是天生的才能，才是專家表現的主要動力。
後來，艾瑞克森本人抗議這個流行的規則扭曲了他的研究。一萬是平均數，不是門檻，而且在不同個人和領域之間差異很大。更根本的是，他堅持要區分刻意練習——由老師設計、費力且有目標、針對特定弱點並有快速回饋的活動——和單純的經驗。多年例行公事般的表現可能讓技能停滯不前；開了幾十年車的駕駛，很少比他們剛開始那幾年開得更好。
更強的主張——光靠練習就能解釋專業能力——就沒那麼站得住腳了。布魯克・麥克納馬拉、大衛・漢布里克和弗雷德里克・奧斯瓦爾德在 2014 年的統合分析估計，刻意練習大約能解釋遊戲中 26%、音樂中 21%、運動中 18% 的表現變異，但在教育上只有約 4%，在職業上不到 1%。對這項統合分析的批評者則主張，它對刻意練習的定義太寬鬆，而關於研究方法的爭論仍在持續。
研究者越來越傾向「多因素」的觀點：練習會和開始的年齡、工作記憶容量、個性、指導的品質以及取得機會的管道等因素交互作用。這種觀點不必是宿命論的：環境和教學可以改善，而且即使練習不是充分條件，它仍然是必要的。

a.title: The Unfinished Task
text: Have you ever stopped watching a TV show in the middle of an exciting part and then kept thinking about it all night? Unfinished things can stay in our minds.

About 100 years ago, in a café in Berlin, Germany, people noticed something interesting. According to a famous story, a waiter could remember long orders that had not been paid for yet. But once customers paid, he quickly forgot what they had ordered.

A young psychologist named Bluma Zeigarnik tested this idea in 1927. She gave people simple tasks, like puzzles and counting. She let them finish some tasks but stopped them in the middle of others. Later, many people remembered the unfinished tasks better. This became known as the Zeigarnik effect.

Later scientists tried the test again. Their results were mixed — the memory effect did not always appear. But one thing seems clear: people often feel a strong wish to go back and finish what they started.
You can use this! If you don't want to start your homework, just begin with five minutes. Once you start, your mind may want to finish.
And if unfinished tasks keep you awake at night, write them down in a to-do list. It can help your mind relax.
tz: 你有沒有在電視節目最精彩的地方停下來，結果一整晚都在想它？沒做完的事會一直留在我們心裡。
大約 100 年前，在德國柏林的一家咖啡館，有人注意到一件有趣的事。根據一個有名的故事，一位服務生能記住還沒付錢的長長點單。但只要客人一付錢，他很快就忘了他們點了什麼。
一位名叫布盧瑪・蔡格尼克的年輕心理學家在 1927 年測試了這個想法。她給受試者一些簡單的任務，像是謎題和數數。她讓他們完成其中一些任務，但在其他任務做到一半時讓他們停下來。之後，很多人比較記得那些沒做完的任務。這後來被稱為蔡格尼克效應。
後來的科學家重做了這個實驗，結果好壞參半——記憶效應不一定會出現。但有一件事似乎很清楚：人們常常很想回去把開始做的事做完。
你可以利用這一點！如果你不想開始寫功課，就先從五分鐘開始。一旦開始了，你的大腦可能就會想把它做完。
如果沒做完的事讓你晚上睡不著，就把它們寫在待辦清單上。這能幫助你的大腦放鬆。

b.title: The Zeigarnik Effect: Why Unfinished Tasks Stay With Us
text: Many people have had the experience of lying awake thinking about an unfinished essay, an unanswered message or a half-solved puzzle. Completed tasks, by contrast, seem to slip easily out of mind. This contrast has a name: the Zeigarnik effect.

According to a popular story, the psychologist Kurt Lewin noticed that a waiter in a Berlin café could remember complicated orders until the bill was paid, after which the details seemed to vanish. His student, Bluma Zeigarnik, investigated the idea in a series of experiments published in 1927. Participants were given around twenty small tasks, such as puzzles and simple arithmetic, and were interrupted before finishing about half of them. When later asked to recall the tasks, they tended to remember the interrupted ones better.
Zeigarnik explained this with Lewin's idea of "tension": starting a task creates a kind of mental pressure that remains until the task is completed, keeping it active in memory.

Later attempts to repeat her findings have produced mixed results. Some studies found the memory advantage; others did not, and it appears to depend on factors such as how motivated people are and whether they expect to return to the task. A related observation has proved more reliable: people who are interrupted often feel a strong urge to go back and finish. This is sometimes called the Ovsiankina effect, after Maria Ovsiankina, another of Lewin's students.

These ideas have practical uses. Writers sometimes stop in the middle of a sentence so it is easier to start again the next day, and television series end episodes on cliffhangers. Research also suggests that making a specific plan for an unfinished goal can quiet distracting thoughts about it.
Unfinished business, in other words, can either nag at us or pull us forward — depending on how we manage it.
tz: 很多人都有過躺著睡不著、一直想著沒寫完的作文、沒回的訊息或解到一半的謎題的經驗。相較之下，已經完成的事似乎很容易就從腦海中溜走。這種對比有一個名字：蔡格尼克效應。
根據一個流行的故事，心理學家庫爾特・勒溫注意到，柏林一家咖啡館的服務生在帳單付清之前，能記住很複雜的點單，付完錢之後，細節就好像消失了。他的學生布盧瑪・蔡格尼克在 1927 年發表的一系列實驗中研究了這個想法。受試者拿到大約二十個小任務，例如謎題和簡單的算術，其中大約一半在完成前被打斷。之後請他們回想這些任務時，他們往往比較記得被打斷的那些。
蔡格尼克用勒溫的「張力」概念來解釋：開始一項任務會產生一種心理壓力，這種壓力會一直持續到任務完成為止，讓它在記憶中保持活躍。
後來重複她的發現的嘗試，結果好壞參半。有些研究發現了記憶上的優勢，有些則沒有；這似乎取決於人們的動機有多強，以及他們是否預期會回到這個任務等因素。一個相關的觀察則被證明比較可靠：被打斷的人常常有一股想回去完成的強烈衝動。這有時被稱為奧夫相基娜效應，以勒溫的另一位學生瑪麗亞・奧夫相基娜命名。

換句話說，沒做完的事，可能一直糾纏著我們，也可能推著我們前進——取決於我們怎麼處理它。

c.title: Open Loops: The Zeigarnik Effect Revisited
text: Some psychological ideas endure less because of their evidence than because they capture something people recognise. The Zeigarnik effect — the claim that interrupted or unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones — is a case in point. Nearly a century after it was first described, it is cited in productivity guides, marketing manuals and screenwriting advice, even as researchers continue to debate whether the memory effect itself is reliable.

The idea emerged from Kurt Lewin's circle in 1920s Berlin. Lewin's field theory proposed that intentions create "tension systems" that persist until the goal is reached. His student Bluma Zeigarnik tested a direct implication: if tension keeps incomplete goals active, interrupted tasks should be more accessible to memory. In her 1927 study, participants who had been stopped partway through a series of brief tasks recalled the interrupted tasks considerably more often than the completed ones.

The finding proved difficult to pin down. Replications over the following decades varied widely, with some showing the effect, some showing none and some showing its reverse. Moderating factors appeared to include participants' motivation, their sense of whether the interruption reflected failure, and whether they expected to resume. A recent meta-analysis concluded that there is no general memory advantage for unfinished tasks, while finding support for a related tendency: the urge to resume interrupted activities, first documented by Maria Ovsiankina in 1928.

That distinction matters. The Ovsiankina effect concerns motivation rather than memory, and it is the motivational component that most practical applications actually rely on. Novelists who stop writing mid-sentence, teachers who end a lesson with an open question and streaming platforms that automatically queue the next episode all exploit the pull of the incomplete.

Later work has added a further nuance. Studies by E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister suggested that unfulfilled goals can generate intrusive thoughts that interfere with other tasks, but that forming a concrete plan for completing them reduces this interference — as though the mind accepts a plan as a temporary substitute for completion.

The history of the Zeigarnik effect thus offers two lessons. The first concerns the mind: unfinished intentions exert real psychological pull, even if not always on memory. The second concerns science: a memorable story and a frequently repeated claim are no substitute for consistent evidence.
tz: 有些心理學概念之所以流傳下來，與其說是因為證據，不如說是因為它們說中了人們熟悉的感受。蔡格尼克效應——主張被打斷或未完成的任務比已完成的任務更容易被記住——就是一個例子。在它首次被描述將近一個世紀後，它仍被生產力指南、行銷手冊和劇本寫作建議所引用，儘管研究者仍在爭論這個記憶效應本身是否可靠。
這個概念誕生於 1920 年代柏林庫爾特・勒溫的學術圈。勒溫的場論主張，意圖會產生「張力系統」，一直持續到目標達成為止。他的學生布盧瑪・蔡格尼克檢驗了一個直接的推論：如果張力讓未完成的目標保持活躍，那麼被打斷的任務應該更容易被記憶提取。在她 1927 年的研究中，在一連串短任務中途被叫停的受試者，回想起被打斷任務的次數，明顯多於已完成的任務。
這個發現後來證明很難確定。之後數十年的重複研究結果差異很大：有些顯示出效應，有些完全沒有，有些甚至顯示相反的結果。調節因素似乎包括受試者的動機、他們是否覺得被打斷代表失敗，以及他們是否預期會繼續。近期一項統合分析的結論是：未完成的任務並沒有普遍的記憶優勢；但它也發現一個相關傾向得到支持——想繼續完成被打斷活動的衝動，這是瑪麗亞・奧夫相基娜在 1928 年首次記錄的。
這個區別很重要。奧夫相基娜效應關乎的是動機，而不是記憶；而大多數實際應用真正依賴的，正是動機的部分。在句子寫到一半就停筆的小說家、用一個開放式問題結束一堂課的老師，以及自動排好下一集的串流平台，都在利用「未完成」的拉力。
後來的研究又加入了一個細微的差異。E. J. 馬西坎波和羅伊・鮑梅斯特的研究指出，未達成的目標可能產生侵擾性的念頭，干擾其他任務；但為完成它們訂出具體計畫，能減少這種干擾——彷彿大腦願意把一個計畫當成完成的暫時替代品。
因此，蔡格尼克效應的歷史提供了兩個教訓。第一個關於心智：未完成的意圖確實有真實的心理拉力，即使不一定作用在記憶上。第二個關於科學：一個令人難忘的故事和一個常被重複的說法，都無法取代一致的證據。

text: November 23 is Fibonacci Day. The date 11/23 looks like the start of a famous number pattern: 1, 1, 2, 3.
In this pattern, you add the two numbers before to get the next one. So 1 + 1 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, and 2 + 3 = 5.
The pattern is named after Fibonacci, an Italian man who wrote about it more than 800 years ago.
These numbers often appear in nature. Count the spirals on a sunflower or a pinecone, and you may find 8, 13, 21 or 34.
Fibonacci also helped people in Europe use the numbers we use today: 0 to 9.
Next time you see a flower, try counting. Maths might be hiding there!

b.title: Rabbits, Sunflowers and a Famous Sequence
text: Every November 23, maths fans celebrate Fibonacci Day, because the date written as 11/23 matches the first four numbers of the Fibonacci sequence.

The sequence starts 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and each number is the sum of the two before it. It takes its name from Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who described it in his book Liber Abaci in 1202 through a puzzle about breeding rabbits.

Fibonacci did not invent the sequence: Indian mathematicians had studied the same pattern centuries earlier. His bigger contribution was introducing the Hindu–Arabic numerals 0 to 9 to Europe, which made calculation far easier than Roman numerals.

The numbers appear surprisingly often in plants. Sunflower heads and pinecones usually have spirals that come in neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55, an arrangement that packs seeds efficiently.

However, popular claims that the sequence is hidden in every famous building or 'perfect' face are usually exaggerated. Scientists warn that if you look hard enough, you can find patterns almost anywhere.

c.title: Patterns, Real and Imagined
text: Fibonacci Day, celebrated on November 23 because 11/23 echoes the opening of the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, honours one of mathematics' most beloved patterns, and offers a useful lesson in scepticism.

The rule is simple: each term is the sum of the two preceding ones. Leonardo of Pisa popularised it in Liber Abaci in 1202 through a whimsical problem about multiplying rabbits, though Indian scholars had described the same sequence far earlier. Ironically, his more consequential achievement was persuading European merchants to abandon cumbersome Roman numerals for the Hindu–Arabic system.

In botany the sequence earns its reputation. The spirals of sunflower heads and pinecones typically occur in adjacent Fibonacci numbers, because placing each new seed at a constant angle produces efficient packing; the mathematics emerges from growth rather than design.

Elsewhere, enthusiasm outruns evidence. Claims that the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa or ideal human faces encode the related golden ratio rarely survive careful measurement, and often depend on choosing convenient starting points.
The sequence therefore teaches two lessons at once: nature genuinely contains elegant regularities, and human minds are so eager for pattern that we readily invent ones that are not there.

tz: 費波那契日在 11 月 23 日慶祝，因為 11/23 呼應了數列 1、1、2、3 的開頭；它紀念的是數學中最受喜愛的規律之一，也提供了一堂關於懷疑精神的實用課。
規則很簡單：每一項都是前兩項的和。比薩的李奧納多在 1202 年的《計算之書》中，透過一道關於兔子繁殖的奇想問題讓它廣為人知，不過印度學者更早就描述過同樣的數列。諷刺的是，他影響更深遠的成就，是說服歐洲商人放棄笨重的羅馬數字，改用印度－阿拉伯數字系統。
在植物學裡，這個數列的名聲是名副其實的。向日葵花盤和松果的螺旋，通常以相鄰的費波那契數出現，因為以固定角度擺放每一顆新種子，就能排列得最有效率；這種數學是從生長過程中產生的，而不是被設計出來的。
在其他地方，熱情就跑到證據前面去了。那些宣稱帕德嫩神殿、蒙娜麗莎或理想人臉裡藏著相關「黃金比例」的說法，很少經得起仔細測量，而且往往取決於挑選方便的起點。
因此，這個數列同時教了我們兩件事：大自然確實含有優雅的規律，而人類的大腦太渴望找到規律，以至於很容易就編造出根本不存在的規律。

topic: Darwin's Big Book: On the Origin of Species

a.title: How Living Things Change
text: On November 24, 1859, a book called On the Origin of Species came out in England. It was written by Charles Darwin.
When he was young, Darwin sailed around the world on a ship called the Beagle. The trip took five years.
On the Galápagos Islands, he saw birds that looked a little different on each island. Their beaks were different shapes.
Darwin thought about this for many years. He believed living things change slowly over a very long time.
Animals and plants that fit their home better live longer and have more babies. He called this natural selection.
Many people were angry about his ideas at first. Today, his book is one of the most important science books ever.

b.title: The Book That Changed Biology
text: On November 24, 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species. The first printing sold out almost immediately, and the book went on to transform how people understand life on Earth.

Darwin's ideas had been forming for more than twenty years. As a young naturalist on the survey ship HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, he collected fossils and observed animals in South America and on the Galápagos Islands, where species differed slightly from island to island.

His central idea was natural selection. Individuals vary, and those with traits that suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so over many generations species gradually change.

Darwin delayed publishing, partly because he knew his ideas would be controversial. He finally acted in 1858 when another naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, sent him a paper describing almost the same theory. Their work was presented together in London that year.
Today evolution is the foundation of modern biology, supported by evidence from fossils and DNA.

tz: 1859 年 11 月 24 日，查爾斯・達爾文出版了《物種起源》。第一刷幾乎立刻就賣光了，這本書後來徹底改變了人們對地球生命的理解。
達爾文的想法已經醞釀了二十多年。1831 到 1836 年間，年輕的博物學家達爾文搭乘測量船小獵犬號，在南美洲和加拉巴哥群島收集化石、觀察動物；在那些島上，物種在不同的島之間略有差異。
他的核心想法是「天擇」。個體之間有差異，而擁有適合環境特徵的個體，比較可能存活並繁殖，所以經過許多世代，物種就會逐漸改變。
達爾文延後了出版，一部分原因是他知道自己的想法會引起爭議。1858 年，另一位博物學家阿爾弗雷德・羅素・華萊士寄給他一篇論文，描述幾乎相同的理論，他才終於採取行動。那一年，兩人的研究在倫敦一起發表。
今天，演化是現代生物學的基礎，並得到化石和 DNA 證據的支持。

c.title: The Long Patience of a Revolutionary
text: On November 24, 1859, a cautious naturalist published one of the most consequential books ever written. On the Origin of Species argued that the diversity of life arose not through separate acts of creation but through descent with modification, driven by natural selection.

The argument had been decades in the making. Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle in the 1830s furnished him with puzzles, notably the subtly different finches and tortoises of the Galápagos Islands, but he spent the next twenty years accumulating evidence, breeding pigeons and corresponding with experts before daring to publish.

That reluctance was strategic as well as temperamental. He anticipated fierce religious and scientific opposition, and he wanted his case to be overwhelming. Only a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace in 1858, outlining the same mechanism, forced his hand.

The book's power lay in its accumulation of ordinary observations into an extraordinary conclusion. Variation exists; more offspring are born than can survive; those best suited to their surroundings leave more descendants. Given immense time, small differences add up to new species.
Later discoveries in genetics, unknown to Darwin, supplied the mechanism of inheritance he lacked and confirmed the theory's core with striking precision.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?

q.why: 主旨：謹慎延後出版、由平凡觀察推出革命性結論，後被遺傳學證實。

q.why: 最後一段：遺傳學補上機制並證實理論核心。

tz: 1859 年 11 月 24 日，一位行事謹慎的博物學家出版了一本史上影響最深遠的書之一。《物種起源》主張，生命的多樣性並不是來自一次次各別的創造，而是透過「伴隨修改的傳承」，由天擇所推動。
這個論證醞釀了好幾十年。1830 年代搭乘小獵犬號的航行，給了達爾文許多謎題，特別是加拉巴哥群島上那些有細微差異的雀鳥和陸龜；但他接下來花了二十年累積證據、養鴿子、和專家通信，才敢出版。
這份遲疑既出於個性，也是一種策略。他預料到會有來自宗教和科學界的激烈反對，所以希望自己的論證壓倒性地充分。直到 1858 年阿爾弗雷德・羅素・華萊士寄來一封信，概述了同樣的機制，才逼得他不得不出手。
這本書的力量，在於把許多平凡的觀察累積成一個非凡的結論：個體之間存在差異；出生的後代比能活下來的多；最適應環境的個體會留下更多後代。只要有極長的時間，小小的差異就會累積成新的物種。
後來達爾文所不知道的遺傳學發現，補上了他所欠缺的遺傳機制，也以驚人的精確度證實了這個理論的核心。

a.title: The Rich Man Who Gave Libraries

b.title: Making a Fortune, Giving It Away
text: Andrew Carnegie, born on November 25, 1835, in Dunfermline, Scotland, is one of history's most famous examples of rags to riches.

His family emigrated to Pittsburgh in 1848, where twelve-year-old Andrew worked in a cotton mill for little more than a dollar a week. He moved on to a job as a telegraph messenger, impressed his bosses, and invested his savings wisely.
By the 1870s he had built a steel empire. In 1901 he sold Carnegie Steel for about 480 million dollars, making him one of the richest men alive.

Carnegie then devoted himself to giving his fortune away. In his essay The Gospel of Wealth, he argued that the rich have a duty to use their money for the public good during their lifetimes. He funded more than 2,500 public libraries around the world, as well as universities and concert halls.
His record is mixed, however. In 1892 a bitter strike at his Homestead steelworks ended in deadly violence, and critics argue that his generosity was paid for by workers' low wages and long hours.

tz: 安德魯・卡內基 1835 年 11 月 25 日生於蘇格蘭的丹弗姆林，是歷史上最有名的「白手起家」例子之一。
他的家人在 1848 年移民到匹茲堡，十二歲的安德魯在一家棉紡廠工作，一週只賺一美元多一點。後來他換到電報送信員的工作，讓上司印象深刻，並把積蓄做了聰明的投資。
到了 1870 年代，他已經建立起一個鋼鐵帝國。1901 年，他以大約 4.8 億美元賣掉卡內基鋼鐵公司，成為當時世上最富有的人之一。
之後卡內基致力於把財富捐出去。他在文章《財富的福音》中主張，富人有責任在有生之年把錢用在公共利益上。他資助了全世界超過 2,500 座公共圖書館，還有大學和音樂廳。
不過，他的紀錄有好有壞。1892 年，他旗下霍姆斯特德鋼鐵廠的一場激烈罷工以致命的暴力收場；批評者認為，他的慷慨是用工人的低薪和長工時換來的。

ph.ex: After the test, we moved on to the next chapter.
ph.exzh: 考完試後，我們接著上下一章。

st.m: Andrew Carnegie, born on November 25, 1835, in Dunfermline, Scotland, is one of history's most famous examples of rags to riches.
st.mz: 卡內基白手起家成為首富，又把財富捐出來，但他的作為也有爭議。
t: His family emigrated to Pittsburgh in 1848, where twelve-year-old Andrew worked in a cotton mill for little more than a dollar a week.
By the 1870s he had built a steel empire.
Carnegie then devoted himself to giving his fortune away.
st.c: His record is mixed, however.

c.title: The Contradictions of a Philanthropist
text: Andrew Carnegie, born in Scotland on November 25, 1835, embodied the American myth of the self-made man with almost theatrical neatness: a penniless immigrant boy who became the richest industrialist of his age.

His ascent combined diligence, shrewd investment and fortunate timing. From a cotton mill and a telegraph office he rose into railways and then steel, ruthlessly cutting costs until Carnegie Steel dominated the industry. Its sale in 1901 for roughly 480 million dollars made him almost unimaginably wealthy.

What followed was equally remarkable. In The Gospel of Wealth he contended that dying rich was a disgrace and that fortunes should be distributed for the public good. He funded more than 2,500 libraries, believing that access to knowledge, not charity handouts, allowed people to improve themselves.

Yet the same cost-cutting that built the fortune also produced the Homestead strike of 1892, in which a clash between strikers and armed guards left several people dead. Critics then and since have asked whether generosity can redeem wealth extracted from exhausted workers.
Carnegie's legacy thus resists a simple verdict, and it raises a question that remains urgent: should society rely on the goodwill of the very rich, or on fairer wages in the first place?

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Carnegie's life combined remarkable philanthropy with harsh labour practices, raising the question of whether charity can replace fair wages.
Carnegie was simply a generous hero.
Carnegie's libraries caused the Homestead strike.
Carnegie's libraries made up for the Homestead strike, proving that generous gifts can fully replace fair wages for workers in his company.
q.why: 主旨：慈善與嚴苛勞動並存，引出「靠富人善意還是公平薪資」的問題。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “shrewd” means ___.
opts: lazy
clever in practical matters
generous
dishonest and cruel to others
q.why: shrewd = 精明的。

q.q: Why did Carnegie prefer funding libraries to giving charity handouts?
opts: Libraries were cheaper to build than paying higher wages for his companies
Handouts were illegal
Workers asked for libraries
He believed access to knowledge helped people improve themselves
q.why: 第三段：access to knowledge, not charity handouts, allowed people to improve themselves。

q.q: How does the writer judge Carnegie's legacy?
opts: As purely good, because he gave money away
As purely bad
As complex, resisting a simple verdict
As unimportant
q.why: 最後一段：resists a simple verdict。

q.q: What is the function of “Yet” at the start of paragraph 4?
opts: To add more praise for the libraries he built around the world in Pittsburgh
To turn from his generosity to the darker side of how the fortune was made
To introduce a new person
To summarise his libraries
q.why: Yet 轉向財富來源的陰暗面。

q.q: A billionaire today pays workers very little but donates millions to schools. Which question does the essay suggest we should ask?
opts: Would it be fairer to pay workers better in the first place, instead of relying on donations?
Which schools got the most money?
Is the billionaire Scottish?
How many libraries could the billionaire build with the same money as Carnegie? in each city
q.why: 最後一段：should society rely on the goodwill of the very rich, or on fairer wages？

tz: 1835 年 11 月 25 日生於蘇格蘭的安德魯・卡內基，幾乎像演戲一樣完美地體現了美國「白手起家」的神話：一個身無分文的移民男孩，成為他那個時代最富有的實業家。
他的崛起結合了勤奮、精明的投資和好時機。他從棉紡廠和電報局起步，進入鐵路業，再進入鋼鐵業，毫不留情地壓低成本，直到卡內基鋼鐵公司稱霸整個產業。1901 年以約 4.8 億美元出售公司，讓他富有到幾乎難以想像。
接下來發生的事同樣驚人。他在《財富的福音》中主張，富有地死去是一種恥辱，財富應該為了公共利益而分配出去。他資助了超過 2,500 座圖書館，相信讓人們取得知識，而不是發放救濟，才能讓人改善自己的生活。
然而，打造這筆財富的同一套成本壓縮手段，也造成了 1892 年的霍姆斯特德罷工：罷工工人和武裝警衛之間的衝突造成數人死亡。當時和後來的批評者都在問：慷慨捐贈，能否彌補從精疲力竭的工人身上榨取來的財富？
因此，卡內基的歷史定位無法簡單下結論，而它也提出一個至今仍然迫切的問題：社會應該依靠超級富豪的善意，還是從一開始就給予更公平的工資？

ph.exzh: 這場暴風雨造成三人死亡。

topic: Charles Schulz and the World of Peanuts

src: Charles M. Schulz Museum · The New York Times · NBC

a.title: The Man Who Drew Snoopy
text: Charles Schulz was born on November 26, 1922, in the United States. He loved drawing from a young age.
In 1950, he started a comic strip called Peanuts. It showed a shy boy named Charlie Brown and his dog, Snoopy.
Charlie Brown often failed. He could never kick the football, and his kite always got stuck in a tree. But he never gave up.
Snoopy was very different. He had a big imagination and pretended to be a pilot, a writer and much more.
Schulz drew Peanuts by himself for almost 50 years, nearly 18,000 comic strips!
Today, people all over the world still love Snoopy and his friends.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How to fly a kite
A dog named Snoopy who was a real pilot in the sky
Charles Schulz and his famous comic, Peanuts
Why Charlie Brown is shy

Schulz drew Peanuts by himself for almost 50 years.

q.why: imagination = 想像力。

Keep trying even when you fail
q.why: 第三段：he often failed … But he never gave up。

Tell him to get a dog instead
Tell him Charlie Brown failed many times but never gave up

tz: 查爾斯・舒茲在 1922 年 11 月 26 日出生於美國。他從小就很喜歡畫畫。
1950 年，他開始畫一部叫做《花生》的漫畫。漫畫裡有一個害羞的男孩叫查理・布朗，還有他的狗史努比。

b.title: Good Grief: The Genius of Peanuts
text: Charles M. Schulz, born in Minneapolis on November 26, 1922, created one of the most popular comic strips in history. Peanuts first appeared in newspapers on October 2, 1950, and ran for almost fifty years.
Unusually, Schulz wrote, drew and lettered every one of the nearly 18,000 strips himself, without assistants.

His characters were children, but their worries were very adult. Charlie Brown is lonely and unlucky; Lucy is bossy; Linus carries a security blanket while thinking deep thoughts. Readers recognised their own fears and disappointments in these small figures.
Snoopy, Charlie Brown's beagle, provided the fantasy. Lying on top of his doghouse, he imagines himself as a fighter pilot or a famous novelist.
The strip grew into books, toys and television specials such as A Charlie Brown Christmas in 1965.
Schulz died in February 2000, just hours before his final Sunday strip was published. Today, his gentle mix of sadness and humour continues to influence cartoonists around the world.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Schulz's Peanuts became hugely popular by showing children with very human worries, mixed with gentle humour and fantasy.
Peanuts first appeared on October 2, 1950.
Peanuts was popular because Snoopy was a real fighter pilot and famous novelist who always won in every single strip he appeared in.
Schulz used many assistants.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：兒童角色、成人般的煩惱、幽默與幻想。

q.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
opts: Peanuts ran in newspapers for almost a hundred years.
Schulz made every strip himself, without any assistants.
Snoopy is lonely and unlucky, while Lucy provides fantasy.
Schulz died a few hours after his last strip was published.
q.why: 第 2 段：Schulz wrote, drew and lettered every one … himself, without assistants。連載將近五十年；孤單倒楣的是查理・布朗、提供幻想的是史努比；他在最後一則刊出「前」幾小時過世。

To list the TV specials based on the comic
To show that the characters behave like real children
To explain why readers connected with the child characters
q.why: 第 3 段：角色是孩子，煩惱卻很像大人——Readers recognised their own fears … in these small figures。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “bossy” describes someone who ___.

is always lucky
likes telling others what to do
always loses at baseball in every game
q.why: bossy = 愛指揮人的。

q.q: Why did readers connect with the children in Peanuts?
opts: Because the children were famous
Because the strips were very long
Because the children always won their baseball games every week
Because they saw their own fears and disappointments in them
q.why: 第三段：Readers recognised their own fears and disappointments。

q.q: A headline says: “Schulz Retired Years Before His Death.” Based on the text, is this accurate?

Yes, assistants drew the last strips
No, his final strip was published just hours after he died in 2000
No, he never stopped drawing until 2010

tz: 查爾斯・M・舒茲 1922 年 11 月 26 日生於明尼亞波利斯，創作了史上最受歡迎的連環漫畫之一。《花生》在 1950 年 10 月 2 日首次刊登在報紙上，連載了將近五十年。
很不尋常的是，將近 18,000 則漫畫，每一則都是舒茲自己編寫、繪圖和寫字，沒有任何助手。
他的角色是小孩，但他們的煩惱卻非常像大人。查理・布朗孤單又倒楣；露西很愛管人；奈勒斯一邊抱著他的安全毯，一邊思考深奧的問題。讀者在這些小小的角色身上，看到了自己的恐懼和失望。
查理・布朗的米格魯獵犬史努比則負責提供幻想。牠躺在狗屋屋頂上，想像自己是戰鬥機飛行員，或是一位知名小說家。
這部漫畫後來發展成書籍、玩具和電視特別節目，例如 1965 年的《查理布朗的聖誕節》。
舒茲在 2000 年 2 月過世，就在他最後一則週日漫畫刊出的前幾個小時。今天，他那種揉合了淡淡哀傷與幽默的風格，仍然影響著世界各地的漫畫家。

ph.exzh: 他喜歡躺在草地上思考深奧的問題。

ph.exzh: 這個小社團發展成了學校的大型校隊。

ph.ex: The rain stopped just hours before the parade.

st.mz: 舒茲創作的《花生》是史上最受歡迎的漫畫之一，溫柔又帶點哀傷的幽默影響了全世界。
